commission. – madam president, before i turn to the specific question of depleted uranium, let me first put the issue in context by saying a word about the environmental situation in the balkans and what the european commission has been doing to tackle it. nearly a decade of regional conflicts, combined with weak institutions, old-fashioned polluting industry and a legacy of years of unchecked pollution, have left the environment of the balkan region in a state of serious neglect. in june 1999, a report conducted for the commission by the regional environment centre in budapest gave a preliminary assessment of the environmental effects of the conflict in the balkan region. in october 1999, the united nations balkans task force then provided its assessment of the environmental damage arising as a result of the kosovo conflict. in our efforts to tackle the health and environmental situation in the balkans, the commission has established a twin-track approach. this combines action on the one hand to address immediate problems with longer term assistance. our longer-term assistance is designed to embed a process of sustainable environmental protection in the countries in the region, all of which are potential candidate members of the union. let me set out briefly what we have been doing. in the framework of the stability pact, the commission has been the driving force in the development of the regional environmental reconstruction programme. this provides a framework in which environmental actions can be pursued at regional level in the balkans. by bringing together the various bilateral donors and the countries in the region, we are providing a focus for the coordination of otherwise disparate and overlapping bilateral actions. to help launch the regional environmental reconstruction programme the commission is currently funding actions to the value of eur 5m. other donors have committed a further eur 2.5m, and others still have expressed their intention to commit around another eur 5.8m, bringing a total of around eur 13.3m. through these actions we have targeted institution building, participation in the activities of the european environment agency in the region and two environmental hotspots in albania and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. our contribution reflects the balance between setting the basis for long-term environmental protection and urgent remedial action. let me now come to the specific issue of depleted uranium and the public concern about the possible health risks associated with the use of depleted uranium weapons in kosovo and bosnia for the local populations, as well as the international personnel serving, or who have served, in the region. the commission is naturally also concerned to ensure that the interests of its own staff and contractors placed in the region are properly assessed. let me stress again that this is an issue which has aroused considerable public anxiety and that anxiety must be addressed. but it can only be addressed on the basis of facts and the provision of all the information on this issue. our watchword must be "openness". that is why it is essential to proceed rationally and on the basis of scientific evidence. what then are the facts? uranium itself, as you know, is a radioactive and toxic element that occurs in several minerals. depleted uranium is less radioactive than natural uranium. it is readily available as a by-product of the nuclear fuel cycle and it is very hard and self-sharpening. as such, it is used to make tips to shells to increase their penetrating capacity. however, there is currently no unanimously held scientific opinion on the health and environmental effects of depleted uranium. at the time that the un balkans task force provided its original assessment of the environmental damage arising as a result of the kosovo conflict, it had not received any official document confirming whether or not depleted uranium had been used during the conflict. when that confirmation was given, unep carried out a mission to collect, for example, soil, water and vegetation samples in autumn last year. we expect that the results of their examinations will be known in march this year. for our part, the commission has acted swiftly in the face of recent concerns to ensure that any commission action on depleted uranium is based on sound scientific knowledge. we have used existing structures to convene a meeting of an independent group of experts under the euratom treaty to give an opinion on the possible health consequences in general of exposure to depleted uranium. in their opinion the experts will be expected to draw upon all available scientific evidence. we expect to have the scientific opinion of the independent experts within a month from now. in the light of the opinion the commission will review whether or not follow-up actions are indicated, for our own staff for example. we will also decide whether it is appropriate to adapt existing assistance programmes within the longer term with the aim of ensuring the sustainable development of the region. the commission will, of course, invite member states and international authorities to share information on their findings and approaches and to discuss any proposed follow-up actions resulting from the opinion provided by the independent scientific experts. the twin-track approach i have set out underlines the value added of the community contribution to addressing the health and environmental situation in the balkan region. the commission confirms its commitment to strengthening our medium and long-term support to improve the environmental and human health situation in the balkan region. (applause)
i have to say, madam president, the public is concerned because there is evidence of a link between this depleted uranium in the munitions and the effects on health and the environment. but at the same time, we also know that it hasn't been proven that this relationship actually exists. this has not been proved in any scientific study or in any of the studies carried out in spain, italy or other countries. for this reason, following what the eu envoy, mr solana, has said here, i would like to say that this debate is not an after-the-fact endorsement of milosevic. the operation carried out by the soldiers of nato and the member states of the european union in bosnia and kosovo was an operation against a war criminal. we should continue to thank these people for their commitment to human rights in this way. those who have political and military responsibility deserve our respect as well. i would like to make that clear on behalf of my group. (applause from the centre) but we hear that when the weapons used hit, chemical processes occur that produce, for example, uranium oxide, which can be problematic. we have heard in the last few days of investigations by the pentagon in january 2000 which have shown that these munitions sometimes contain small amounts of plutonium. there are risks involved and soldiers must be reminded of the need to exercise extreme caution in areas where these munitions have been used. in view of these considerations, it is indeed necessary to carry out studies in order to provide certainty. these investigations are not a sign of weakness but a sign of the credibility of democracies which look into such issues and do not sweep anything under the carpet. we owe this to the soldiers who have been affected, to the staff of non-governmental organisations who have been affected and also to the civilians of this region. we must determine whether there are any health and environmental effects, and then either give warning or permanently withdraw such weapons from circulation. it is also necessary to use, during the period of study of these weapons and their effects, alternative munitions of equal potency which cannot produce any of the effects feared. i would like to thank mr solana and the commission for agreeing to inform the european parliament so that we can make our final decision on this basis at the appropriate time, in order to ensure the safety of our citizens and our soldiers and to ensure the credibility of our military operations in the future, which are essential for the realisation of human rights.

proposed by the commission. we support this community mechanism, which is intended to provide funds for operations in the context of crisis management and conflict prevention, without combat operations. it can only be right if the european union helps to maintain or restore public order, to promote dialogue, reconciliation, mediation and the prevention of human rights violations. but all this can only be effective if the special facility is able to react really quickly. we therefore expressly support the commission's proposal for implementation, namely the comitology, including an advisory committee. the emphasis is on 'advisory'. the commission has, over the years, with the backing of parliament, pursued the concept of communification. in other words, activities have been going to go. but the necessary resources must be allocated to heading iv of the financial perspective. but the fact that our finances are so tightly packed under the heading 'foreign policy' has been known to all members for at least two budgetary procedures. the council has always had the most serious conflicts with the council on the budget. it doesn't take a fortune teller to predict something above all how they intend to divide responsibilities between themselves and how they intend to finance the measures, and secondly, to include a recital in the text which clearly states that the appropriations for the special facility must be financed under heading iv. if this is not possible, a revision shall be provided for. we also want parliament to be consulted on every measure. the commission. – mr president, i am delighted to be able to respond to the excellent report by mr newton dunn, on the rapid reaction facility. he is a friend and colleague. we used to be, indeed, fellow tribesmen before he wandered, i hope temporarily, off the reservation, but i am not at all surprised, knowing the author, that this is such an excellent report. the rapid reaction facility, as it is called in the report, is of course now called the rapid reaction mechanism to avoid any possible confusion with the rapid reaction force over which, let me repeat for the benefit of readers of parts of the press from the country i know best, i have no responsibility whatsoever. that is a negative "no" rather than an affirmative "no", just for the benefit of the correspondence columns of the daily telegraph. i have to say i did listen to the speech by my friend, mr van orden. i thought that it was a good example of dancing on pinheads. i must say that his principal objection concerned what i think is amendment no 9 and, as i shall say shortly we are opposed to amendment no 9. but, if there is some confusion about the nature of what we are attempting to do, i have to say that it is partly because of what some of those who agree with the honourable gentleman have been saying about these proposals. if conservatives like my honourable friend do not approve of this, i have to ask the question, not entirely rhetorically, what the hell will they ever approve of? in the days when i was chairman of the party of which the honourable gentlemen is a member, we actually believed in trying to speed up the delivery of financial assistance. we actually believed in trying to cut through red tape. so, i wonder what the hell my honourable friend and his colleagues actually believe in these days. i think it would be desirable to look beyond those correspondence columns of the daily telegraph for one's information on an important subject like this. now, i am responsible for ensuring that the commission is able to respond swiftly and effectively in a crisis both on its own and, as is perhaps more likely to be the case, as part of an overall european union response to crises including those in which the european union rapid reaction force might find itself deployed. the lesson of recent years has been very clear. responding to crises very often involves the deployment of a wide array of tools, sometimes encompassing the military, frequently including policies and programmes for which the commission has a responsibility or involvement from trade policy to humanitarian aid, from the provision of election monitors to assistance on the ground with customs missions, border management, assistance to the independent media and so on. too often in the past, take the balkans for example, we have just not been able to respond with the efficiency or timeliness that developments in the real world demand. or, we have had to wade through procedural treacle in brussels which has bogged down officials who should have been devoting every effort to getting the job done in the field. that, i fear, was my impression when i came into this job. we are trying to rectify these deficiencies. weakness is exposed by real events, not theoretical models. i have devoted a great deal of my attention since i became a commissioner to trying to improve that delivery on the ground. i think we have started to make progress, as i believe our response to recent events in serbia has demonstrated. there the commission was in the all too unusual position of being praised by the local government and by other donors for the rapidity with which we were able to deliver. but this is still too rare, and getting help where it is needed fast still requires a great deal of effort on the part of our officials to cut their way through bureaucratic thickets. we owe it to them and to those we are trying to help to equip them properly to do the job. that is what this proposal for a rapid reaction mechanism is all about. just as the wider reforms which we are introducing to our external assistance programmes across the world are designed to ensure that the european union aid programme begins to earn and to deserve a reputation for excellence. the rapid reaction mechanism will allow us to activate very rapidly and to disburse quickly community funds in response to crises or emerging crises. the draft regulation under discussion in the council reflects the amendments submitted by parliament. we want to ensure maximum flexibility both geographically and bureaucratically, dispensing with complex comitology rules, for example, in favour of straight provision of information to the council and the european parliament and simplifying as much as possible the decision-making process. the aim will be for the rapid reaction mechanism to be activated to cope with the initial limited period of a crisis, pending the coming on stream of the regular community programme, be it cards or tacis, or whatever. interventions under the mechanism will be limited in time and amount up to eur 12 m each time. just before coming specifically to the amendments let me respond to one or two points in the debate. both mr newton dunn and mr wiersma – who spoke shortly after him – suggested that i should give examples of when the rapid reaction mechanism would be useful. almost the first problem i had to deal with when i became a commissioner was how to deliver oil rapidly to the democratically controlled municipalities in serbia. frankly, it strained our administrative creativity to get that done. we have actually managed to do it in a way which i believe satisfied the court of auditors as well as getting assistance into those municipalities very rapidly. the only other country, the only other donor which actually got involved as well, because of the complexities of what we were taking on, was norway to which i pay particularly warm tribute, but it was a difficult job, it would have been easier if we had had this mechanism in place in order to do it. i was asked about conflict prevention and i very much agree with what the honourable gentleman, my honourable friend i might say even though we are not members of the same party, mr hume, had to say about this, who knows more about conflict prevention than most of the rest of us put together. the important thing about conflict prevention is that it should be quick and effective, and i repeat the word "quick". now, mr howitt challenged me to say whether i believed that development assistance is the best form of conflict prevention. of course i do. sensibly used development assistance along with a generous and sensible attitude to the trading relations between countries is by far the most effective way of trying to cope with conflicts, a point made admirably the other day in an excellent article in the financial times by martin wolf bringing together the findings of a number of academic studies on conflicts in africa and in other societies. so of course i agree with that, but the commission will actually be bringing forward in the next month or two a communication on conflict prevention in which we will try to pull together some of the imaginative ideas which are being developed both in the commission and elsewhere for conflict prevention which is increasingly, as we have to cope with the dark side of globalisation, the major subject on the agenda of foreign and security ministers. but in providing the assistance, in providing the resources to deal with conflict prevention, i just want to make one point. it is not a question of the commission raiding one budget in order to find money elsewhere. the commission only has the money which the budgetary authority provides, which the council and which parliament provides, and my view, which i will be rehearsing once again in the general affairs council next monday, is the commission for too long has allowed others to get away without setting priorities and has been landed with all the political odium of setting priorities itself. i think we need to engage parliament and ministers much more in discussing the relationship between our political and development priorities and our external spending around the world, because if we only have a limited amount of money to spend, as we will have for the foreseeable future, for ever as long as there is a finance minister, we will always have to make very difficult choices between priorities, and not everybody will like what those choices are. but i agree with what the honourable member said about development assistance and with his view that it should be primarily directed towards the alleviation of poverty. let me deal with the amendments proposed by parliament. of the 38 put forward, the commission can take on board 34, either as they are or with small drafting changes. that is a measure of how close we are on this issue. we have difficulty with four amendments. firstly, amendment no 9: the first part talks about the need for the rapid reaction facility to be supported by the setting up of civil headline goals. we are happy with that notion, but we cannot go along with the european public security force suggested in the second part of the amendment, which is plainly well beyond the commission's remit. i hope my honourable friend, mr van orden, took note of that and that i can at least dismiss that nightmare. amendment no 14 adds a new recital on the financial rationale behind the budget line created for the mechanism and its budget provision. this amendment seems to stem from an earlier misunderstanding of the whole mechanism which later discussions in the european parliament have cleared up. it is now very clear that there is no question of moving activities or budget out of cfsp or to hijacking options under that pillar into a community framework. the mechanism is wholly a community instrument, and so is the origin of its budget. we cannot accept amendment no 28, because the "community" is not the budgetary authority. only the budgetary authority is entitled to determine annual financial provisions in the budget. finally, the commission would not of itself have been against amendment no 29, but we have in a spirit of compromise accepted the demand put forward by the council to limit the duration of operations, given the considerable flexibility achieved in other respects. these are not, i am sure as honourable members will appreciate, exactly fundamental differences. that is because basically we share the same objectives: to improve our performance considerably, to improve our response in crises. that is, i repeat, what this mechanism is all about. i very much welcome the support which overwhelmingly most honourable members have given it thus far. i hope very much that honourable members will give it a fair wind this week because, like you, i want to have it operational as quickly as possible. this is all about the credibility and the effectiveness of the european union around the world. if honourable members do not support this, i repeat, god knows what they think the european union is for. president of the commission. - madam president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, it is with great pleasure that i stand before you today, at the beginning of a new presidency, and i wish you all a very happy new year. in welcoming your incoming presidency, mr persson, i welcome the choice made by sweden to adopt a particularly powerful slogan, based on the letter e. the letter e stands first and foremost for 'europe', which is our common objective and to which sweden will devote its best efforts over the next six months to make progress, particularly in the fields of enlargement, employment, the environment. but the letter e also stands for "euro". 2001 is the year that marks the beginning of the physical circulation of the single currency and is also the last year of many national currencies, some of which have a history of more than a century and which we, even personally, are fond of. the swedish presidency will therefore accompany us for part of the way towards the historic date of 1 january 2002. i should like to dwell for a moment on the three e's of the swedish presidency, as outlined by prime minister persson. these three priorities are well chosen because they cover all three areas where the union, and europe as a whole, will face enormous challenges and will be able to seize enormous opportunities. these are not just priorities for the next six months, to be forgotten immediately afterwards, but long-term challenges, chosen as the main objectives for the entire five-year term of the legislature. and as an enlargement, an enlargement. enlargement - it is worth repeating - is the greatest challenge facing the european union. we are at a crucial stage for the future of europe as a whole: we have the opportunity to create an area of peace, prosperity and stability extended to 500 million citizens, united by the same values. to make this process possible, we had to adopt a number of internal reforms. the treaty of nice, although not entirely satisfactory, is still a step in the right direction and allows us to continue along the road we have taken. for this reason, and also because nice, aware of its own limitations, envisages an after-nice, i would like to urge you to join this house in recommending to national parliaments, at the appropriate time, the ratification of the treaty of nice. i think it is clear that peace, stability and prosperity cannot stop at the borders of the european union, but must involve as many neighbouring and friendly countries as possible. i am therefore pleased to see that relations with russia are also among the priorities of the incoming presidency. the same strategy, which is aimed at building a substantial neighbourhood policy, is reflected in my recent trip to north africa. in fact, in the process of reuniting our continent, we must be careful not to neglect this dimension. the euro-mediterranean partnership is also central to our interests, and we are looking at ways of reviving and strengthening it. nor should we forget - and the presidency will certainly not forget - the nordic dimension of the union, which is of fundamental importance. the second e stands for employment. this priority is largely in line with the new economic and social agenda we agreed in lisbon. i fully share the commitment to take it forward. in particular, the commission welcomes the emphasis placed by the presidency on the modernisation of the labour market and the need to ensure equal opportunities for women and men in our society. modernising our economies means more jobs and promoting equal opportunities for men and women is an important aspect of the fight against discrimination. the commission will work closely with the presidency to contribute to the success of the stockholm summit, which will be largely devoted to these aspects. in this context, the commission intends to propose a new strategy for the creation of a european labour market by 2005, the details of which will be set out in the synthesis report we are preparing for the stockholm meeting. the third e is for environment, that is, environment. our fellow citizens are concerned about environmental and consumer protection issues, including - and this is particularly important these days - food safety. the recent events of the mad cow crisis are a most dramatic reminder of this and the commission has already taken concrete measures to deal with this emergency. we have a responsibility to future generations to ensure the sustainable development of our societies and to make our economies compatible, in the long term, with the balances of the planet. i look forward to working with the swedish presidency to provide the european union with an effective and coherent strategy for sustainable development. the gothenburg summit will have to take concrete and operative measures - i repeat, concrete and operative measures - in this fundamental area. in this context, the union must remain committed to taking a leading role on climate change issues. we must respect the commitments made in kyoto and keep up the pressure on our international partners to respect their own commitments made in kyoto. in this respect, the letter e also indicates a more conscious commitment to energy and a deep reflection on all aspects related to the supply, use, conservation and environmental compatibility of energy sources. i therefore welcome the emphasis the presidency has placed on these aspects. i have repeatedly called for a deeper european policy on transparency when speaking before this house, and i am pleased that prime minister persson has insisted on this and devoted a considerable part of his speech to it. citizen participation, both in the major decisions and in the daily life of europe and its institutions, is a priority for the commission. i would therefore like to assure the presidency of our full support for its efforts to promote openness and transparency. madam president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, the initiatives planned for this six-month period are ambitious and are bound - i am sure - to leave a lasting impression on the minds of our fellow citizens. however, i do not see the six-monthly presidencies as isolated acts, but rather as a continuous effort, as something that lasts over time. i therefore fully appreciate the effort made by the swedish prime minister to assure us that his work will build on the foundations laid by the intensive work of the previous presidency to enable the next one to carry on its work effectively. this is all the more true when we consider the decisive theme of the so-called post-nice period, namely the particular debate on the future of the union. the last time i spoke before this house i made clear my disappointment not only with certain aspects of the treaty just agreed but above all with the atmosphere which prevailed throughout the summit. fifteen member states, each of which was understandably concerned with its own national interests, could only reach an imperfect agreement in nice. (applause) moreover, most heads of state or government - and this is the most important point - have shown themselves more inclined to seek to secure the possibility of blocking future action by the union than to find a way of advancing the common cause. (applause) in this way, nice has clearly demonstrated what is meant by agreement on the lowest common denominator. it would be dangerous to delude ourselves that we can go on this way. i returned from nice with the confirmation of a conviction that i already had and that i had already manifested before you: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the financial resources of the community are used to the full. (applause) we must therefore draw some lessons for the debate on the future of the union, which takes us up to 2004, although it is still too early to have a complete picture of it. the first lesson is that nothing positive or lasting can be done to secure europe's future without involving the european forces at work immediately, including, of course, the forces of all the candidate countries. in my view, the path leading up to 2004 can be divided into three distinct phases: the commission has already started a first phase, which we could call open reflection - we are doing it today - during which it is good that the widest possible debate on the future of europe takes place at all levels of civil, political and scientific society. each of us must contribute to stimulating and multiplying the discussion. we must therefore give concrete meaning to our objective of achieving a balanced and stable system in 2004 which will enable the enlarged union to function in a democratic, legitimate and effective way. the contribution of european democratic political parties is crucial to anchoring this debate in civil society. in this connection, i should like to arrange a meeting with the leaders of the political groups in this parliament in the near future. i hope that through this exchange of views we can reach operational conclusions on the objectives to be pursued and the instruments to be used to achieve them. this debate must be open and without pre-established limits. in particular, it goes without saying that the worst way to deal with this would be to confine ourselves to the four themes of the nice declaration, because this is the 'post-nice' era. these issues - the charter of fundamental rights, the simplification of the treaty, the clarification of the powers and the possibility of a second chamber - are obviously very important. some have been the subject of considerable work, as in the case of the restructuring of the treaty, but these issues are only elements of a basic reflection which must be both wider and deeper (applause) and which is effectively summed up in the very title of the declaration of the heads of state and government, when they asked themselves the question: "what do we want for the future of europe? i hope that this house, through the political parties represented in it, will play its full part not only in expressing the democratic legitimacy of the community's decisionmaking process but also in bridging the gap between national political parties and the public opinion which they represent. (applause) i would like to thank i urge you to do so, and i will be at your side in this endeavour. i believe that is necessary for the future of europe. the commission, for its part, intends to engage in a broad and open dialogue with european companies and with the actors in the union's political systems. this is the first stage. the second stage should begin immediately after the laeken summit in december. this phase, which we might call structured reflection, is the most delicate and will have to be centred around an operational summary of the opinions gathered during the previous phase. it cannot be confined to purely intergovernmental negotiations behind closed doors. this is the lesson of nice. in laeken we will have to invent a new formula, one which meets the needs of openness and legitimacy. the third and inevitable stage will necessarily be a new intergovernmental conference in the proper sense of the word. i think this conference could be brief, conclusive and decisive. all three adjectives are important: short, conclusive and decisive. as i said, the debate we are launching must be open-ended, because, as has been stressed in recent days, it is essentially a question of the structure of political life in a union of 25 or more members. but i would be failing in my convictions and duty if i did not recall, once again, as they remain relevant, the concerns i expressed in this house on 3 october last. i am firmly convinced that the community method, its rationalization, its simplification and its enlargement are the future, not the past, of the union. concern. it calls upon the turkish authorities to seek a peaceful solution. in any event, the turkish security forces should exercise restraint. concerning the operations conducted by police and army partnership, the improvement of the detention conditions to bring them into line with the un standard minimum rules for the treatment of prisoners and other international norms is considered as a priority. turning now to algeria, i can say the following: the commission backs the algerian authorities' efforts to bring about national reconciliation and end the violence. democracy, the rule of law, human rights and fundamental freedoms are key principles that the european union applies even-handedly to all its partners. we applaud algeria's acceptance of the relevant clause in the negotiations for an association agreement. the violence, however, produces new victims every month. we are particularly concerned by the upsurge of violence during ramadan which claimed many lives and educating the police force, making it able to work as a police force should in a democracy.

i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. in fact, it is quite confusing when even the parliamentary administration is unable to distinguish between two persons with the same name. sometimes the mail gets a little confused. the united nations revived the idea of an international criminal court after the horrors of world war ii. the violations of international law in yugoslavia and the massacres in rwanda were also reasons for this. some ask: what is the international criminal court's jurisdiction in contrast with the existing courts? the court of justice of the european union, based in luxembourg, decides on the application and interpretation of the treaties of the european union. the international court of justice in the hague decides on disputes between states. the international court of human rights in strasbourg rules on state violations of the rights of the convention on human rights. the international criminal court is now being set up for the four most serious crimes: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and crimes of aggression. the united nations has so far authorized special tribunals, such as the ad hoc criminal tribunals for the crimes in yugoslavia and rwanda. in the future, the international criminal court will clearly signal that each of these crimes will be prosecuted and punished. war criminals can no longer hide behind the borders of sovereignty. the new court of justice is an important achievement for the community in bridging the gaps in the criminal justice system. i would therefore like to call on all member states to ratify the statute soon and i recommend that the resolution be adopted.
mr president, if you look at the list of eu states which have already ratified it, you will see that five of the six founding states have done so. the only country missing is the netherlands, which has made a special effort to promote this court and its seat. so you wonder what's behind it. of the other nine member states of the european union, only three have already ratified, including austria, which has been criticised by many. i would also like to appeal to the other countries of the european union to start the ratification process as soon as possible. we need this criminal court so that international crimes against humanity, which unfortunately have not decreased but rather increased, can finally have an objective global dimension. we were talking about cambodia earlier. we are talking about the former yugoslavia. the special courts that are being set up are certainly justified. but we must also be aware that it is sometimes defamed by nationalist forces in these countries as a victorious justice. in order to prevent this from happening again, it is extremely important that there should soon be a unified criminal court in the world, so that we no longer have to operate with special courts. the hague-based tribunal for the crimes of the former yugoslavia is very meritorious. he needs our support. but you have seen that president kostunica, who has just recently made solemn speeches in parliament, refused to receive mrs del ponte two days ago because she was not his equal in terms of protocol. this is a scandal! we have to be very careful not to let the european union become a victim of the international community, which is the only one that can do so. this is the first and foremost criminal court. we've worked hard on this, and it's high time he started his work.
commission. – even though the setting-up of the international criminal court does not come within its remit, the commission hopes that the required number of 60 ratifications will soon be reached so that the court can become operational. as of 31 december, the statute was signed by 139 countries and ratified by 27. the commission notes, with satisfaction, that the united states signed the rome statute on 31 december and the yugoslav federation earlier on 19 december. in its relations with third countries the commission will make every effort to recall the necessity to sign and ratify the statute as swiftly as possible. in the meantime, the commission will continue to provide grants to initiatives in support of the international criminal court. so far, approximately eur 4.8 million of grants have been provided to support the activities of ngos or institutions working on information campaigns concerning the international criminal court. the commission will provide further support for these activities this year. we want to promote this and use our cooperation with ngos to keep up the momentum to make this court a reality.

commission. – mr president, let me reply to mr seguro, who talked about the situation in honduras. i want to make it clear that as part of our decision last year, supported by this house, to increase our stake in the whole hipc initiative – eur 1bn, we decided to spend it globally, not just on the acp countries. the reason for this was that, as a consequence of hurricane mitch, honduras was included in the hipc initiative. we needed to find a budget line outside european development fund money to make it possible for the european union to be even-handed and support honduras. honduras will receive eur 15m as debt alleviation from us because of this. this is, of course, in addition to what honduras is receiving from the hurricane mitch mid- and long-term rehabilitation and reconstruction follow-up as part of the regional programme. several members have raised concerns about the slow delivery of the more long-term reconstruction part of the hurricane mitch follow-up. i can only agree with the criticism. i myself have characterised this as a real scandal. it took almost one and a half years for the commission services to find the six to seven people to send to managua to form the unit to run the implementation of the regional reconstruction programme of eur 250m. this is pathetic. it is not just bureaucracy, it is a totally dysfunctional set-up of different parties who do not talk to each other. this is exactly why i am still in the market for more tnt to blow up those kind of structures which are blocking good performance in the commission. the situation today for the implementation of this programme is that these people have now been working in managua since early autumn. of the eur 250m, we have specifically earmarked and started the execution in a number of the states covered by the reconstruction programme of more than eur 80m. so eur 80m out of eur 250 are now set to work. things are finally starting to happen on the ground. i still want to make the very clear distinction – which i urge everyone who has spoken in this debate to note – between the immediate humanitarian short-term response to disaster and the long-term reconstruction work. they are two totally distinct types of activity and this has to be borne in mind. nothing has moved slowly in the hurricane mitch follow-up, except, as i mentioned here, finding seven people to send to managua. but this is bad enough. let me now turn more specifically to the terrible situation in el salvador. of course, the commission fully shares the consternation and solidarity expressed in parliament's resolution on the terrible earthquake which struck several countries of central america, and in particular el salvador. the commission – president prodi, mr patten and myself – immediately expressed its condolences to the families of the victims and the authorities and announced a quick and efficient community response to this catastrophe. as in the past, when it assisted el salvador after the 1986 earthquake through the construction of a new hospital and provided very substantial humanitarian and reconstruction aid to the countries stuck by hurricane mitch, the commission stands ready to help central america and el salvador to face the present dramatic challenges. as soon as the earthquake occurred the commission humanitarian aid office, echo, directed a field expert stationed in honduras to go directly to the scene and he was there by sunday. echo also arranged this monday for a mission to be sent to make an initial assessment of the needs as regards cooperation with other donors and the local authorities. it left yesterday. on monday i decided that the first response in terms of money should be eur 2 m. this would cover the things that we knew would be necessary in any case. without any type of coordination or further studying, it was clear that drinking water, sanitation, shelter, food aid and medical supplies would be needed. we also were immediately clear as to the organisations we should ask to take care of this on behalf of the commission, namely a couple of european ngos and the red cross family. we will follow up these initial decisions with further commitments, depending on the feedback we get on what we are going to do compared to other donors and so on. let me add here that this terrible catastrophe once again proves that poverty as such is dangerous. most people think that earthquakes and these types of catastrophe are much more damaging in our sophisticated societies with all the elaborate infrastructure we have, yet in el salvador the immediate consequence has been that more than 50% of water provision to the whole nation is cut off because of damage to pipes, electricity etc. so the secondary impact is enormous, often because the systems are vulnerable, not functioning very well. for instance the flooding in mozambique caused much greater damage to dams, road, bridges and so on than it would have done if the country had had normal, well-maintained, strong and more expensive infrastructure. so poverty is dangerous, and this has to be kept in mind. for this reason, we are giving more emphasis to disaster preparedness activities as part of our humanitarian assistance. we are also considering as favourably as possible the requests for a re-orientation of resources available in commission-supported development projects in the zones and sectors affected, including those foreseen in the framework of the post-mitch reconstruction programme. my view here is that we need additional resources for this. it is not acceptable to divert money from the post-mitch reconstruction programme which has had enough problems already due to our bureaucratic difficulties, but it is an asset that we have a unit in place in the region which consists of people who are specifically engaged in these kind of reconstruction activities. of course, this is an asset and we will definitely come back to the more long-term problems for el salvador when we get beyond the immediate humanitarian response. so i thank you for the very strong support here. we will come back on how to do these things.

representatives of the european parliament, we succeeded, in the evening of 22 november, in making significant progress in the conciliation procedure on the three basic directives on railway liberalization, namely the further development of the railways, railway authorizations, and the allocation of track capacity, namely progress towards further opening up the railway sector. i shall summarize them in three points, and i welcome you, madam vice-president! we have made three points to the council. firstly, it was decided to open all national rail networks for crossborder freight traffic once and for all, starting in 2008 at the latest. we have thus achieved that from that moment on all member states must open not only the lines of the so-called new trans-european rail freight network, but their entire network to railway companies from the other eu countries. secondly, the derogation which would have allowed member states - originally planned by austria - to escape the strict european requirements for the respective national regulatory authority has been removed. i think that this has led to the fact that in all the member states it is not the national railway companies or their subsidiaries that have to decide on the licensing of railway undertakings, the allocation of tracks and the charging of tolls, but actually independent bodies. so these are the two essential components: opening up all networks to cross-border traffic and setting up an independent regulatory authority in all member states to ensure fair competition. if i may say something about my colleague's report, the third essential thing that i think has been achieved is that we have incorporated the long-term objective of making users bear the costs of using rail infrastructure by means of a new provision. we have thus succeeded in raising road tolls in the long term to cover the costs, so that the construction, maintenance and also the expansion of the networks are borne by the users and not by the taxpayers in the long term. i think that in the long term we still need to separate the grid from the operation. but in any case, we need the network to be maintained by the users. that is why we need the long-term objective of covering costs through fees. i believe that these three essential steps will break up the national railway structures and open up new opportunities for competition among railway companies. the european parliament has fought for this, in cooperation with the commission. the commission was not so enthusiastic at first, but in the end it fought with us to achieve this liberalization, and i can therefore express my special thanks to the vice-president for her cooperation in the conciliation procedure. i believe that the european parliament, together with the council and the commission, has thus set the framework conditions for an attractive railway sector with a greater offer of customer-oriented crossborder freight services in the future. we want to modernise the railway sector by means of competition so that ultimately more goods are moved from the road to the railway, because for environmental reasons it is extremely important to move goods down the road and up the railway over long distances. let me make a comment in the meantime: the conciliation procedure has once again demonstrated the importance of the codecision procedure, which has been in force in the transport sector since the treaty of amsterdam. it is only because of the codecision procedure that we have been able to break the council's position. i would like to remind you that the french president-in-office of the council thought that after the first reading of the council's common position, all negotiations would be over and we would have to accept it. no, we have managed to move forward through a fair mediation process and achieve the internal market at least for crossborder freight traffic by 2008 at the latest. allow me a quick look. it is not enough to simply make laws, directives and regulations, nor is it enough to simply implement them into national law. my group calls on the existing railway companies - and i see one of them in the gallery, for which i am grateful - to make arrangements now so that they can make use of the new provisions when the european law we are now adopting has to be implemented in 2003. the german federal railways, for example, together with the dutch federal railways or other railways, should really take advantage of the opportunity to carry out cross-border freight transport. i think that the traditional railways are now really called upon to enforce the market opening that we have created. however, if the traditional railways do not take advantage of the new opportunities offered by liberalisation, then some industrial companies will consider doing business with small railway companies themselves and using european law. you'll have the right to do so. in germany there are 180 licensed railway companies, and they are licensed wherever they want to operate, even if they have only been operating regionally. so i think we should call on all the parties involved, the railway companies and the economy, to take the necessary measures now, to use competition to move more goods from the road to the railway!

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner and commissioners! i should like to take this opportunity to present to you, at a late hour, the commission proposal for a council regulation on the implementation of projects to promote cooperation and trade relations between the eu and the industrialized countries of north america, the far east and australasia, and my report on the subject. apart from the somewhat misleading packaging of the title, which refers to the industrialized countries and does not, of course, include all the industrialized countries of the world, but only those industrialized countries with which we do not have free trade areas or cooperation or partnership agreements, i would like to express my gratitude to the commission for the proposal for a regulation it has put forward. i think that not only has it done a great job in this area, taking into account all the difficult political debates that have taken place in the council and also the perhaps not always easy cooperation with the european parliament, but it has also done something great by actually bringing together the many different small existing projects and programmes that exist in the areas of the countries mentioned in one budget line and thus also creating a legal basis. i would like to thank the commission and the excellent cooperation it has shown with you. the aim of the commission's present proposal for a regulation is to provide a sound legal and budgetary framework for the measures taken under the various existing bilateral agreements between the eu and the six industrialized countries mentioned. these measures are currently financed from a number of different budget lines. some of them have to be run as pilot projects or preparatory measures, as there is currently no legal basis for the budget lines concerned. the commission has now provided a legal basis in this proposal for a regulation. in drawing up the proposal, the commission took care to ensure that the main responsibility for promoting exports remained with the member states. community action is therefore limited to measures which complement the efforts of the member states and other public bodies of the european union and thus create, as we always say, european added value. the proposal provides for the reporting to the european parliament and the council on a regular basis in future. we have corrected this in some places, and we have also corrected and added that the regulation is due to expire in december 2005. i have also tabled an amendment which i hope the commission and the council will support, namely that the commission should submit a new proposal as early as 2003 in which it would then outline the framework for a new trade policy and philosophy. it would also solve the dilemma we still have at the moment, namely that we have no positive clause on trade policy in our treaty, but only a negative one, by excluding what does not belong. the commission should make this positive provision in future. i think the post-nice process is a great way of doing that, and in that context i would also ask the commission to always bear in mind, as a background, that we are not satisfied with the current wording of article 133 as a parliament. i am not surprised, mr commissioner, but i assume that you are aware of parliament's views on this matter. i would also ask you to include in this new wording your position which you have just expressed with regard to one of the countries, the united states. you have given a very comprehensive overview of our relations with the united states. i would also like to see the reflections that are taking place in the commission at the moment, especially under commissioner lamy, who wants a policy statement in the field of trade policy in the future, that these reflections will also be included in a review in 2003. the projects now being financed concretely under this budget line include cooperation projects, they include company-related training programmes, and they include programmes to promote trade relations. this includes the programmes in the united states already mentioned, and particularly those with japan. in conclusion, i would like to thank you once again for all the experimental projects you have tried in relation to the various countries. it would be desirable for you to draw conclusions from this and summarise what should be transferred to programmes with other countries, what you think may have been less successful, what you think has no chance of surviving the period after 2005. if you do this review, i think we have an excellent basis on which to base a real trade policy and philosophy. in the context of globalisation, in the context of the next world trade round, i believe you have created an excellent basis. thank you again for this!

the climate agreement. i also consider it a great advantage that this system is now being applied practically worldwide to the field of office equipment. the european union has a common labelling programme not only with the usa but also indirectly with japan and a number of other countries. this is how we respond to the global market. this helps to remove barriers to trade. the telecommunications and computer sectors appear to be the most important. in the context of the establishment of an energy star office of the european union, i believe it is urgent that national experts in energy policy should be involved in addition to interested actors, so that national interests can be clearly represented. the energy star bureau is required to produce an annual report on the market penetration of products bearing the energy star logo. i think that annual rates are appropriate in view of the technological development of computer and telecommunications equipment. this is the only way to ensure that the label is awarded only to appliances with significantly higher energy efficiency than the market average. in this context, i would ask you to support my opinion, which is attached to this report and which was adopted in its entirety by the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i would like to join in the thanks to the rapporteur, mrs mcnally, but also to the rapporteur for the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, mrs emilia müller. energy saving and the reduction of greenhouse gases such as co2 are important objectives of the european union. these goals are not always achievable without effort and loss of comfort, but sometimes they are quite simple. sometimes we have to use only the technical means that are available today, and sometimes the political will to do so vigorously is lacking. in my country, germany, 11% of household electricity consumption is due to standby losses. if you add up the private and public sectors, it's 20 terawatt hours a year, which is the equivalent of two large power plants, which we use for nothing! so the device's power is not demanded, and yet it consumes electricity. the simplest thing, of course, as mrs mcnally has already mentioned, is to turn off the machine when you do not need it. this is a solution in many areas; for example, in the case of television, it should simply be more publicly advertised. but in some areas the machines cannot be switched off at all, and in the computer sector in particular it is necessary that they fall asleep quickly and wake up quickly, as mrs mcnally says, because you need the computer to be very fast and you do not want to start it up slowly. there are technical problems, but you can solve those problems without using energy. there are new innovative approaches to reduce idle losses to almost zero, you just have to put them in. technically, none of this is a problem anymore. so it's good that we're here discussing the energy star and rewarding devices that take advantage of these new technological possibilities and are very efficient. that is correct, and that is why the epp group supports the commission's proposal and mrs mcnally's report. but i think that's not enough. when i took over as the epp's shadow rapporteur, i asked experts from the various organisations, ngos, ministries, the commission, but i also asked people who deal with the subject on a daily basis, such as a computer dealer friend. i asked him, "what do you think of the energy star?" he said, "that's a good thing. at first, there were technical problems, the computers went to sleep, but they didn't wake up fast enough. now we've solved all the technical problems, but nobody cares whether a computer has an energy star or not. it's not a selling point! we should therefore consider whether we are not simply applying the principle we are proposing here, namely to give a positive label to very efficient devices, or whether we are not also removing very bad devices which are very inefficient from the market, simply not allowing them after a transitional period. i think we must also think about this - it is also in mrs mcnally's report - and then we will have a comprehensive approach to energy efficiency in this area. i therefore ask you to accept these amendments as well.

damage cannot usually be repaired. that's why there's pain money. i don't know anyone in my legal practice who wouldn't have gladly given back the money if it would have prevented the damage to their health. i'm allowed to take a little ride. i think this whole procedure is also a good example of how the council should be public in future, because some of the things that were put forward would have been of great interest to the citizens of greece to ireland and of italy to finland, and they would have thought, what are my governments doing, we want more protection! the interest in these commission. – i am pleased to have the opportunity to update parliament on the most recent events in relation to bse. many of you were present when i spoke to the agriculture committee last week. nonetheless, let me very briefly summarise the main events of recent weeks. important new measures came into effect on 1 january. these included the ban on meat and bone meal and the testing of all animals over 30 months destined for the food chain. the commission wrote to ministers for agriculture on 4 january and asked for replies to an extensive questionnaire on the implementation of bse-related measures. a working document summarising the responses was circulated to the agriculture council on monday last. the opinion of the scientific steering committee on a number of bse-related questions from the commission was published on 17 january. this set the agenda for the agriculture council on monday. following the usual, very lengthy discussions, member states agreed on the following main orientations. a ban on mechanically recovered meat. the heat treatment of ruminant fats for inclusion in animal feed and the removal of the vertebral column, the backbone, from cattle. all three of these orientations follow directly from the previous discussions in the council on the measures necessary to restore consumer confidence. they are also based on the opinion of the scientific committee. i intend to present proposals within the next several days on all these issues to the standing veterinary committee. they will, of course, result in further controls and potentially very significant costs. however member states are prepared to accept virtually any measure to ensure that beef is now safe. it is surely a matter of very great regret that this determination to tackle bse has taken so long to emerge. only seven months ago, the commission failed to obtain a qualified majority to ban brain and spinal cord from food for human consumption and from animal feed. equally, not all member states implemented a ban on the feeding of meat and bone meal to ruminants in a satisfactory manner. i would like now to turn to the proposals which the commission will put to the standing veterinary committee. firstly, the one relating to mechanically recovered meat. the commission will shortly consider a proposal to ban the use of mechanically recovered meat from all bones of ruminants of all ages. there is a case that material from bones other than the skull and vertebral column or from bones of young animals is safe. however, this involves important control problems and in the circumstances it is believed a total ban is necessary. i might add that the use of mechanically recovered meat is increasingly repugnant to consumers. the processed meat industry has also called for this ban. the proposed measure should therefore be very welcome to both industry and consumers. on the question of rendered fat, the commission will propose that ruminant fats to be included in ruminant feed should be pressure cooked in addition to the current requirement that they be ultrafiltrated. the commission will equally act on the opinion that such ruminant fats should only be sourced from discrete adipose tissues when fed as milk replacers to calves. we also need to reflect however if these changes can be properly enforced. for example, might there be control problems in distinguishing between different fats. if so, is there a need for a need for an outright ban on the use of ruminant fats in ruminant feed? if so, how do we ensure that the replacement fats are safe? one final point on the issue of ruminant fats: it is surely incredible to the public that there should be higher standards relating to the use of ruminant fats in animal feed than applies to their use in food for human consumption. however that is the current situation and i intend to put this right. on the vertebral column, the commission intention is to require the removal of the vertebral column where there are doubts over the effectiveness of the ban on meat and bone meal or whenever it cannot be demonstrated that animals are highly unlikely to be incubating bse. this is in keeping with the opinion of the scientific steering committee. again, however there are important issues which need to be addressed. where should the vertebral column be removed. if it is done at the abattoir, the most easily controlled location, there are implications for the storage and transport of beef carcasses. there are also risks of microbiological handling due to the increased handling involved. if instead removal is required at the butcher or retail outlet, there will be control problems in the recovery and the destruction of the bones. similarly we need to be aware of the impact on consumers. a strict implementation of the scientific committee recommendations would require removal of vertebral column in animals aged over twelve months, as is currently the case in france. this will entail a ban on certain cuts of meat which are very popular – t-bone steaks and bistecca fiorentina for example. finally, which member states should be exempt from the requirement? should for example member states like austria, sweden and finland which continue to be bse-free be exempt? these are all issues which the commission is urgently considering and will address in its proposal. i hope that these observations help to highlight the very complex issues which arise for what might appear at first sight to be a relatively simple measure. i am aware that the issue of controls is a concern. in this respect, the replies of ministers to my letter of 4 january is reassuring. all member states now insist that they are giving top priority to the secure implementation of bse-related measures. the food and veterinary office will continue its programme of inspections in this regard. finally, as a further incentive to improve compliance, i am considering a proposal in the very near future to require member states to present monthly reports on their implementation of bse control measures. the uk and portugal are already required to provide such a report under the restriction measures on their exports of beef. i believe it has been invaluable in ensuring that controls are actively implemented. it should therefore, i believe, be replicated at community level. (applause)

the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. first of all, i should like to make it clear that we will have ample opportunity to discuss general aspects of fisheries policy during the coming week in strasbourg, when the green paper on fisheries policy reform will be presented. i would therefore like to say a few words here today on the report which is just about to be presented. i think it is quite clear, and it is certainly not wrong, that we are faced with cod stocks in the irish sea at historic lows. it is certainly not wrong to say that if we want to protect the cod stock, there is only one thing to do, and that is to leave the stocks alone during the spawning season. it is therefore very important to close the spawning grounds in good time before spawning begins, even if this is very painful and even if it naturally causes problems for the fishermen. time is running out, for the spawning season begins in the middle of this month. i know that all those involved, and i thank the committee on fisheries and the rapporteur in particular, have made a great effort so far to ensure that we achieve this objective in time. they will vote on the report tomorrow and then there is just enough time left for us to get a decision in the council and the regulation is there on 15 february. the commission fully agrees with this report and i would like to thank you again for your support. the amendment tabled is very important. i am sorry to say that i must reject this amendment. why would you do that? we have made a number of experimental catches with semi-pelagic trawls in the last year, precisely in the second half of the closure period. these tests have clearly shown that the risk to the cod is very high during this period and that there is a very high amount of cod being caught. but we in the commission are prepared to allow semi-pelagic trawls during the first half of the closure period, under the conditions that mr nicholson has indicated, namely that there is a specific monitoring system under article 3 and that if too much cod is caught, the activities will be stopped immediately. we also know that this second condition, which i have mentioned, involves a certain risk, but with the monitoring system we can know exactly next year in the event of another closure whether or not this exception for the first part of the closure period can be carried out next year.

president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it is certainly a good thing that once a year there should be a general debate on the state of the union. i would like this debate to be a step forward on the road to 2001. this road is obviously marked by many events and many priorities which we shall describe in this speech, but above all it is the road which has already been taken - indeed i would say it is almost finally being taken - towards the direction of europe of tomorrow. the commission, which i have the honour of chairing, has always asked to be judged on the basis of facts and it is therefore very important to me that cooperation between the commission and parliament and fruitful relations between the commission and the member states in the council lead to serious and concrete results. that is why i hope that this annual meeting will become a privileged occasion for joint, open and free reflection, for discussing our successes and our problems in a constructive way, in order to achieve the projects that are important to the european citizens. i know that, on such occasions, the protocol tradition requires the president to describe in detail the policies implemented, but i do not think i am doing anything unwelcome by suggesting that i depart a little from that tradition, preferring to limit myself to the main priorities for 2001 and the broader question of the future of europe. in fact, i shall say very little in the last 12 months. when i stood before you a year ago, i announced the four strategic objectives which my commission had set itself: first, to promote new forms of governance at european level; secondly, to stabilise europe and strengthen our presence worldwide. thirdly, to redefine economic and social priorities and, finally, fourthly, to improve the quality of life for all. to improve the quality of life for european citizens, we have published our white paper on food safety and a proposal for a regulation laying down the basic requirements and principles of food law. we have also proposed the establishment of a european food authority, which will be operational this year. we have also proposed the establishment of a european aviation safety authority and, after the erika disaster, we have drawn up new, strong legislative instruments on maritime safety. to promote a new economic and social agenda for europe, we presented strong and detailed proposals to the lisbon european council, which have given the european union an integrated strategy to transform it into the most dynamic and competitive knowledge-based economy in the world. the key factor in the stabilisation of our continent is our strategy for enlargement of the european union. throughout the year, the commission stepped up its negotiations with the applicant countries and launched a public debate on a proper immigration policy. (applause) i would like to thank finally, we have started work on promoting new forms of european governance and we expect to publish a white paper on this subject by the summer. on the whole, ladies too long under such stress, whatever the objective requirements imposed on the changes required. i have therefore decided to complete the internal reform quickly, in full compliance with all our commitments and in a climate of concertation and transparency. the commission's policy choices are set out in its work programme for 2001, which was adopted at the end of january and sent to the most significant initiatives of this year. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, all our work since lisbon and in the context of stockholm has been guided by a constant objective: the european the communities in which they live. on the basis of the commission's contributions, the lisbon summit last year produced a strategy to achieve this objective. the european council in stockholm next social capital and our environment. to achieve this balance in the long term, a sustainable development strategy is required. this is precisely the strategy that the commission is developing and which the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. i thank you for giving me the opportunity to present the seven-point plan for the conversion of beef production just adopted by the commission. what's the matter? we all know that the beef market is in a serious crisis; the european union consumption has fallen massively, with prices for young bulls falling by 39.2% in germany and 41.8% for cows. these historic lows have already triggered the intervention safety net in germany and the netherlands. i am sorry to say that our exports have also collapsed. there is a need for swift action. i'm sure that storing meat is not enough. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's beef and veal market is not affected by the introduction of the single market. we must therefore also change course quickly. the commission's seven-point plan is a kind of emergency package to prevent overproduction in the coming years by taking another step towards extensive production, towards sustainability and towards organic farming. but this plan is not a systemic revolution either, and for one simple reason: we must first give a chance to the reform that has just begun. the agenda 2000 reform has only been partially implemented. we have only taken the first step towards a total reduction of 20% in intervention prices, and this year and next year we will take another 7.1% reduction. the increase in direct payments and the tripling of extensification premiums are far from being implemented. in short, the full implementation of agenda 2000 in 2002 will in itself contribute to more extensive cattle farming and to more decoupled support. today we are talking about the crisis package in the wake of bse, which neither anticipates nor replaces the mid-term review of agenda 2000. i am not going to change my mind: in 2002, that is to say next year, the whole of the agricultural policy will be put to the test, as was requested in berlin. the commission will use 2001 to carry out in-depth analyses of the individual sectors in order to present a comprehensive, well-thought-out approach to the future. we must take this time to avoid being the victims of hasty political action. the seven-point plan is not a robbery of the european farmers either. it is the only chance of reducing the loss of income for farmers, at least in the medium term. the commission is unfortunately not in a position to make up the full loss of revenue with its financial resources. unmarketable beef, consumer distrust and skyrocketing costs are a highly explosive amalgam that can cause enormous damage to cattle farmers and agricultural policy. our seven-point plan is designed to help us remove the trigger from this ticking time bomb. but our plan also aims to ensure that beef is safer for the consumer than ever before, and that consumers can have confidence in beef again. let me now briefly outline these seven points. firstly, we propose to reduce the permitted stocking density for the special premium for male and female bovine animals from 2 to 1.8 livestock units. secondly, we want the member states to respect the so-called 90-head limit without exception, i.e. that a holding can only receive the special beef premium for a maximum of 90 head of cattle. both measures will increase the incentive to extensive production. thirdly, to make organic farming more attractive, we propose that organic farmers can grow fodder crops such as small grass on land that is being set aside. fourthly, the commission also intends to set the number of rights for the special premium for male bovine animals on an individual basis per holding. this measure will also reduce the incentive for intensive production. fifthly, our package also provides that a higher percentage - at least 20% and at most 40% - of the eligible animals, i.e. suckler cows, must be heifers. this should also help to reduce beef production, which is very much dependent on the number of suckler cows. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. ladies and gentlemen, let me say that the measures the commission is proposing today will not be fully operational for one or two years. there's no other way. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not disrupted by the introduction of new forms of production. in the short term, we have to think about what to do with the huge quantities of unsold beef. with all our understanding of ethical discussions, with all our sympathy for those who say that the elimination of cattle is a tragedy, we should have no illusions. hundreds of thousands of cattle have been crowding into european stables for months, and farmers have been unable to find buyers for their old cows. the safety net has already been set up in two member states. this week alone we are likely to be stocking up to 30,000 tonnes of meat! but it's not enough. this brings me to the last point in the package of measures. once bse testing for animals over 30 months old is made compulsory in all member states, we want to replace the harmless disposal programme with a new special purchase programme. the member states can then decide whether they prefer to store the meat from cows at their own expense or whether they want to withdraw it immediately from the market. in any case, we will be reimbursing farmers together with the member states 30% of the value of the animal for the member state and 70% for the eu. this measure is nothing more than a temporary emergency measure which is intended to last until the end of this year at the latest. in the medium term, there is only one way forward: act today to limit the beef production of tomorrow, promote less intensive production methods and promote organic farming. i would therefore ask you to give your opinion on this proposal as soon as possible. thank you for your attention.
