the rapporteur. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. when we talk about supplements, we mainly mean vitamins, minerals, fatty acids, amino acids, and many more. so we are not talking about fortified foods or food additives. we are talking about nutrient concentrates, which are offered individually or in combination in the form of capsules, tablets, powders and similar dosage forms. vitamins and minerals are involved in a wide range of biochemical processes in the human body. an optimal intake of these substances is crucial for human health and performance. i think that the possibility of supplementing our daily diet with vitamins and minerals is very positive. the directive on food supplements is a means of approximating the laws of the member states. some member states currently classify food supplements as foodstuffs, others as medicinal products. the directive now clearly classifies foodstuffs. we are therefore correcting the imbalances for the producers. it also removes existing barriers to trade in the internal market. at the same time, we are creating legal certainty for european consumers. the commission proposal is generally welcome. however, the discussions in parliament have made it clear that amendments are necessary to certain points of the proposal. the area of application is highlighted. the commission proposal for a directive takes a narrow approach to the substances covered. this applies first of all to the permitted minerals and their compounds. the commission proposal does not cover some important minerals, although they are used in many countries of the european union. in principle, these minerals should be accepted. of course, the chemical compounds still need to undergo scientific review. this must be done before the directive enters into force in order to avoid the need to withdraw important food supplements from the market. in addition to vitamins and minerals, there are other substances that are classified as 'nutritional supplements'. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is agreed that other substances, like vitamins and minerals, must undergo scientific examination before they are covered by the directive. however, a definition of these additional substances under the heading 'physiological' would create new problems of differentiation, particularly with regard to medical devices and medicinal products, and would lead to a completely unclear market situation, contrary to the objective pursued by the directive. a blurring of the distinction between medicinal products and food supplements would lead to a confusing situation regarding health claims, which have not been regulated to date. all this cannot be the aim of the directive on food supplements. the system of safe maximum quantities is to be welcomed as regards dosage and thus consumer health. however, we must also ensure that the consumer does not run the risk of exceeding the daily requirement for supplements by a large margin with the daily vitamin tablet. this would be detrimental to health, for example, in the case of vitamins a, d, b6. the commission proposal clearly takes account of this fact. i fully support this. the proposal for a directive provides for effective communication with the consumer with regard to the labelling of food supplements. the labelling is intended to guide the consumer in the proper handling of vitamin and mineral products. the highest standards of purity and quality are set for the products. both the individual substances and the product as a whole should be produced in accordance with good manufacturing practice. mandatory notification of products is the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr korakas, and the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for the report and the thorough discussion of the commission's proposal. the aid per hectare for cotton - and this is something to bear in mind when discussing the whole matter - is three to four times as high as for other crops. the commission considers that this particular effort by the community, and in particular this financial effort, can be justified only by the economic and, in particular, social importance of cotton in certain regions of the community. however, in recent years, the area under cultivation has increased considerably, and yields per hectare have also increased strongly. this is a new risk for the household and for the environment, because we must not forget that cotton is a very intensive crop, requiring a high level of fertiliser and pesticides. the commission's proposal is therefore aimed mainly at reducing the minimum price we calculate more than before in the event of an excessive increase in production. the amendments tabled by the committee on agriculture and rural development, if they were to be implemented, would lead to a substantial increase in the budget for the cotton sector. this means that the incentives to produce are not decreasing but increasing, and that environmental requirements are also being eroded. to make it clear what we're talking about here: the committee's amendments would add up to an additional cost of some eur 650 million per year, even assuming a constant income and an average market price. this would mean an increase of 85% in the budget. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. in short, amendments nos 1, 3, 4, 9 to 13 aim to increase prices by 10% and the maximum guaranteed quantity by 50%. in addition to the resulting cost explosion, this could mean an increase in production of 60%, i.e. by 900 000 tonnes, with the consequences i have already described. amendments nos 5 and 14 propose an indexation of the minimum price depending on the quality of the unseasoned cotton, to be approved by the member states if the trade associations cannot reach an agreement. we have had some experience with such ideas in the past. because it has become clear that it is simply not possible to create and manage such a system centrally, because there are simply too many factors that affect the quality of raw cotton. we can therefore only maintain that this question is still decided between the parties concerned, that is to say between the purchasers of the raw cotton and the suppliers of the raw cotton. we do, however, propose the introduction of a criterion, namely conformity with the price level index on the world market for cotton fibres. this will provide a framework which will facilitate the negotiation of future contracts. amendments nos 7, 8, 16 to 19 concern the drawing up of an official statute for producer groups and their activities to be supported by community aid. this is particularly true of environmental measures. i should like to draw your attention to the fact that such a system already exists in the form of eec regulation no 389/1982. the creation of producer groups has been financed by the community for ten years. as in other sectors, they have to use the resources provided for in the market organization and environmental aid to cover their operating costs. the amendments cannot be accepted because they would lead to two different arrangements for producer organizations and two different types of financing. furthermore, taking into account the increase in production that would result from the required increase in the maximum guaranteed quantity, this alone could result in costs of the order of eur 80 million per year. as regards the environment, amendments nos 6, 15 and 20 call for a wide range of possibilities for member states to amend the rules of the common organization of the market not only for environmental reasons but also and above all for economic and social reasons. this is unacceptable because it completely undermines the environmental regulations. so we are left with amendment no 2, which is basically aimed at correcting a textual error in the spanish text. in reality, however, there is no problem of translation and no mistake, because the term precio de objetivo refers to the target price and not the real market price. i very much regret that the commission cannot accept the amendments tabled by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection in this case, but i believe i have explained the reasons in detail.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. first of all, i would like to thank you, mrs izquierdo rojo, for your report, and also all the others for the effort you have put into the 22 amendments. before i go into these, let me say a few words about the basic principles of the proposal. the current scheme for nuts has been in force for 10 years and the first quality schemes expired in 2000. during this 10-year period, 92 producer organisations received community funding totalling eur 750 million to improve production and marketing in the shell fruit sector. there have also been some successful restructuring and competitiveness has increased. as a result, they are generally in a stronger position than in the past to secure sales markets and to compete with other third country suppliers. a further eur 250 million is earmarked for contracts still in progress and for measures still in progress. the commission considers that the ten-year programme has in principle been sufficient to achieve the objective set ten years ago, namely to create a stable basis for economically viable producer organizations. however, the council has asked the commission to propose that payments to shellfish producers be continued in the 2001 financial year. the commission proposal was drawn up on this basis. your requests show that you are not going far enough with this proposal. the amendments, some of which refer to the european parliament's resolutions of june and october last year, concern three main areas. the first group of amendments, namely nos 14, 15, 17 and 20, aims to maintain the support measures for improving quality and marketing beyond 2001 and to consider all expenditure on work carried out by the end of 2002 as eligible. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. the second group of amendments, namely 8 and 18, aims to maintain the special aid for hazelnuts until the end of 2002. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the following should be noted: firstly, the scope of this proposal has been limited to the financing of programmes under the 2001 budget. it should not be extended to the 2002 financial year, which will again generate additional costs of eur 82 million. secondly, specific support for hazelnuts is not included. in total, this amendment would create additional budgetary expenditure of some eur 110 million, in addition to the eur 24 million proposed. amendment no 16, which refers to chestnuts, does not fall within the scope of the regulation under discussion. the third group of amendments, namely 6, 7, 12, 13, 21 and 22, seek to secure the future of the shellfish sector in the long term by other support measures. amendments nos 9 and 19 propose that support under the common agricultural policy and regulation 2200/96 should continue. in the context of this third group, let me say how the commission sees the future of the sector and its promotion. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's agricultural policy is not disrupted by the introduction of new varieties of fruit and vegetables. these producers have made good use of the money we have made available over the last 10 years and a number of them can certainly benefit from the extension now in force. on the other hand, there are unfortunately also producers and producer organizations who have to work in extremely difficult conditions, for example in disadvantaged areas, often in remote mountainous regions, and who also have no irrigation available. there are in fact thousands of families here who are still dependent on this production in part or in full. because of these natural disadvantages and the overall disadvantages of location that these producers have, they will always have a problem with being able to withstand imports from third countries. we therefore think it is much more sensible - and this is indeed an objective we set ourselves in 1999 - to support this second group of producers, who are concerned above all with a social issue, in the context of rural development. we have therefore built this second pillar of the agricultural policy, and it should be used in this context. the principle of subsidiarity means that responsibility for this is transferred to the member states. the member states must include such measures in their programmes and give them the appropriate priority, and then they can decide on such development projects themselves.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i would like to begin by thanking all the members for their support of my report on the authorization directive. the commission has already made a number of very good amendments which i am happy to incorporate in my report. i would also like to thank the commission and the respective council presidencies for the very constructive cooperation they have had in recent weeks and months. i now come to the licensing directive and my report. what is the current state of play with regard to authorisation procedures for the operation of communications services and networks in the european union? the fifth and sixth commission reports on the implementation of the telecommunications reform package and the reports of the european telecommunications office have shown that member states have developed their authorisation regimes in completely different ways. this is particularly difficult for operators offering cross-border telecommunications services. in practice, therefore, a telecommunications activity cannot in principle be started until a decision has been taken in advance by an authority, i.e. until an individual authorization has been granted. the types of individual authorization vary widely from one member state to another, with some requiring extensive information and others requiring no information at all. as a result, the length of the authorisation procedures varies from one member state to another, the content of the authorisations differs and the level of the fees varies greatly. the aim and purpose of the authorization directive presented by the commission is to remedy this. the directive aims to provide for more harmonised and less burdensome rules on market access for electronic communications services and networks in the community. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the environment. this is already the practice in some member states. it is therefore good and right that the commission should propose to introduce this throughout europe. two sentences on the substance of the proposal for a directive. in future, network operators or providers of communications services will no longer have to obtain individual authorisations, i.e. they will no longer have to ask for permission from an authority before offering their services. they only have to comply with the requirements of general authorizations. at the same time, the conditions that may be imposed on service providers will be reduced and harmonised at european level. the proposal also provides that service providers will no longer be required to provide comprehensive information. in future, national regulatory authorities may only be required to provide information which is objectively necessary for the authorities to verify compliance with the conditions for authorisation. the change in authorisation regimes will ensure that providers can offer their telecommunications services and networks quickly and unbureaucratically across europe. i think this is certainly a milestone towards a dynamic and competitive market for electronic communications in the community. let me address a problem that is currently plaguing operators in practice. there are always great difficulties in the allocation of rights of way. here too, the rules in the member states differ greatly in terms of procurement procedures, fees and conditions. this, of course, makes it more difficult to build infrastructure in an unnecessary way. the installation of telecommunications cables of a certain length is already a considerable effort. you have to apply for a lot of rights of way from cities, municipalities, counties. you have to get building permits. they often need the approval of hundreds of landowners before they can start operating. the directive therefore aims at least to oblige member states to publish a list of fees, procedures and conditions relating to the award of rights of way. this will at least give operators an overview of the legal situation, which can save them a lot of time when applying for rights of way. finally, another critical issue is the issue of administrative fees. the level of administrative fees must be more closely aligned with the overall costs of administering and controlling general authorisations. the directive provides for a disclosure obligation for member states to make costs transparent. the proposal for a directive provides for the administrative fees to be apportioned among the various undertakings providing a service under a general authorization. the commission's proposal is that the administrative fees should not be distributed according to the turnover of the undertaking concerned, but should be distributed proportionately among the applicants. smaller companies with an annual turnover of up to eur 10 million should be fully exempted from these charges in order to facilitate market access for smes. so much for the introduction to my report. i would also like to draw attention to an important aspect of mr paasilinna's report. as mr paasilinna has already pointed out, the commission's proposal provides that national regulatory authorities will no longer be able to take all major regulatory decisions in the telecommunications sector on their own in future. instead, they are to produce only drafts, which the commission will examine and, if necessary, approve or reject within one month. in the event of a negative decision, the commission may submit a decision to the regulatory authorities concerned within a further two months. the commission will also decide whether and on which frequencies broadcasting content must be transmitted. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i therefore expressly oppose this proposal, which is also contained in amendment no 33 by the committee on industry, trade, research and energy and which was adopted by a large majority in the committee at that time. i personally believe that the national authorities are closer to the market than the commission and therefore better placed to decide in individual cases how and to what extent to further liberalise the telecommunications markets. the liberalization of telecommunications markets in particular is a success story. today, consumers have a choice of many operators, and telephone costs have fallen rapidly. in particular, at this stage of the procedure, there is no reason to take the scepter from the successful national regulators and to transfer the decision-making powers to the commission. this would only make decision-making processes cumbersome and slow. i have now tabled the amendment again, which will also be voted on in parliament tomorrow. that is amendment no 78. i ask for your support for this request and thank you for your attention.
draft opinion of the consultative committee on culture, youth, education, media and sport. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the so-called telecommunications package, the main elements of which parliament must now decide, is an ambitious undertaking which should be supported in principle. it is quite reasonable to want to make the existing legal framework of 28 different legal texts more uniform and clearer. the fact that a horizontal approach has been adopted is consistent and to be welcomed. in its opinions on the various reports, the committee on culture and the media has unanimously called for all regulation of electronic communications networks and services to ensure that access to the infrastructure does not create conditions which may ultimately have a negative impact on the diversity of content. in other words, it must be ensured that offers of general interest are sufficiently disseminated. the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport also sees the need for harmonisation measures in line with the internal market, but in a much narrower sense than the commission, which wants to expand its powers in this area. after years of arduous debate, there is now agreement among the institutions that different legal frameworks are needed for infrastructure and content. but there is also agreement that there are links between transport modes and content disseminated through them, and that these need to be adequately recognised and taken into account in the interests of cultural diversity and journalistically relevant contributions to democratic opinion-making. the market can do many things, but not everything. in the light of the above, the commission considers that the proposed amendments to the directive on the protection of the consumer are not compatible with the internal market. it must be clear that the european level has no right to interfere in national and regional broadcasting. the bottom line is therefore that coordination comes before harmonization.
- mr president, commissioner, rapporteur and other rapporteurs, ladies and gentlemen! the greens are generally in favour of these three reports. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the telecommunications sector is not left to the discretion of the member states. this liberalisation of state enterprises, whether in full or in part, has already been completed throughout the eu. the question was no longer whether liberalisation would take place, but merely how. the position of the european greens on liberalisation is clear. while we believe that the state has not always provided the best solution for its citizens, we fear that privatization will undermine public services and we are opposed to a digital divide in society. there is a lot of talk about technological neutrality. on a purely legal level, that may be the case. a technology is never socially neutral. we want development for the people, which is good for the people, which benefits all and does not harm many. that is why we have set up the greatest possible monopoly in the telecommunications sector. this may not prevent us from having only three big telecom giants in the whole eu in ten years' time. but it can prevent it, because if at least the national regulatory authorities are strengthened and the commission also plays an arbitrator role, then - and only then - is monopoly control within the realm of possibility. we have also worked to ensure that new companies can offer services on fair terms to compete with the former state-owned companies. this is a chance for more people to have access to the internet, even if we do not believe in the invisible hand or in the logic of the market. where does this discourse lead? the aim is to regulate an economic sector which can give people more independence and self-determination. we want to help ensure that all people who want to have access to these technologies can also take advantage of this opportunity. and we want people to be able to communicate digitally, to be able to organize, in short, to be able to unfold, globally. we need fair access to that. not just in private homes, but in public. in libraries, in schools, in public places. this communication must be free. it must be possible anonymously and it must be possible, if at all possible, equally. that is why we also say "no" to the many attempts to restrict, censor or criminalize the internet. although this is not specifically stated in the directives here, censorship and the desire of the surveillance authorities to control people more and more seem to be becoming more and more the essence of any attempt to design the digital space. that is why it must be mentioned here that we, the greens, are in favour of open access for all. we want open digital communication, and we don't want any more surveillance, we don't want any surveillance! that is the only reason why we have been involved in the design of privatisation, which we do not want to see as privatisation.

the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the chairman of the committee on culture, mr gargani, for his clear explanation of the question on a subject which the commission also considers to be of the greatest importance. i shall try to answer the various questions in the question in the order in which they are worded. firstly, the communication on information policy announced by the commission will be presented by the end of the summer and will then be submitted to the interinstitutional committee, the committee on culture, chaired by mrs gargani, and the committee on budgets of parliament. as regards the second point, the commission takes account of developments in information technology in several ways: the commission will continue to support the development of the european union's information society, and will continue to support the development of the european information society. thirdly, the commission is drawing on experts and professionals in the development of its information policy, especially as regards the strategy for widespread campaigns, such as those mr gargani himself has rightly emphasized, on the enlargement of the union and the euro. the commission also uses these professionals for training in information technology; the citizens are consulted through the numerous dialogues on europe which have been organised within the framework of the intergovernmental conference and which will be intensified around the issues of the future of europe. representations and networks of information centres for the general public are the voice of the practical concerns of citizens, and their input allows the information strategy to be adapted to the country or other specific factors. fourthly, what are the pillars? the main pillars, announced in april 2000 by commissioner reding, will be reflected in the commission's communication; the commission will also take account of the principle of subsidiarity, which is clearly underlined in the lisbon conclusions. fifthly, the commission intends to develop a regional dimension to its information policy, first of all by listening more closely to the regional press and to the requests of local authorities. it also intends to continue to develop information centres - infopoints - information centres known as rural carrefours, european documentation centres, in order to achieve adequate regional coverage. the large communication centres, such as those in paris, lisbon or rome, often integrated by a regional and local network, are a good example of cooperation between the institutions and the member states and are points of reference for information intended for the general public. the internet is accessible at regional level; the commission also has eight representative offices in different regions of the union. the commission has sought to bring together all the communication instruments in one single service, in order to listen more closely to opinions and to react quickly and in the most direct way. it has established, through its network of regional representations and branches, a rapid alert system capable of identifying communication difficulties posed by certain topical european issues in order to be able to react with targeted messages better suited to a certain type of audience. in terms of public relations, the commission will launch, as part of the 'future of europe' action, a wide-ranging operation to listen to citizens in order to better identify the information they wish to receive, from whom they wish to be informed, where and by what means. this action is part of the continuation of the dialogue for europe, in which the european parliament has been very much involved. the commission will put in place evaluation mechanisms and parameters for measuring efficiency. the first way of assessing an information policy is by conducting opinion polls in the 15 member states; the standard eurobarometer has been enhanced by a special eurobarometer which provides a more refined analysis by country. cost-effectiveness studies at the level of representative offices will be launched in 2001. other evaluation tools will be developed as part of the modernisation of the commission's resource management policy and in particular its press and communication service. finally, mr president, on the last and eighth point, the commission has instructed its press and communication service to draw up a new initiative on cooperation between parliament and the commission in the field of information. a technical cooperation group has begun its work and all the main issues concerning the institutions, the euro, enlargement and actions relating to the future of europe will be the subject of joint communication strategies. the euro was the subject of the first agreements between the commission and the member states for large-scale information campaigns. this effort must be continued and widely expanded. the commission's information budget is currently eur 90 million, the equivalent of one newspaper per inhabitant per year. the importance of the task to be carried out means that each member state must support the investment which falls to it, since information on europe concerns all public authorities. i would like to thank you again, mrs gargani, for drawing attention once again to these very important issues. i have offered, as far as i was able, the main lines of the responses and i can assure you that my colleagues in the commission are working very hard to meet this great challenge.

commission - madam president, you will recall that on 7 september i spoke to parliament to inform it of the commission's position on the reform of fifa's rules governing international transfers. on that occasion i announced the commission's intention to engage in discussions with fifa and other interested parties, under the chairmanship of my colleague mario monti and with the collaboration of anna diamantopoulou, in order to make fifa's rules compatible with community law, while respecting, on the one hand, the specific nature of sport and, on the other hand, the autonomy of sports organisations. the declaration on the specific characteristics of sport adopted by the european council in nice last december fully confirmed this approach. today, after intensive discussions between the commission services, fifa and the other interested parties, i am pleased to be able to announce the result we have reached. this result, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, is in keeping with the principles i have just mentioned and to which we are all committed. in this whole affair, the commission has been accused very often of not understanding sport, and worse still, of wanting to destabilize football. the result of the discussions shows that these were unfounded accusations, and i believe that the discussions have allowed us to demonstrate once again that community law and the specific nature of sport are perfectly compatible. i therefore believe that there is no need to amend community law. the commission has shown in this case its flexibility in incorporating sport-specific features into existing texts. the discussions have led to clear progress in at least three key areas. firstly, and this has always been the wish of the european parliament, to protect young players who are moving around the european union by ensuring that they receive adequate general and sporting training. these principles will be reflected in a code of conduct to be drawn up by the football federations, and i attach particular importance to this because i believe that it is much more effective to provide players with proper supervision than to impose restrictions on their mobility - restrictions which are incompatible with the principle of free movement. let's not forget that in football there are many called but few chosen, and not all players will become stars of the ball. it is therefore essential to provide both sport and vocational training. with the new provisions, the commission wants to send a strong signal to all those young people who are involved in sport: they will not all succeed in sport, but they will all be taken into account in terms of human and individual development. the second element is to encourage and compensate clubs for the effort they make in training young people and thus giving a social dimension to their sporting activity, a social dimension which is also the characteristic of the european dimension of sport. to do this, fifa will have to introduce rules on: first, the compensation of training costs up to the age of 23, on the basis of the real cost, as defined by the court in the bosman judgment, and, secondly, the creation of a solidarity fund which will be fed by a levy of 5% on each transfer compensation payment, this fund being intended for training clubs which will thus receive a part of the added value of the player. the detailed application of these principles now belongs to fifa, and the commission will ensure that, within its competence, the transposition of these principles into the fifa rules is actually carried out, and i am sure, madam president, that the commission will not be alone, but that it will be followed in this monitoring work by both the ministers of sport and the parliamentarians engaged at national level. we are therefore convinced that it is possible to strike a balance between the mobility of the player and the necessary compensation of the training club, within the limits of what was established by the court in the bosman judgment. the third point is the introduction of elements of stability in sports competitions to ensure fairness and regularity. here are the mechanisms. first, unilateral termination of the contract will only be permitted at the end of the season. this will give the fan the assurance that he will see the same team play throughout the season. but he bought his membership to watch the team play, not another, sometimes with its best players. secondly, sporting sanctions are provided for against players and clubs who terminate contracts without good reason during the first two seasons of the contract. other important points complement these principles, such as the time-limited transfer periods or the duration of contracts, which vary from one to five years. ladies and gentlemen, in the course of these discussions we met with fifpro, which represents the players. some of their demands were met. the fifa rules will no longer prohibit players from going to court, but an arbitration tribunal will also be set up, composed on an equal basis and able to rule in an emergency, which will be able to decide disputes relating to training allowances, transfers and sports sanctions. i attach particular importance to a fair and independent arbitration. the introduction of such a body, which can be used by both players and clubs, should resolve disputed situations in a fair, timely and efficient manner. i would also like to point out that the commission has emphasized throughout this case that its discussions with fifa and other interested parties do not in any way prejudge the compatibility of the revised fifa rules with the applicable national law, and in particular with labour law. it is the responsibility of fifa to ensure that these rules are applied in compliance with national legislation, from which there can of course be no derogation. fifa has announced that the agreed principles will be implemented by a revision of the fifa rules at its world congress in buenos aires in july. the commission encouraged fifa to seek a close dialogue with the other interested parties for this implementation and more particularly, of course, with the players. in the commission's view, the transfer case has clearly demonstrated that dialogue at all levels is becoming a necessity and that all means of organising it, including through collective agreements at european level, should be explored. in addition, mrs diamantopoulou offered her assistance in encouraging a permanent dialogue at european level. let me conclude this statement by reminding you that fifa will prepare a report on the implementation of this system two years after the new agreement enters into force. we will then have both quantitative and qualitative information to draw the appropriate lessons. in the meantime, i think we should welcome the outcome of these discussions. but, madam president, it has not always been easy to achieve this. the pressure exerted by certain heads of state and government, strong but unnecessary and above all harmful, has delayed the conclusion of the case on more than one occasion. in any event, the commission stood its ground and was able to demonstrate in the end that it was not necessary to amend the treaty rules to respect the specific nature of sport, and it therefore maintained the course in strict compliance with its powers. this result allows my colleague, mario monti, to decide not to propose to the commission to adopt a negative decision on the fifa transfer rules.

the commission. the accession negotiations are based on the principle that the candidate countries will recognise and apply the non-negotiable acquis communautaire as from the date of accession. transitional measures postponing the application of part of the acquis may be granted only in duly justified cases. in the enlargement strategy paper which the commission adopted on 8 november last year and which president prodi and i presented to this parliament on the same day, the commission set out principles for dealing with requests for transitional measures. the member states have agreed to these proposals and they are now the basis of our work. they can be summarised as follows: transitional measures should not concern the nature of the acquis but merely the postponement of its application for a certain period. they must not cause significant distortions of competition. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the internal market is not a one-off event, but a one-off event. the free movement of persons, the freedom of establishment and the free movement of capital are fundamental elements of the internal market. the negotiating timetable agreed by the european union commits the union to formulating a common position on these chapters by the end of the first half of the year at the latest, if the information provided by the candidate countries so permits. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used to support the implementation of the community's policies. this applies also to poland and the czech republic, and i would also point out that part of our negotiating basis is that the commission may also make proposals for transitional measures if this is in the interest of the union as a whole.

and the agenda. let us take the time, in the few weeks ahead, to work on these principles, this method and this agenda. this is and will be the subject of a joint effort by us, in particular parliament and the commission, throughout the swedish and belgian presidencies, because we must achieve a high level of ambition in laeken on this debate and the future reform. first, a basic principle: the content of the debate, the future of the union, must be the inspiration for its form and remain its priority. what kind of europe do we want tomorrow? what do we want to do together? what 's our plan ? do we want more integration or not? do we want more political europe or not? i would add another question: how can the community model be renewed? although it may seem difficult to provide simple answers to these complex questions, and perhaps because it is difficult, the debate must allow citizens to become aware of them, to participate in them. the first principle is therefore that of transparency, of objectivity, with which this debate must be conducted without refusing, and on the contrary encouraging, the expression of contradictory opinions - and we are well aware that in each of our member states opinions are diverse and often contradictory - even if, to respect this principle of transparency, it is necessary to ask - as i have just said - troubling questions. the second principle is proximity. such a reflection cannot be properly initiated by being conducted only from brussels or strasbourg. the internet is certainly here, and it is an indispensable tool for information and dialogue, and this debate is already taking place on the website, although i admit that it is still imperfect. however, dialogue via the internet is not enough. the european debate must be open to people where they live, work and study, and to their elected representatives, whether national or territorial. it must therefore naturally take place at european level, but first and foremost it must be based on debates in each member state, at the most appropriate level, which in my view is the level closest to the citizen. if the community institutions can help to organise them, and the commission is playing and will play its part in this, then these national debates must first be organised by the member states. the third principle could be that of anticipation. even if the candidate countries are not yet members of the union, it will take very few years for them to become members. the future of this union therefore concerns them as much as it does the present member states. and i think we have to find a way and make sure that they are present in the debate, that they are actively involved in it. after the principles, ladies and gentlemen, the method. the final decision-making stage, which we hope will be as short as possible, as you have said, madam minister, of this reflection, will of course be an intergovernmental conference in 2004. we hope to do so as soon as possible in 2004, as president romano prodi has suggested. it is only in this way, with an intergovernmental conference as provided for in the treaties, that the treaties can be reformed or changed. this is, as we know, the only possible method. but we also know that this future igc must be prepared carefully and, no doubt, in a different way from what was done for the previous igcs, in amsterdam or nice. the issues raised in the public debate will have to be translated into concrete proposals for revising the treaties. the structure or the competent body will, in our view, have to be inspired precisely by the model or the precedent of the convention, which, within a few months, gave the european union a charter of fundamental rights, solemnly proclaimed in nice. in other words, it must be a structure or an institution not only for debate but also for work and proposals, bringing together the various sources of democratic legitimacy in europe: representatives of the member states, the european parliament, national parliaments and the european commission. having said that, there are still many questions that remain open. what will be the decision-making procedures of this body or of this future convention? what will its composition be, and in particular the place to be reserved for the representatives of the candidate countries? what will be his mandate? should this preparation follow the public debate or is it desirable to carry it out in parallel throughout the process leading to the igc? the commission is very attentive to the answers which the european parliament is proposing and will be proposing to these various questions of procedure. and we're working on it ourselves. i also believe, madam president, that our proposals, yours and ours, must and will have to be adjusted to each other as precisely as possible in the light of the laeken european council. and so i think we must now intensify the joint work between our two institutions, in consultation of course with the two presidencies, the swedish and the belgian. to this end, it will also be essential that the structure for reflection is not a place reserved for experts only, but a permeable structure, open to external contributions. finally, i should like to say a word about the principles and method of the agenda for this debate. throughout the last few years and during this very long cycle of institutional negotiations, which began in maastricht and ended, at least temporarily, in nice, parliament and the commission have always joined forces to ensure that real reform can take place. and i would like at this point, madam president, to pay tribute and thank you, and in particular president napolitano and the members of the constitutional committee, for the intelligent effort we have made together in close cooperation. this was particularly true, i think, at the last igc, where parliament had wished, in its resolutions of november 1999 and february 2000, that a comprehensive institutional reform be discussed, in the same spirit as the commission had expressed its wish. it seems to me that we must keep this convergence intact today, even if we have to, beyond our joint work, open doors and windows, reach out, listen, participate in a wider debate. if we are to take stock of all the challenges facing the future of the union, the next igc cannot be satisfied with examining only the four subjects mentioned in the annex to the treaty of nice, which are constitutional subjects. it could be, especially since it must be said frankly that some of these four subjects - i see at least two of them - can have, depending on how they are approached, a negative or even regressive effect on the level of integration of the union. so we should not be afraid to address these four topics and not just address these four topics. however, with regard to these four themes - simplification of the treaties, the legal scope of the charter, the articulation of competences, the place of national parliaments in the european architecture - let us be careful not to weaken the community acquis or the community method, depending on how we approach them. madam back the progress of european construction. for these two reasons at least, which may be of crucial importance as the enlargement of the union approaches, the european commission, its president and all the members of the college will be fully committed to bringing to life this great debate promised by the heads of state and government in nice. the council. mr president, mr brok and other members! first of all, i would like to thank mr brok for raising this important issue. i would also like to take this opportunity to give a broad answer to the swedish presidency's view of the work on prevention within the union. "all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights". thus begins the united nations universal declaration of human rights - the cornerstone of our work for the freedom, security and dignity of the individual. in war and armed conflict, as we know, all basic principles are destroyed. rather, it is the right of the strong to prevail by force of arms and oppression. the 20th century was the century of war, with world wars and wars in the middle east and the balkans. each time the alarm bells rang, but the international community was usually too late. now we can show that we have learned from the past. by actively working to prevent armed conflict, we can help make this century something different. the eu has a key role to play here. let me quote what hume said in parliament when he was awarded the nobel peace prize: "let us not forget that the eu is the best example of conflict resolution we know of in the history of the world". today, conflict prevention is also a central part of the emerging european security and defence policy. the esdp, security and defence policy, rests on three pillars: military crisis management, civilian crisis management and conflict prevention. these are closely related. at the same time, prevention is different from military and civilian crisis management because it is not about responding to an already flared-up crisis, but about promoting in good time the fundamental values we have agreed on: children going to school instead of going to war and democracy at all levels. the eu has a very large number of instruments that can be used to prevent armed conflict and manage crises. we must use them in a more deliberate and coherent way, both in the field and in brussels. these issues must involve the whole union and all the institutions. we already know that the eu can make a significant contribution. our unarmed monitors in presovo and the police mission in albania are just two examples. the experience of the balkans has clearly shown that conflict prevention must be based on a long-term commitment. the root causes of armed conflict must be eliminated. development cooperation therefore plays a central role. the decision by the commission and the development council to integrate prevention into development cooperation is central and must now be translated into practical guidelines for projects and programmes. it is about strengthening human rights and democracy in the long term and about how crisis management and disaster relief are integrated into development cooperation. the commission's forthcoming communications on conflict prevention, human rights and democracy, and disaster relief, reconstruction and development will therefore be significant. we also need to detect potential conflicts earlier. for example, water issues are often a source of conflict today. but we can also see right next to us a telling example of how the eu can make resources of common interest generate cooperation and development. the river that runs through strasbourg used to be a poisoned watercourse, a border. now it's a shared ferry and a source of fish. the eu must also develop sustainable and effective partnerships with other key actors. we are now seeking to establish a long-term close cooperation at all levels between the eu and the un. similarly, we are strengthening relations with the osce. in africa, we want to work with the subregional organisations sadc, igad and ecowas, which also work in conflict prevention and crisis management, to help them build capacity and support local processes. the ecowas light weapons moratorium is a good example. we are also setting up a joint expert group on conflict prevention with canada and developing contacts with the g8. of course, cooperation with others must be driven by real needs and comparative advantages. when i recently visited the south caucasus with patten and solana, it was obvious to build on the knowledge and presence of the osce and the council of europe in the region. we are now discussing how the eu, together with the osce, can develop the monitoring of the border with the north caucasus. the troika's visits to the caucasus in february and to israel and gaza yesterday and the day before are also examples of the eu's role in conflict prevention. i would also like to stress that relations with civil society and ngos are crucial to our success. mr president, i would like to thank you. there has been a request for a council statement on the situation in the northern fyrom, and i would like to take this as an example of how the eu can work: we have for some years been trying to prevent conflicts through unarmed monitors, through assistance for political and economic reforms and central and local institutions, through the trade and cooperation agreement of 1998 and through the stabilisation and association agreement which is expected to be signed shortly. on 22 february, the first reports of the entry of albanian armed groups into the north of fyrom were received. their aims are unclear, but there was clear opposition to the ratification of the border agreement recently signed between fyrom and fry. to prevent further unrest, the eu and the local presidency in skopje established a close dialogue with the fyrom government. the troika called the leading albanian parties together and urged them to vote in favour of ratifying the border agreement, which a majority did. following the clashes, the mine explosion and the exchange of fire, the eu condemned the violent attacks and cooperation between kfor, unmik and the authorities of the fyrom and expressed support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the fyrom, but at the same time called for restraint. the important message to the public has been that the future of the fyrom lies in a rapprochement with europe and the eu and that stability and security are an important precondition for this. the will of move forward with what the european council has said civilian police, judiciary, civil administration and the emergency services. we're working hard to turn the goal of 5,000 officers into concrete lead police operations and in common standards for, among other things, equipment and training. furthermore, we have started work on the other capacity areas strengthening the judiciary and civil administration in times of crisis and conflict, and the council working group on emergency services is developing concrete objectives in its field. we know that armed conflict damages all the vital functions of a society. crisis management must therefore include support for everything from justice to waste management. human rights, international agreements and humanitarian principles must be upheld, not least as regards safe access to help those affected. we therefore also want to initiate the discussion of other areas of capacity than those we have identified previously. observers and commission. – i note what the honourable gentleman says about the difficulty of getting to strasbourg rather than murmansk but i suppose one difference is that you cannot get to strasbourg by nuclear submarine. it is a great privilege for me to follow on from the minister with whom i have spent a good deal of time on troika visits in the last few weeks, i guess dealing with conflict prevention, debate unless there are specific questions which people wish me to respond to, in which case of course i would be delighted to do so, not least in the minister's absence in murmansk. as the minister reminded us, the european union is not new to the whole field of conflict prevention, crisis management and post-conflict reconstruction. we recognise that conflict prevention and crisis management are long-term undertakings. all of our regional cooperation programmes, cards, the alure latin america programme, phare, meda, tacis and so on, the cotonou agreement as well as our pre-accession strategies and stabilisation, association and cooperation agreements with third countries – all of them contain conflict prevent and crisis management provisions. rehabilitation programmes such as that in rwanda after the genocide, economic reconstruction programmes such as that in kosovo today, bilateral aid programmes built on peace agreements such as those in guatemala and el salvador are practical examples of how we are helping every day to prevent conflict and to build peace around the world. no one disputes that recent history in the balkans, in africa and elsewhere has taught us that we need to equip ourselves better to try to prevent the outbreak of violent conflict and to react more effectively when it occurs. we have taken some important new initiatives in relation to conflict prevention. last december the commission and the high representative jointly presented a report to the nice council with recommendations for improvements. we focused in particular on developing better methods of analysis, closer coordination within the union and more effective coordination with our international partners – and this follows a point that my honourable friend made – especially the united nations and the osce. we are now working with the high representative to follow up the recommendations of the nice report. we are looking at the development of conflict indicators and early warning systems so that we can focus our attention much better on countries or regions in difficulty. we are also examining how cfsp instruments such as political dialogue can be adapted so that they are more robust, flexible and timely. the commission is working with the presidency on the action programme which the presidency, as the minister made clear, will present at the european council meeting in june. the commission is also preparing a communication on conflict prevention which we will present to the council in april. this communication will focus particularly on addressing the root causes of conflict through community external aid and development instruments. we will put forward proposals, for example, to build the objectives of peace and democratic stability more clearly into our assistance programmes. we will place greater emphasis in future on support for the building of stable institutions and the rule of law including, of course, the police and the administration of justice. we will also ensure through our assistance programmes that we take account of indicators of political exclusion, ethnic, social or regional marginalisation, environmental degradation or other factors which can contribute to violent conflict. we intend to contribute to international initiatives, for example through the g8 and the oecd, on issues such as international crime, the diamond trade, drug-trafficking and child soldiers. we have also to exploit to the full other means such as trade policy instruments and trade and cooperation agreements, or our skills on border-management police training, customs assistance missions – which have been such a success in the balkans – or expertise in migration, social or environmental policy. i look forward to returning to this parliament to present the communication once it has been finalised. but i am acutely conscious that while we are working on these issues, events in the real world are not put on hold. in southern serbia and on kosovo's borders with macedonia we have a real-life example of a crisis that needs managing, as the minister said, and a further conflict that must be prevented. let me be clear. what is happening on these two borders threatens, if it is not tackled firmly and rapidly, to reverse much of the recent, very heartening progress that has been made in the region. it threatens fresh conflict, fresh instability, just as we were putting those things behind us in the balkans. plainly, the straight military security issues involved are for the council, and above all for nato, not for the european commission. i know how hard the presidency, the minister and my colleague, javier solana, have been working on these issues, as has nato. i very much welcome the cease-fire negotiated on monday in the presevo valley. i very much hope that it will hold. however, i have been determined that the commission should contribute as rapidly and fully as possible to support the wider efforts to tackle this crisis both in southern serbia and on the fyrom border. as parliament may know, we have already announced that we were prepared to provide about eur 1 million in assistance for southern serbia, for the presevo valley. we have made available another eur 900 000 and agreed on 24 projects with deputy prime minister covic of serbia and with the local mayor. the 24 projects are in areas like improvement of water and improvement of schools, which we are prepared to undertake as well. that raises our immediate assistance to almost eur 2 million. i think that is the right way to support deputy prime minister covic's commitment to try to resolve these issues through dialogue rather than conflict. we are also prepared to put some of the eur 240 million that we are providing for serbia in reconstruction assistance this year to doing more in the presevo valley. we still have a long way to go in improving our capacity to respond to crises in the short term. i would characterise the challenges we face under three headings. first, we have to react more quickly in crisis situations. the commission is responding to this challenge. as parliament knows we are engaged in a process of the reform of our external aid, which will mean that we are able to deliver assistance more rapidly and more efficiently across the whole range of community aid programmes. last month, on our initiative, the council also adopted the regulation establishing a rapid-reaction mechanism. second, we must be able to deploy appropriate personnel in sufficient numbers, which is a real difficulty and a challenge for all of us. the rapid-reaction mechanism will give the commission the possibility to do this and we will shortly start to negotiate framework contracts for this purpose with member states, international organisations, ngos and others. the major problem we face in this area, however, is the lack of suitably qualified and available personnel in the member states. it is a problem faced not just by the union but also by the un, osce and other bodies engaged in international peace missions. in the commission's view, the best way to build up the union's capacity in this field is by developing common recruitment standards and training programmes. the commission is encouraging member states to work together and with the un and osce in this area, and is prepared to support such training programmes from community funds. third and last, we have to develop more effective coordination. in the commission's view, effective crisis management does not necessarily require major changes in existing decision-making procedures laid down in the treaty. it requires the establishment of improved mechanisms for day-to-day coordination at headquarters level, in the field, and between the field and headquarters. for its part, the commission is engaged in reorganising itself internally in order to ensure better coordination of community instruments in crisis situations. the commission has established a conflict prevention and crisis management unit. within that unit the commission intends to establish a crisis management cell, which will coordinate various community initiatives and provide a focal point for the council situation centre. the crisis management cell should be operational by the summer. furthermore, in the context of the on-going debate in the council on crisis management procedures, we have suggested to council that the coordinating mechanism provided for in the conclusions of the helsinki european council should be relaunched. we are prepared to play our full part in the functioning of this mechanism. finally, with regard to both conflict prevention and civilian crisis management, the commission intends to play, in full association with the work of the council's political and security committee, an active role in helping to take forward efforts in this area with the council. we want to work with the high representative, the policy unit and the council secretariat in this spirit. we will work closely with parliament, as well as the council, on these issues. we will certainly keep parliament fully informed. i very much hope that the communication which we bring forward in april will provide a focus for a debate which gives us the opportunity to bring together in a more creative and constructive way the responsibilities with which the commission is charged, the responsibilities which we have agreed to share on a europe-wide level. we can take initiatives in this field which are not available to others and if we do that constructively we will make a reality of the construction of a common foreign and security policy.

mr president, the committee on economic and monetary affairs welcomes the report by the wise men and has underlined this in a resolution adopted unanimously. it is in the interests of the european union, in the interests of the three institutions, that we overcome the fragmentation of the european financial market and find solutions that meet the interests of industry, investors and consumers and contribute to the stability of the financial market in the context of globalisation. we therefore consider it important to speed up and make more efficient the legislation in this area. the three institutions must all contribute to this. the report by mr wise does not make clear how the relationship between the actors and the institutions should be shaped at the various levels, and therefore calls for a dialogue between the european institutions. the question therefore arises to the commission and the council, because it is not clear to the european parliament how the institutional balance here in the european union can be guaranteed within such a proposal. we have therefore drawn up proposals and are awaiting the council and commission's replies. unlike most member states or the united states, the treaty does not provide for the possibility of secondary legislation, not least because there is no executive body at community level to which these powers can be delegated. in addition, unlike the national parliaments, the european parliament has no right of initiative. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection has already taken a number of important decisions, and i am sure that the commission will take them into account in its future work. this means that if clear links are established between political and technical matters within a framework legislation, the empowerment for implementation in the technical field and for adaptation to technological change must be designed as quickly as possible and this must also be underlined by giving the european parliament a clear right of recourse in the event of a breach of the empowerment or if the requirement of transparency is not respected, for example in the consultation. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. i would say that if there is good will on the part of the council and the commission, this right of withdrawal could be interinstitutional agreement which makes clear that the basic principles and the clear distinction between political and technical implementation are regulated in the laws on a case-by-case basis. we the council. mr president, i would like to thank you for your reply. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i am grateful for this opportunity to develop the council's position on the proposals in the report of the wise men, chaired by baron lamfalussy. we have already had many informal contacts between parliament and the council on this matter. i would like to take this 12 march 2001. the council welcomed the report, but discussions will continue. a new ecofin council will take place immediately before the stockholm summit. the presidency's ambition is to reach an agreement as soon as possible. the council considers that the functioning of financial markets is essential for the growth of the economy. it is therefore natural that this particular issue should be discussed in the context of the stockholm summit, which has as one of its objectives the modernisation of the european economy. the ability of financial markets to move capital between savings and investment, to manage payment systems and to allocate risks in a cost-effective manner is crucial for growth and employment. at the same time, we must ensure that markets provide good consumer protection and that they are stable. the financial and venture capital markets in the union must be integrated and made more efficient. the financial services and venture capital action plans provide a good basis for achieving precisely these objectives of integration and efficiency. the focus is on the implementation of the action plan. to keep to the timetable, we must make the necessary efforts now. we therefore believe that the institutions concerned and the member states should jointly review the legislative process in the financial area and make more effective use of its possibilities, so that important and necessary decisions can be reached more quickly. the council considers that community law governing the securities market must provide a degree of flexibility in order to meet developments and create a competitive community market, responsive to new international trends. the legislative process must be speeded up, but the limits of the treaty must of course be respected. this can and must be achieved while fully respecting the provisions of the treaty, the rights of the institutions concerned and the balance between them. the council broadly supports the four-level approach proposed by the wise men to make the regulatory process more flexible within the framework of the current treaty. i do not wish to comment today on the details of the future work of the securities committee. i would just like to emphasize that the council and the member states, as i said just now, are aware of the need to speed up the legislative procedure. the procedures the wise men proposed for making decisions on what are called levels 1 and 2 are not really new. they are based on existing possibilities, namely the full legislative procedure and implementation by committee. the basic rules and their effects are therefore well known in relation to the issues raised by mrs randzio-plath in her oral question. the commission is also proposing that the council should be able to adopt a decision on the basis of the recommendations of the european parliament. the legal framework for the delegation of implementing powers is clear from the treaty, the 1999 council decision on committee procedure, the case law of the court of justice of the european communities and the decision of the legislator when delegating implementing powers in each specific case. in all these areas, both the council and the european parliament follow already established rules. we are jointly obliged to comply with this legal framework. the co-decision procedure allows us to decide jointly, for each act, what is to be delegated to the committee procedure and according to certain rules. in addition, the new 1999 framework decision on committee procedure guarantees parliament a greater role than ever before, while guaranteeing a high degree of transparency. this new openness is beneficial and important for the european parliament but also, of course, for the general public. the european parliament shall be guaranteed full information at all times on the work of the securities committee and shall receive all documents relating thereto: agendas, draft measures, voting results, minutes of meetings and attendance lists. if parliament considers that the draft measures presented by the commission exceed the implementing powers of the basic instrument, the commission should review those measures without delay, taking utmost account of parliament's resolution. an independent committee of regulators will advise the commission in the preparation of draft implementing measures for the framework principles. for this system to work properly, all the institutions involved must act in good faith and respect the basic conditions for the multi-level approach proposed in the wise men's report. randzio-plath also asks me to ensure that 'the securities committee does not intervene to substantially alter or stop implementing provisions proposed by the commission' and to give political assurance as to the willingness of the council to speed up its procedures. i must emphasize the fundamental constitutional difference between the council as an institution and a committee of inquiry, which is made up of representatives of the member states themselves, and not of the council. this distinction is important and, as everyone knows, it is the basis of the whole structure of the committee procedure. i would like to emphasize that the main task of the securities committee will be to assist the commission in the exercise of its delegated powers in accordance with the committee procedure. as regards the council, i would like to repeat what i said earlier, namely that all the institutions concerned will have to act in good faith and respect the basic conditions of the report of the wise men. the structure proposed in the lamfalussy report respects the codecision procedure and the institutional balance established by the treaty. the council therefore considers that no further institutional framework is needed in this area. i would also like to mention that the ecofin council is in favour of the idea of setting up an interinstitutional monitoring system to evaluate the progress towards an integrated economic market and identify bottlenecks. regular reports could be submitted to the european parliament and the council as part of this monitoring process. in addition, the comprehensive and transparent review proposed for 2004 would allow us to evaluate the functioning of the system and to address any shortcomings. as i said, on 12 march the ecofin council welcomed the report and the proposed four-level strategy and made good progress in establishing the general rules for solving the institutional and organisational issues raised by the strategy. however, some questions remain. the commission has also adopted a communication on the implementation of the european union strategy for the environment and sustainable development, which sets out the main priorities for the period 2007-13. the ecofin council has now called for further work on these issues, and i hope, as i said at the outset, that we can reach a comprehensive solution as soon as
