commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by saying that the commission broadly supports the main thrust of the report of the committee of wise men, chaired by mr lamfalussy. in order to achieve the integration of security markets by 2005, the commission considers that community legislation must become more efficient and flexible in order to respond rapidly to developments in financial markets. eu legislation must also be implemented swiftly and consistently, and enforced more rigorously. mrs randzio-plath has raised five main points on the commission's position on the report. i should like to try to answer all five, although perhaps in a slightly different order. first, on accountability and transparency of the process, i recall that the essential elements of an act must, according to the treaty and the jurisprudence, be defined by the legislators and therefore it will pass through the so-called level 1 normal codecision procedure. implementing measures, however, shall, in accordance with the comitology decision, be delegated to a level 2 process, as is clear to any person who has read the lamfalussy report. the commission shares the view that it is essential that consumers and industry are fully consulted on all such implementing measures affecting them. in adopting directives or regulations at level 1, the council and parliament will jointly define the scope of technical implementing measures by codecision, as has been stated, on a case-by-case basis. on level 2, the commission is also ready to consult widely with market participants and end-users in an open and transparent way before adopting tactical implementing measures. the commission also agrees that the european securities regulators' committee should carry out a full consultation process on draft implementing measures, with the european parliament being fully informed. as regards the commission’s right of initiative, i stress that the commission, in preparing its proposals for level 2 technical implementing measures, looks forward to benefiting from the technical expertise that the european union's regulators will bring – after all they are the experts in these matters. there can therefore be no question at all of the commission's right of initiative being affected by any such advice. the commission believes that encouraging european regulators to work in this way will also facilitate over time the convergence of regulatory structures throughout the european union. i now come to the third matter raised by mrs randzio-plath: the question of the symmetry of the codecision powers of the two legislative pillars and of the transparency of the securities committee. it seems to the commission that such a symmetry is guaranteed by the codecision procedure provided for in article 251 of the ec treaty. that procedure gives parliament the power to decide, together with the council, on the scope of the technical implementing measures to be adopted at level 2. parliament must decide, together with the council, on the difference between the general principles and the implementing measures. for those measures the 1999 comitology decision – referred to earlier by the representative of the council – confers on parliament "the right to be informed by the commission on a regular basis of the proceedings of the committees involved in committee procedures." in conformity with articles 1 and 2 of the interinstitutional agreements on procedures for implementing the 1999 comitology decision, the commission will send to parliament all necessary documentation, draft measures and agendas of the european securities committee, as the council representative just mentioned. the commission is also prepared to follow the committee's recommendation that it should take the utmost account of any parliamentary resolution adopted concerning a proposal to the european securities committee. let me now turn to the question raised about proposals for implementing measures. if the european securities committee were to fail to give a positive opinion to the commission and the council were to oppose the measures or parliament were to express a view that the implementing measures exceeded the delegated powers in a resolution adopted by an absolute majority – the so-called ultra vires case – the commission would, following the 1999 comitology decision, re-examine its proposal. in such circumstances the commission would be prepared, as i mentioned earlier, to take the utmost account of parliament's position, as expressed in such a resolution. in those circumstances, and even if the european securities committee had already given a positive opinion on the proposed implementing measures, the comitology decision still gives the commission the possibility of putting forward a legislative proposal on the basis of the treaty, i.e. through codecision. the commission is, however, convinced that all sides will have major incentives to make this system work. it is willing to work with the council and parliament within the scope of the treaty and of the comitology decision to clarify any outstanding points. furthermore, the proposed interinstitutional monitoring committee – on which, of course, this parliament will be represented – will have a significant role in ensuring all of this. finally, on this point, there will be a full review of the whole process in 2004. to conclude, and before i answer the questions put by mrs randzio-plath, the commission's fundamental objective in the securities field is to create an integrated european financial market through the completion of the financial services action plan, and the sooner the better. the commission believes that substantial long-term benefits will flow from that objective. to deliver it, the commission considers that community legislation must become more efficient and flexible in order to respond rapidly to developments in financial markets. as the council representative also stressed, legislation must be delivered in a way which is in conformity with the treaty and with the 1999 comitology decision. all interested parties will have to be satisfied and have an adequate role within the limits of the treaty. i know i shall have the chance at the end of the debate to provide some additional comments, but i should like to reply to some remarks made by mrs randzio-plath. indeed the commission welcomes very much the positive attitude shown by mrs randzio-plath, as chairperson of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, vis-à-vis the report of the committee of wise men under the chairmanship of mr lamfalussy. she said that every effort must be made to speed the process up – and the commission totally agrees with her opinion – otherwise we shall be adopting yesterday's measures for tomorrow's developments. she also said – and here again we concur – that the procedures must be absolutely transparent, and the report of mr lamfalussy and his colleagues is very clear on this. once again, there is a monitoring committee on which, as i have said, parliament will be represented, to monitor this whole process. if there is insufficient transparency, then no doubt the monitoring committee will make the appropriate observations. thirdly, in the case that parliament should adopt by majority vote the opinion that the commission has acted ultra vires, then once again the commission agrees with the lamfalussy report in saying that it will take utmost account of parliament's opinion and act accordingly. that is an important safeguard for parliament to see that it is not bypassed by any sleight-of-hand. so, there again, we can reassure mrs randzio-plath.

the agenda calls for the oral question (b5-0010/2001) by mr rocard to the commission, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the commission proposal on the status of assistants. i would ask the author of this question, mr rocard, to explain the matter.
commission. – the commission attaches a great deal of importance to the matter of assistants to members of the european parliament. in 1998 the commission, with parliament's agreement, drew up a proposal to amend the conditions of employment for other staff so that parliamentary assistants would become auxiliary staff. i happened to be the commissioner responsible at the time. this would have ensured equal treatment for assistants in terms of their salary, employment conditions and tax, with a choice of a social security system. as you know, however, this proposal was not accepted by the council. by agreement with the european parliament and the council, the commission then commissioned an expert study with various solutions that would be compatible with community law and the interests of the assistants and the members of parliament. the experts suggested that one aspect of the assistants' legal status could be dealt with by another community instrument, namely regulation no 1408/71, which coordinates the social security schemes of the member states. the assistants are already covered by this regulation and it brings them, in principle, under the social security system of the member state where they work. vice-president onesta has contacted my colleague, commissioner diamantopoulou, suggesting that the commission puts forward a proposal to the council and parliament for an amendment to this regulation, allowing assistants to chose between the member state where they work, the member state where they were last insured or the member state of which they are a national. a similar option is already available to auxiliary staff of the institutions. such an amendment would only resolve a very specific and small part of the assistants' legal position and would not exonerate them from the obligations of national law in regard to labour conditions, tax and social security. however, the commission has committed itself to finding solutions which are in the interests of both assistants and members of parliament. the suggested amendment can indeed clarify the legal position of the assistants as far as their social security rights are concerned. it seems that the application of regulation no 1408/71 to this category of workers still gives rise to uncertainty, which can be removed by the amendment. once they have made a choice there should be no further misunderstanding as to which member state 's system they are subject to. moreover, it seems justified to derogate from the general rules of the regulation for persons working on a temporary basis for members of community institutions, such as auxiliary staff. my draft then reads as follows: ‘therefore the commission intends to propose shortly to parliament and council the suggested amendment to regulation no 1408/71’. if asked what ‘shortly’ means, i can say that it will be before the summer. that means that this issue can be decided during the belgian presidency.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. when we legislate in this house, we always assume that it will be an improvement on the present situation. i therefore have the right as rapporteur to claim that the seventh amendment to the cosmetics directive is an improvement on the current situation. and is she now? and then many in this room with me will say, "no, she's not". the sixth amendment to the cosmetics directive, which i was also able to be rapporteur on a few years ago, clearly states in some stages that, for example, animal testing for cosmetics should be given an absolute end date, after which no animal testing should be carried out. i would ask all of us to bear in mind that there are now more than 8,000 ingredients that have been tested and that we can use. now the question is, what happens to the new ingredients? the commission has converted this ban on testing and marketing, i.e. the ban on selling, from the sixth amendment into a pure ban on testing on the territory of the european union. so that means that in the future, you can do animal experiments for as long as you want, but a few kilometers away. i now hear from all sides, including the commission, how sympathetic and friendly they are to my amendments, but unfortunately they cannot accept them because they are against the commercial point of view. is that right? the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. my report is intended to put an end to the discharge procedure in 1998. the first thing the prodi commission had to face was a tense situation. however, what was achieved by postponing the discharge for 1998 in april 2000 and by granting discharge in july 2000 leaves much to be desired. i shall only mention three areas of particular concern. in 1998, for the fifth consecutive year, the court of auditors refused to give the commission a positive statement of assurance, that is to say, to certify that the european taxpayer's money was being handled with care and economy. parliament has therefore done more than enough to oblige the commission to achieve a so-called positive das by the end of the financial year 2003. unfortunately, the commission has so far failed to identify concrete, measurable intermediate steps along this path. the commission's constant reference to the general reform programme cannot be sufficient here. i therefore ask the commission: is not the careful handling of european taxpayers' money a matter which must be the commission's first priority? or will the commission celebrate the tenth anniversary of the refusal of a positive declaration of assurance in 2003? we measure the commission by its actions, not by its words. i therefore expressly welcome the deadlines we are now setting for you to achieve this objective in the report. in particular, the fléchard case has shown that the role of the independent financial controller is decisive for whether a case of fraud becomes known or not. you now want to abolish this independent financial controller and, as part of the reform programme, place him in a hierarchical position under the director-general responsible for the specific subject. we cannot agree to that! the result would certainly be a glaring reduction in the error rate, but not because there would be no more mistakes or fraud, but because the directors-general in charge would ensure that such things would not arise in the first place. the establishment of an independent disciplinary chamber, capable of fair and impartial disciplinary proceedings, with corresponding consequences for the officials responsible, is also a longstanding demand of parliament, which the commission has not complied with. nor is it serious about the introduction of a european prosecutor to prosecute fraud cases. on the subject of access by members of parliament to information and documents, i ask the commissioner seriously: how are we to control if you deny us the information and documents? the commission has, at the beginning of its mandate, put transparency and openness at its heart. i myself have seen in the 1998 discharge proceedings how the claim and reality here are clearly at odds. the 1999 discharge procedure also showed no significant improvement. a look at annexes i and ii to the blak report shows that the rapporteur has received 22 requested reports and has not written 11 reports! these figures, i think, speak for themselves. the lack of access to information is being fatally exacerbated by the framework agreement between the commission and parliament. it was adopted, as you know, in july 2000 here in the plenary without any opportunity to discuss it. this framework agreement is driving a wedge between members and creating a two-class parliament. it is promoting a policy of divide and rule. we cannot tolerate this, nor can we tolerate the denial of access to public documents. i would also remind you that in the morgan report last december we decided to postpone discharge in the future if all the documents requested were not submitted by the commission. this case actually came to pass sooner than many expected. i would like to say again very clearly about the fléchard case: the commission cannot blindly ignore the clear recognition that what was done was wrong at the time and that everything must be done in the future to prevent such an illegal decision from being taken again. the opportunity to make such a statement is yours, mrs schreyer, as the responsible member of the commission. please take advantage of this opportunity today! i want to make it very clear that my decision whether or not to grant you a discharge will depend on how you speak today.

commission. - mr president, as parliament knows, and mr posselt in particular, for the member states bound by title 4 of the treaty establishing the european community, the principles relating to the control and surveillance of the external borders of the european union are governed by community law, in accordance with the protocol integrating the schengen acquis into the european union as decided by the treaty of amsterdam. in my opinion and in the commission's opinion, there are several reasons today for considering the creation of a european external border guard. several member states seem to be keen to deepen this approach in order to strengthen the means of combating illegal immigration. the countries applying for membership of the european union are destined, and i emphasize this, to participate in the full schengen and community acquis, including in the area of control of the union's external borders and the free movement of persons without internal border controls. even from the point of view of the development of community law, the function of external border controls is not to control people for the sole purpose of migration. they also want to ensure control of external borders in the fight against crime, the enforcement of customs regulations and the observance of certain technical regulations applicable to vehicles or dangerous or illicit goods. i can therefore confirm that the italian government has asked the commission to support a feasibility study on the possibility of creating a european border guard corps, an initiative which has been supported by several other member states and which has the sympathy of the commission. as you know, any decision on such a programme supported by the odysseus programme is up to the management committee. what i can tell you is that the commission supports the italian initiative. as regards the european police college, which was set up by the council decision of 22 december 2000 - commission. – mr president, i should like to begin by thanking both mr galeote quecedo and mr gasòliba i böhm for the questions they have put which indeed touch on an important aspect of the internal market. may i begin by saying that the communication of 19 july 1997 on certain legal aspects concerning intra-eu investments to which both speakers made reference was adopted by the commission, as was the case for a series of other communications, on the basis of its exclusive competence stemming from its role as guardian of the treaties. as is specified in the communication itself, its objective is to indicate to national authorities and economic operators in member states how the commission interprets the provisions of the treaty on capital movements and the right of establishment in order to reduce the risk of divergent legal interpretations. the principles set out in that communication are essentially based on the jurisprudence of the court of justice of the european communities, which remains, of course, the sole competent institution to provide a definitive interpretation of community law. in accordance with article 56 of the ec treaty all restrictions on capital movements between member states, be they discriminatory or non-discriminatory, are prohibited. the communication, being devoted to intra-community investment, goes more deeply into the respect for this fundamental principle insofar as two specific forms of capital movements are concerned: the acquisition of domestic securities and direct investments. all restrictions applied to these capital movements can pose compatibility problems with, in particular, article 56 which deals with the free movement of capital, and article 43, which deals with freedom of establishment. the communication to which i referred a little while ago states that, in conformity with the very notion of direct investments, nationals of other member states of the european union should be free to acquire controlling stakes, exercise their voting rights attached to those stakes, and manage domestic companies under the same conditions as are laid down in a given member state for its own nationals. while the freedom of establishment and the free movement of capital are among the fundamental freedoms of the treaty, certain exceptions to the general rules exist which allow member states to impose certain restrictions. as far as the freedom of establishment is concerned these restrictions may be motivated by the exercise of official authority or on the grounds of public policy, public security or public health – article 46. as far as the free movement of capital is concerned they may be justified on the basis of requisite measures in the field of taxation, prudential supervision, or the use of declaration procedures, or by considerations in relation to public policy or public security – article 58. finally, member states may take measures which they consider necessary for the protection of the essential interests of their security which are connected with the defence sector – article 296. in accordance with the jurisprudence of the court of justice it is necessary to interpret those exceptions narrowly in order to satisfy the criterion of proportionality. all interpretation based on economic criteria should be excluded. an exception should not constitute a means of arbitrary discrimination or a disguised restriction on the freedom of movement of capital. in the light of the principles which i have just set out, and taking into account that the treaty is neutral insofar as the private or public nature of companies is concerned, it clearly appears that all restrictions aimed at preventing subsequent purchases by investors of other member states of controlling rights in privatised companies under the pretext that the capital of these investors is to different degrees in public ownership cannot be justified by the exceptions of the treaty in the area of capital movements or the rights of establishment, exceptions which i delineated a few moments ago. in conclusion, may i say that as members of this parliament may be aware, the commission will shortly have a debate on restrictions on intra-community investment.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the resolution we are discussing this evening raises two questions. the first is the problem of community legislation. if we look at the sources of community law, we have on the one hand the original law of the treaty and on the other directives and regulations adopted with the participation of the council and parliament. but in between has come what is often considered a source of law - the communications. we shall be discussing one of these communications today. commissioner, you have rightly pointed out that this communication is only an interpretation and is also based on the case law of the european court of justice. but it can often seem that the commission is the one who interprets the law alone, without the involvement of the council and the european parliament. the commission acts as the sole legislator, as was the case in ancient byzantium under emperor constantine. my legal teacher in freiburg sometimes referred to this commission procedure as the imperial-byzantine method of legislation. i therefore believe that in such important cases it is absolutely necessary that directives or regulations should be put forward and adopted, as they should be, with the involvement of parliament and the council. the problem we are discussing raises a second question, namely that of competition in the european community. liberalisation, the abolition of monopolies, is one of the success stories of the european union. in the telecommunications sector, we have seen that reducing costs and prices has actually brought benefits to citizens. but there is a very great danger here. we are faced with a situation where some liberalize and open up competition, but others do not. we can then observe that those who have not done so, on occasion even win with monopoly, as long as the others buy up, until the old, public monopoly has been replaced by a private monopoly. the citizens are still faced with a monopoly and are not benefiting from the benefits of liberalisation. i believe that the commission must take this fact more seriously in its future action.
president of the council. president. - the debate is closed. ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament! i will give my and the presidency's view of the stockholm summit. the meeting was divided into two parts: a follow-up to the lisbon process, a discussion on the union's external relations and a short discussion on agricultural policy. i would like to begin by commenting on the lisbon process. the lisbon summit gave a strong impetus to the union to create a competitive, world-leading, dynamic economy with social cohesion. at the stockholm summit we added four different areas to the lisbon process. firstly, the demographic developments in europe, which will have a strong impact on the social agenda that must be formulated for europe. the demographic challenge will eventually include both a fiscal problem and a shortage of labour. meeting this challenge is a common concern for all 15 member states. this will require major efforts, not least in the social field. we can therefore also link up with the social agenda which the french presidency launched so successfully in nice. demographic issues are thus added to the lisbon process. secondly, the biotechnology. in lisbon, the focus was on information technology. we must not forget this, it is still important, but we must also add biotechnology if we are to be a region and part of the world that leads economic development. this too must become a priority for the union. we must not give in to the difficult moral and ethical issues that are associated with this technology. they must also be addressed in our discussion. the third point we add is that we want a link between social development, economic development and ecological development, i.e. no sustainable social cohesion and no sustainable economic growth unless this is also based on an ecologically balanced social development. the fourth point we add is that the candidate countries will continue to participate in the lisbon process. these four elements are therefore added, but the lisbon process is clearly a process, a development. it is therefore important for us to realise that we do not get everything from the social agenda and economic liberalisation at once. it's going to be a gradual process. the european council in stockholm has given and reaffirmed this direction. the focus is on full employment and active welfare states. as regards economic liberalisation, we took another step forward in stockholm. it did not go as far as we as the presidency had wished, but it did take decisive steps in the right direction. firstly, there is the creation of a single european market for financial services. a major breakthrough in the area of financial services and venture capital was first achieved by the ecofin council meeting in stockholm, which was then confirmed by the european council. we also agreed to move forward with the directive on postal services. we also agreed to abolish the monopoly and open up the gas and electricity markets to competition. we have not got the timetable we had hoped for, but it will happen, and we stress our determination to go in that direction. the european council held an intensive debate on the following: if some member states open their markets to competition in the gas and electricity markets, it is an unsustainable situation in the long run for other member states to avoid doing so, because this eventually leads to a situation where some companies in monopoly markets create profits for themselves which are then used in market offensives in other countries which have opened their markets. it will build tensions in the union that will be difficult to manage. it is therefore important that we proceed with the liberalisation of the gas and electricity markets in the way we have proposed in principle, but it must also be done according to a timetable. in june, the question of european airspace will be raised again in gothenburg. we have made progress in this discussion and i hope that we will reach agreement on the single european sky before the end of the swedish presidency. in the economic field, we will also see the internal market directives transposed into national legislation, with 98.5% of the directives to be adopted by 2002. we also want to start a new round of wto negotiations. we have highlighted the importance of making all activities linked to eeurope safer. we also said in stockholm that we wanted to go ahead with the galileo project. it's important, you know. there are still some things that need to be clarified, for example as regards funding, but we believe that this is a project of social benefit that should be implemented as quickly as possible. as early as tomorrow, our transport ministers will discuss the matter further. we also decided that the distortive state aid in the single market will be reduced by 2003. to this end, a scoreboard will be set up and made available to all. this is essentially what was agreed at the discussions on economic issues held in stockholm. as i said, it's a step in the right direction, but it's not going to get us where we want to go. it is a process, and the direction of the process is unambiguous. it is the economic side of the lisbon process. the other side of the process is the social agenda. the europe that is emerging is not a europe that can be built only on the deregulation of markets, but there must also be an expression of the political will to distribute the growing wealth that exists in europe in a fair way, so that our citizens can live a rich life. the swedish presidency has sought to strike a balance between the conclusions of the stockholm meeting on economic liberalisation and social responsibility. on the social side, a new employment objective has been established: it is particularly important that we concentrate on those aged 55 and over in the european workforce. by 2010, 50% of this group will be employed, compared with 38% today. we have a new target for the general employment rate for 2005, namely 67% for all and 57% for women. by 2052, we will have measured childcare in europe to contribute to a social agenda that allows young men and women to combine the responsibilities of a professional career with those of family and children. in the field of gender equality, we are striving to create not only a social europe but also a modern europe. discriminatory pay differentials must be prevented. indicators of this are therefore highlighted to make these differences visible. the equal treatment directive is to be adopted and tightened up this year, which is also a result of the stockholm summit. the creation of quality jobs, i.e. the ability of people to stay in their jobs longer without being forced into early retirement, requires the development of workplaces so that people who are not fully healthy or fully capable find their place in working life. the transition from mass unemployment in europe to a situation of labour shortages and the continuation of economic growth requires the full exploitation of the experience of mature older people. the quality of workplaces must also be improved. the following are important to consider: lifelong learning, equality between men and women, how we treat all those who have come to europe in recent years, perhaps as refugees, i.e. the fight against segregation and discrimination also in the workplace. we will also return to a first evaluation of european pension systems in gothenburg. if there is one thing that weighs on ordinary wage earners, civil servants and workers, it is the question of having a secure livelihood in retirement. how do we manage pension systems in europe at a time when we see fewer and fewer people in working age and more and more people in retirement? this too should be discussed together in the context of open coordination. we shall return to this in gothenburg. this is the structure of the social agenda, and it is in this way that these two elements form a whole: economic liberalisation and modernisation on the one hand, social responsibility and solidarity on the other. this is how the policy is put together to make europe the most competitive, dynamic and socially cohesive region in the world. that's our vision. this was the subject of the lisbon process at the summit. in addition to the lisbon process, we discussed external relations. there were four main reasons. firstly, our relations with russia. president putin was invited to participate. he met the group of 15 heads of state or government in a direct discussion. at the same time as president putin met with us, foreign minister ivanov met with the foreign ministers. we have, of course, reiterated our concern about developments in chechnya and other phenomena in russian society which we do not accept. however, our main discussion was on economic developments in russia and the prospects for economic cooperation between russia and the european union. some concrete results were achieved: firstly, we are opening up the eib's lending to russia, albeit limited, but it is a breakthrough for environmental efforts. secondly, we will give russia all possible support in its preparations for wto membership. the wto opens up the russian market to fair competition and also opens up possibilities to resolve old trade conflicts that we have between the european union member states and russia. we want to give russia all the support we can in this process. thirdly, we have said that we want to take an active part in the forthcoming anniversary in st petersburg in 2003. it is a splendidly beautiful european city which is regaining its old beauty and certainly its old position in european cooperation. it is a clear signal from the european union that this is also our concern. this was raised during the discussion with president putin. i would stress that it was mainly economic, but we of course reiterated our concern about developments in chechnya. we also had a visit from president trajkovski of fyrom, the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. he was invited more as a gesture of solidarity. when we, the heads of state and government, met, it was natural for us, in view of the crisis situation that was developing in macedonia at the time, to meet him and express our solidarity, but also to stress the importance of treating the different groups of the population in fyrom in such a way that they all feel that they have a place in society and a right to participate and be present. we also stressed the importance of avoiding violence, while allowing the foreign ministers to present concrete proposals in the field of aid. this is part of a balkan strategy. we are now ready to sign the stabilisation agreement for the former yugoslav republic of macedonia in april. it will be followed by a similar agreement with croatia. this shows that the union has a role to play in the balkans, and that it is a future that is now beginning to emerge for people living in the balkans as well. president trajkovski's visit was an expression of our commitment to the balkans. i also received a mission from my colleagues to travel to the korean peninsula. it is done in the context of our wish to express our support for the process of reconciliation and détente now under way on the korean peninsula. there we have the last major, four-year conflict of the cold war and the aftermath of the second world war, with enormous suffering for the people involved and with enormous risks also from a military perspective. if we can do something to speed up the process and support it, that is of course our common concern. in this area too, the union was able to come together around common principles and common commitment and to give me the task of going there on behalf of the union, together with javier solana and chris patten, sometime during this six-month period, and to discuss directly with the political leaders of both the north and the south: about the process, about human rights, about de-escalation and disarmament. the fourth foreign policy issue discussed was the situation in the middle east, which is always present in the daily lives of all politically engaged europeans. the middle east is our neighboring region. we have a huge responsibility to ensure that the peace process is restarted. peace and security are thus indivisible. war, conflict and destruction in the middle east are something that affects us too. all of us in the union, no matter what country we live in, have a deep, personal commitment to this part of the world. the union's member states enjoy excellent bilateral relations with the region and often with both sides of the conflict. however, the union has not played a major role in initiating solutions to the conflict or in various types of measures to deal with the pain experienced by people in the middle east on a daily basis. in stockholm we asked javier solana to come back at the latest to the summit in gothenburg, preferably earlier, on how the union can increase its presence and improve its activities in the region, how the union can contribute to the resumption of the peace process - of course, with the united states, but always on the basis that it is the parties to the conflict who must make an appeal, a request for participation. it's not unusual for a petition like this to come in. the union must also be prepared to assume its responsibilities. these were the four issues on the international agenda - a practical but modest way of expressing a common foreign policy within the union. madam president, i would like to thank you. we also discussed the situation of european agriculture. we expressed solidarity with those affected, we expressed confidence in the veterinary authorities and in the ability of our agriculture ministers to deal with the situation, we stressed the importance of safe food and we said that the european budget in this context is already fixed or locked. we did not think that we would be in a position to have a debate on agricultural policy in stockholm, in the circle of heads of state or government. we believe that our agriculture ministers have already done so. preparations are also under way for a review of the european agricultural policy for 2003. in this context, we had no reason to start a big debate, but we wanted to express our solidarity with those affected and, of course, also to show that we are aware that we have agricultural ministers, veterinary authorities and a commission that is doing an excellent job in this context. finally, we also touched on the state of play in the climate negotiations. it is unacceptable that any party should withdraw from the kyoto negotiations. (applause from the centre) ) the kyoto negotiations are the instrument we have to deal with the change in the basic conditions of life that the climate represents. when we see that this signal is being sent, especially in the united states, it is not possible for us to accept it. i have written to the president of the united states with the president of the commission to express our concern. the swedish environment minister is currently in the united states with the commissioner responsible for environmental affairs and will then go on to iran, japan and china to hold talks there too. we also have every reason to emphasize the statement adopted by the stockholm european council as a supplement to the conclusions, so that the kyoto protocol applies. this is the process we should be adhering to. this is, in short, what was discussed at the stockholm summit, a meeting which, in a way, once again became the everyday life of the union. we returned to questions that affect people in their daily lives. we've had an intense period of a lot of internal accountability. the french presidency successfully resolved questions about the future decision-making and accountability of the union. now we are lifting the perspective again and aiming at things that affect people directly in their daily lives. there were not successes in all areas, but there is no doubt about the direction the union is moving in. that's what politics is all about: compromise, step by step, and you get results. this is also the ambition we have had with the swedish presidency. i am also very confident in my belief that the presidency which will be handling the follow-up next spring, spain, will make some further steps forward. in this way we create the union we have dreamed of, a union that is dynamic, successful and socially cohesive. we realize that we cannot survive without considering the ecological conditions. (applause) i would like to thank you.
president of the commission. - madam president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, the last time i spoke before this house was to present the first 'spring report' of the commission to the european council. as you will recall, our report takes stock of the progress made by europe in implementing the economic and social agenda agreed in lisbon. the stockholm summit was the first summit specifically devoted to assessing this progress and setting priorities for the next 12 months. i would like to take this opportunity to thank prime minister persson for the firmness, calmness and energy with which he chaired and organized the stockholm proceedings. i also very much appreciated the opportunity he offered us to meet president putin and discuss with him the partnership between the european union and russia. this meeting was very encouraging and confirmed russia's strategic role. president putin has assured us that russia and the european union share common values. for our part, we have made it clear that we want to contribute to russia's full integration into our community of values; we want to identify the most appropriate instruments of cooperation, not only in the economic, environmental and energy fields but also in defence, security and the safeguarding of democratic rights. in this respect, while we welcomed yesterday's announcement of a further reform programme, we cannot hide our concern at the current trend towards progressive government control of the television system. the discussion, as prime minister persson said, focused mainly on economic reforms in russia, but also looked at the situation in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. the european council, as expected, assured president trajkovski of its full support for the territorial integrity of the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, and at the same time, however, the union asked president trajkovski to take account of the demands of the albanian minority in his country. it would be a mistake, however, to allow the current crisis in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia to divert us from our objective of promoting greater integration of that country with the european union. the forthcoming signing of the first stabilisation and association agreement with the former yugoslav republic of macedonia is in line with this approach. i would like to stress that the credibility of the european union depends to a large extent on our ability not only to set political and strategic objectives but also to act quickly and effectively on the ground. at the same time, we must work for the long-term stability of the balkan region, and that means using all the instruments at our disposal to achieve the gradual integration of the whole region into the european union. milosevic's exit from the scene marks an important step in this direction, putting an end to years of hatred and war. i would now like to return to the debate on the economic and social agenda in the european council. i agree with prime minister persson that there was a climate of legitimate optimism among the heads of state and government in stockholm. a year ago in lisbon, in the face of the strength of the american economy, we still had a kind of inferiority complex. today, things have changed and we can see that europe is in a strong position in three respects. first of all, we have started to modernise our economy. secondly, we have a social agenda which aims to rebuild the european social model without distorting its character. thirdly, we are seriously working towards sustainable development which also includes the environmental dimension. the position recently adopted by the united states on this matter is worrying. our concern was reflected in a letter, signed by prime minister persson and myself, to president bush. in any case, europe must continue to act consistently and it has an obligation to take the lead in this very important area. a month social model in the framework of the nice agenda. i would like to stress again the need for clearer strategies to deal with the issue of our ageing society. this is precisely the commitment the commission has made by announcing the presentation of a communication on the quality and sustainability of pensions in the light of demographic change. the commission therefore urged the european council to commit the member states to taking the initiative in at least six key areas where new impetus is needed. first of all, we still need to improve skills and training in information technology. last wednesday, the commission also adopted the e-learning action plan, which includes specific measures for teacher training and partnerships between schools, businesses and industry. commitment to the rapid implementation of this project. i would also like to take this opportunity to reiterate that this is no longer the time for equivocation: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. what the prime ministers decide should be implemented by the sectoral ministers who are to preside over the practical implementation of the projects. (applause) i would like to thank thirdly, the financial markets. the commission has long advocated the need for an integrated financial market at european level. we need a regulatory system that allows us to keep up with this rapidly changing market. i am therefore pleased that the council has stressed the importance of this sector and its enormous potential in terms of job creation and cost reduction. as recommended, a european committee on tendering will be set up, chaired by the commission. this body will act as a regulatory committee and will assist the commission in deciding on the measures to be taken to give practical effect to the legislative acts agreed between the council and parliament in codecision. we will thus be able to intensify our efforts to achieve an integrated securities market, which is one of the main shortcomings of our internal market. the commission will therefore be putting forward important proposals in this field before the summer, and i call on addressed in the context of a wider european strategy for sustainable development, which will be one of the main topics of the gothenburg summit in june. in addition, the commission will in future preparatory work more transparent and clearer. we are therefore in favour of the introduction of a european system of taxation, which is a very important one. ladies and gentlemen, stockholm has - doc. a5-0093/2001 by mrs sanders-ten holte, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council (com (2000) 340 - c5-0294/2000 - 2000/0145 (cod)) amending regulation (ec) no 2027/97 on air carrier liability in the event of accidents.
- may i ask you for a little discipline tonight? if each speaker speaks one minute longer than his speaking time, madam president, we will have 40 minutes more work and we will have to stay here until 1 a.m. instead of midnight. your speech was very interesting.
the commission - mr president, i would like to congratulate mrs sanders-ten holte on her excellent report, which stresses the importance of rapidly applying the montreal convention and of thoroughly informing passengers of the rights it confers on them. the commission fully supports the report, since it supports our intention to provide air passengers with a high level of protection in the event of an accident, it seeks to modernise the rules on liability for delays and damage to luggage and, above all, it seeks to improve the information of users about their rights, since the biggest problem is often that users themselves do not know what they are. i am glad to say that the transport council is due to adopt a decision at its meeting tomorrow to ratify the convention and for the community to ratify the convention at the same time as the member states. the community must also bring its rules on airline liability into line with those of the montreal convention, which is the aim of this proposal. the amendments tabled are perhaps the most important ones concerning the information to be given to passengers on the provisions relating to the liability of airlines. the commission's proposal requires airlines to provide passengers with detailed information. the report seeks to strengthen the wording of the regulation by requiring community companies to submit an information note, as set out in the proposed annex. this would ensure that airlines provide passengers with the necessary information in an accurate manner, which, as experience shows, does not always happen. the commission therefore accepts amendments nos 13 and 18. the other two amendments, nos 19 and 20, would have the consequence, if adopted, that third country airlines would be exempt from the obligation to inform their passengers of the rules relating to their liability and therefore we cannot accept this discrimination and we reject both amendments. however, we have some doubts about amendments nos 9 and 10, which state that the liability of airlines will be governed by the relevant provisions of the montreal convention without specifying the relevant articles. the commission proposal, however, provides that liability is governed by the provisions of seven articles of the montreal convention, explicitly numbering them. ladies and gentlemen, changing this question could provoke a hostile reaction from some member states, and the subsequent debate would slow down the adoption of the regulation to the detriment of passengers. that is why we cannot accept amendments nos 9 and 10. we cannot accept amendment no 11 either, since the article cannot be deleted if the text continues to refer to specific articles of the montreal convention, in line with the previous rejection. the commission can, however, accept all other amendments which reinforce or clarify the text. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam rapporteur, i have just summarized the commission's position on this report. i would like to thank mrs sanders-ten holte once again for her excellent work and support for the early incorporation of the montreal convention into community law, and she is quite right, because this new incorporation will mean a shift from the international regime agreed 72 years ago - which was ultimately intended to restrict the liability of airlines - to another modern system which is intended to do just the opposite: to give a high level of coverage to the protection of passengers' rights.

- doc. a5-0096/2001 by mr camisón asensio, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council (com (2000) 5 - c5-0402/2000 - 2000/0023 (cod)) on aid for the coordination of transport by rail, road and inland waterway.
mr president, madam vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your kind words. first of all, on behalf of my group, i should like to thank my colleague, mr felipe camisón asensio, for his report. he made it very carefully. the commission has not been able to reach a decision on the matter, and i am afraid that the council will not be able to reach a decision on the matter. the vice-president and mr camisón asensio were well ahead of the european council. but the european council can still be cited. the stockholm european council stated that it is necessary to reduce the level of state aid in the european union and to make the system of aid more transparent. that is the objective here. i believe that by replacing the old regulation 1107/70 with the new regulation we have made the system more transparent. as far as the use is concerned, i believe that the aid only compensates for the so-called uncovered costs in terms of infrastructure development and the use of transport infrastructure. we have another problem here, because it is not clear what the external costs really are. i'll give you an example. the theory that it is always better to move freight from road to rail in the interests of environmental protection is not automatically correct. we're discussing noise near airports. we're about to ban night flights. remember when you hear a really beautiful freight train at night, it's loud, it stinks, and the brakes squeak. i mean, we're asking the questions, what are external costs? how do you scientifically record them? and how do you charge it? i've got a lot of work to do. i am glad that we have mentioned this in the report. this is a task which the commission has yet to accomplish. i wish the commissioner luck in getting this done soon.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur on behalf of my group. he was very cooperative in preparing his report. the principle applies to the internal market: aid distorts competition and is therefore inadmissible. my predecessor has pointed this out. exceptions to this rule require a specific justification. in this regulation, the reasoning is given as follows: coordination of inland transport. the first objective of aid in this sector is to ensure fair competition between road, rail and inland waterway transport. this is the only way to optimise the overall european transport system in the long term, especially in the area of freight transport. this is the only way to achieve the much-vaunted intermodal transport chains. in order to make these transport chains as flexible as possible, we want to extend the scope of the regulation to short sea shipping. state resources for the construction, maintenance and distribution of transport routes are not covered by the prohibition of aid if they are available to all users without discrimination. this should apply irrespective of the legal form of the infrastructure manager. this is the only way to equate railways and ports with roads. the commission has already made a number of proposals. aid for the use of transport routes should reflect the different burdens imposed on society by the choice of means of transport. this means that infrastructure and external costs must be included in the aid calculation. the difference between the costs of two modes of transport not borne by the users of each is allocated to the more social and environmentally friendly mode of transport as an aid to make its use cheaper and more attractive. unfortunately, as has already been mentioned, there is no politically legitimate model for calculating these costs at european level. i therefore, after much back and forth and careful consideration, have agreed to the supplementary model which provides for the transfer of transport from road to rail and inland waterway by means of contracts. that is what amendment no 48 expresses, and i ask the house to support it. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on competition are applied in the community. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the aid is notified to the member states. we therefore propose exemptions for terminals which are included in a national or european development plan or which are part of the transeuropean freight network. we also support a de minimis scheme of eur 100 000 over three years. as regards the aid for the use of transport routes, we call for a five-year period and for renewability. overall, the regulation will contribute to a clearer structure in the award of aid for the coordination of inland transport and will help to reduce distortions of competition also between member states .
the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster. this proposal for a regulation on state aid to the inland transport sector develops article 73 of the treaty, which states that aid to transport coordination is compatible with community law. we therefore intend to create a transparent, coherent and clear framework which will allow for no distortions in the market. it is also important that the same rules apply to different modes of inland transport which compete with each other. the commission proposal therefore lays down common criteria for granting exemptions which apply equally to all types of inland transport. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. however, some of them go in a very different direction and therefore we cannot accept them. i'll mention some of them. first, the concept of state aid is a cornerstone of the union's competition policy. according to this concept, any public aid to an undertaking carrying out an economic activity, whatever its legal status, constitutes state aid to which the rules of the treaty apply. neither amendment no 21 nor amendment no 37 can alter this fundamental principle of community law. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the transport of dangerous goods by road. we cannot agree with the proposals put forward, although we share the concern and the need to promote the railway. but, ladies and gentlemen, we shall achieve that if the railways are able to provide a good quality of service and therefore be competitive, and for that i believe that the measures we are putting in place are the best. a key element of the proposal is to create a level playing field, so that there is a level playing field between companies based on the user-pays principle, which takes account of external and infrastructure costs. state aid should therefore be limited to compensating for certain external costs, and all this in a framework of fair competition. aid above these costs and uncontrolled does not give these companies the right incentives to improve efficiency and competitiveness. other amendments propose that aid to transhipment facilities, with combined transport terminals, should be exempted from any notification procedure, as terminals are often operated by private companies and compete with other terminals to attract traffic flows, there is a clear risk of distortion of competition. we cannot therefore accept that they should not be communicated. it has also been proposed that undertakings providing passenger transport services may be eligible for aid to offset external and infrastructure costs. however, aid for passenger services under article 73 is regulated in the commission's public service rules, which propose a comprehensive and appropriate framework on how public authorities can support the provision of inland passenger transport services. the aim of these amendments is therefore ultimately to change this legislation and the commission cannot therefore accept them. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competition' in the context of the directive. the evaluation of external effects is a subject of constant debate, as mr jarzembowski has pointed out. there are now methodologies for such evaluation, but despite the efforts of the commission, member states are very reluctant to agree on common formulas. the commission is not at all reluctant to put forward a proposal in this respect in the future and i would like to thank mr costa once again for the work he has done in his report on this subject. but we cannot in any case make the need to evaluate specific public aid schemes dependent on agreement by the european institutions on common rules. the commission, acting pragmatically and in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, leaves it to the member states to decide how to assess these costs in each individual case, as long as we do not have commonly accepted standards. in view of the arguments put forward, the commission accepts amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 13, 16, 18 (in its second part), 19, 20, 24, 27, 33, 36, 40, 44, 45 and 51. we cannot accept amendments nos 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18 (in their first part), 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34, 35, 37, 38, 39, 42, 43, 46, 47, 48, 49 and 52, which are not in the same spirit as the amendments tabled by the committee on the rules of procedure, the verification of credentials and immunities.

matter to discuss today. it is about combating money laundering, and there is a very close link between money laundering and international crime. international crime - especially organised crime - is no longer worthwhile when money laundering is no longer possible. that is why it has been a concern of this house from the outset to fight money laundering intensively. i recall that in 1995 - when i was rapporteur on this subject for the first time in this house - we called in the report on the commission's report on the application of the first anti-money laundering directive that, because it was not sufficient and only set a minimum standard, the commission should make a new proposal for a second anti-money laundering directive. we have confirmed this a few years later in the report by mr newman - i was then shadow rapporteur for my group. we therefore thank the commission for initiating this legislative procedure. we have tried to complete this legislative procedure as quickly as possible, as was called for at the tampere summit. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this was not possible at the time, because the council could not agree on what it wanted until the summer of last year. we then completed our first reading at the council's request. the negotiations continued. unfortunately, it was not possible to reach agreement on the parliament's and the council's positions until the council's common position was adopted. this is essentially because the council was not led by the ministers of justice and the minister of the interior, but unfortunately by the ministers of finance, who did not approach a number of important issues with the necessary sensitivity. the result is that we now have to bring back 27 amendments from the first reading for second reading. we have to do so because the council has virtually ignored parliament's views. it is therefore a clear mockery that the council's explanatory statement says that parliament's arguments and positions have been taken over in essence! what are the main problems? the core problem is not the question of the prohibition of money laundering. it's been decided a long time ago. in all member states there have been laws for many, many years prohibiting money laundering, by anyone, whether he is a criminal, a lawyer, a banker or whatever. the point is to establish reporting obligations. it is quite clear that the inclusion of new occupational groups in the scope of money laundering is partly problematic because of the obligations of these occupational groups to certain measures. for example, lawyers are bound by confidentiality, confidentiality in the face of what they are told by their clients. this is a fundamental right of clients, a fundamental right of clients, which is also laid down in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which has just been adopted in nice. i can only say that what the council of finance ministers has decided here is far too much and goes far beyond what is compatible with fundamental rights. it was therefore absolutely necessary for the committee on fundamental freedoms to ensure that the amendments in question were tabled in plenary at second reading. i would also point out that the provisions of article 6 (3) in its current version, which relate to an assessment of the legal situation, are interpreted very differently by the respective delegations in the council, but also by the commission, and are in urgent need of clarification. the identification requirements contained in this directive, as currently set out in the common position, are excessively bureaucratic and unusable. for example, they provide that complex identification requirements arise even in a minor legal dispute, even when lawyers and clients are hundreds of kilometres apart. the parliament considers that the aim is to prevent money laundering and that it is therefore sufficient to trigger the identity obligation from a certain threshold and only when involved in financial transactions. the last point is the question of equal treatment. we have the situation that in this common position the different professions are treated in a completely different way, although there are member states where they can work together in a partnership, and it is not conceivable that in the same company the rule x should apply to one of the parties and the stricter rule y to the other. that is why we are calling for a new directive on the protection of workers from the risks of exposure to asbestos. the european parliament will continue to advocate the swift adoption of this directive. but we expect the council to cooperate in the conciliation process and not to obstruct the finance ministers! (applause from the centre)
- mr president, i have to go. money laundering means concealing the origin of money obtained by criminal means so that it can appear to be taken from a legally operating enterprise. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat money laundering, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. the european community adopted very early on a directive on combating money laundering, which has triggered legislation in member states which did not have such legislation. this law was good in its day, but today it needs renovation, like any older building, because nothing is more inventive than criminal intelligence. if the directive were adopted as mr lehne and the committee have drafted it, we would have the most modern, best and strictest anti-money laundering legislation in the world in the european union. there are only two problems with enforcement. the first problem is that there is a certain uncertainty in the house about how to deal with the special relationship, say between lawyer and client, because there is a requirement to report suspicions of money laundering. the proposal which mr lehne and the committee have then developed is a good one. it is a simple and workable proposal. it basically says: when a lawyer provides legal advice, the relationship of trust between client and lawyer is further protected. if he's involved in any form of money transfer - purchases, investments, whatever - then he's no longer covered by this protection and is fully reportable. this is both to protect the relationship of trust and to meet the requirements of the fight against crime. the second problem is the council, and there is no solution for that at present. the council did not accept substantive proposals. the reason may be, as my colleague mr lehne has pointed out, that the finance ministers are responsible, who have little experience of codecision legislation and no experience at all of fighting crime. the only way left for parliament is to follow the path proposed, namely to maintain the amendments at first reading. we will have a consultation procedure. since representatives of the council are present, i say to you, dress warmly for this concert. we will not allow an excellent bill to be destroyed by amateurs in the field of crime prevention! i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the rules of procedure of the european community bar association state: 'it is the essence of the profession of a lawyer that his client confides in him and that he receives other confidential communications. if confidentiality is not guaranteed, no trust can be established. for this reason, professional secrecy is both a fundamental right and a fundamental obligation of lawyers. other this basic obligation, which must be and applies to all members of the legal profession, is also a fundamental right of every person in need of advice, i.e. potentially every individual. we cannot allow another dismantling of fundamental rights, even if it is justified by the alleged need to combat organised crime. we therefore agree with mr lehne on this proposal and will vote in favour of the amendments.
commission. – mr president, this subject rightly commands a lot of attention, both in this parliament and elsewhere. i should like to assure members that these proceedings attract a lot of attention in institutions outside this parliament which are engaged in fighting money laundering. perhaps the money launderers themselves are also following these proceedings with a great deal of interest since it would be a happy outcome of our discussions if their life were to be made more difficult. apart from that, i would first of all like to thank the rapporteur, mr lehne, and also the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights, justice and home affairs, for their sustained efforts to achieve a rapid adoption of this important but highly sensitive proposal. the fight against money laundering, as several members have stressed, is a top political priority and is now an integral part of the campaign against serious and organised crime. international pressure is increasing on third countries and on offshore financial centres considered insufficiently cooperative in this area. at the same time, the european union, which has always been at the forefront of international efforts to fight criminal money, must continue to show the way by developing and refining its internal anti-money laundering defences. that was the reasoning behind the clear calls from this parliament and the member states for a proposal to update and extend the 1991 anti-money laundering directive. the commission believes that the common position adopted unanimously last november represents a reasonable compromise on the question of the criminal activity covered – the matter of the so-called predicate offences – and also on the safeguards for the inclusion of the profession, in particular lawyers, within the scope of the directive. in response to concerns in parliament about cases where the lawyer is defending or representing a client in legal proceedings or helping the client to determine his legal position, i should like to stress that there is no question of any obligation to report suspicions of money laundering. it seems to me that the fundamental human rights mentioned are protected. they will not come into play when this proposal becomes reality. i agree with baroness ludford when she says that in this respect the proposal is a good compromise between protecting fundamental rights when lawyers defend their clients in court or help the clients to determine their legal position, but not when they are participating in preparations leading up to an activity covered by this directive. i would also like to recall that our work is the subject of considerable international attention, for example within g7 or the financial action taskforce (fatf). the international community is looking to the european union to find solutions to those difficult questions. i would now like to turn to the individual amendments in the draft second reading recommendation. amendments nos 1 and 10 deal with predicate offences and would mark a major step back from the ambitious common position. the decision was made to move gradually to the coverage of all serious crime. having agreed on this wide coverage, the commission cannot accept these amendments. numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 13 and 22 deal essentially with the treatment of the professions. the commission is regrettably unable to accept the amendments as worded. in its view, the legal profession constitutes a special case and requires special treatment. the commission, therefore, does not accept the principle of giving all the professions exactly the same treatment as that envisaged for the lawyers and notaries. this relates, for example, to the activities which bring the professions within the scope of this directive. the commission is also reluctant to envisage a member state option to allow all the professions the possibility of reporting their suspicions to a professional body, but it firmly backs this possibility for the legal professions. on the difficult question of advice, the commission continues to believe that financial investment and corporate advice should fall within the scope of the directive as long as it is unrelated to current or potential legal proceedings or to the wish of the client to establish his position under the law. of course, the commission concedes that drawing this line may not always be easy. nevertheless it also insists on this point. i ask members of this parliament what they would think if a lawyer had a suspicion that his client was preparing some money laundering activity? what would members think if that lawyer decided not to report his suspicions, for example, to the bar association of his country? that has nothing to do with human rights; it has everything to do with an efficient campaign against money laundering activities, which is a serious matter. i would like members to keep that in mind. amendments nos 7 and 11 relate to the role of the competent authorities. the commission believes that the text of the common position is clear and satisfactory and so, cannot accept those two amendments. amendment no 9 would extend the definition of financial institutions to include certain market authorities. the commission does not believe that such an inclusion would be appropriate. amendment no 14 would change the coverage of non-financial activities in a way that is unacceptable to the commission. amendments nos 15 and 16 deal with client identification. some remarks were made earlier this evening to the effect that client identification might be unduly cumbersome and bureaucratic. i should like to read out article 3 of the proposal where it says that: "member states shall ensure that the institutions and persons subject to this directive require identification of their customers by means of supporting evidence when entering into business relations". this is not about a client ringing up for a prospectus or something like that: this is entering into business relations. can anyone here imagine that a bank or some other financial institution would enter into business relations without ascertaining the identity of his client? i cannot. if i were to enter into business relations i would want to make very certain that i knew who i was dealing with, where they lived, their nationality and so on. i cannot see at all why that is unduly bureaucratic or cumbersome. the commission therefore believes that the common position in this regard provides the necessary scope for flexibility. amendments nos 17 and 28 – the latter of which reached us today – are concerned with identification where there is no face-to-face contact. the commission is afraid that amendment no 17 would make the text too inflexible with possible negative repercussions for e-commerce. amendment no 28 retains the flexibility sought by the commission, but the precise wording still poses certain problems. therefore the amendment, as it has now been put forward, is regrettably unacceptable. amendment no 18 seeks to amend the exemptions from client identification for certain insurance contracts. in the commission's view, a detailed technical examination of this question would be necessary before these amounts could be revised. amendments nos 19 and 20 deal with identification requirements for casino customers. the commission considers that these amendments do not improve the common position. in the commission's view, amendments nos 21 and 24 breach the basic anti-money laundering rule that the customer about whom a report is made should not be warned. the commission could not accept this breach. amendments nos 23 and 25 amend the provisions of the 1991 directive on suspicious transaction reporting, which have not given rise to any problems in the past and, in the commission's view, do not need to be changed. finally, amendments nos 26 and 27 refer to olaf. in deleting all reference to olaf in the common position, the council invited the commission to make a separate proposal under article 280. the commission is currently preparing this proposal. the commission considers, therefore, these amendments unnecessary.
- thank you, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at noon.

freedoms of citizens. this is the one thing. i now come to the european judicial network in civil and commercial matters. the establishment of a judicial network in criminal matters was decided in 1998. the network operates through national contact points which provide advice to local authorities. the network is now making a decisive contribution to simplifying criminal investigations in the crossborder area, after initial difficulties, which were mainly of a technical and linguistic nature. the commission proposal extends the method of cooperation between national contact points to the field of civil and commercial law. a measure which, in my opinion, was long overdue. i welcome the initiative as a way of simplifying judicial cooperation between member states and, in particular, facilitating the handling of crossborder legal proceedings. the activities of the network are ultimately intended to benefit the citizen, and the improvement of judicial cooperation is only an intermediate objective in order to create an area of law for the citizen. the committee's amendments therefore specify that citizens can apply to the courts and authorities in any other member state justice and to ensure that proceedings are conducted in a timely and reliable manner. i can imagine that this network can also be an accompanying instrument for the implementation of the brussels ii
