the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. i do not want to go into what mr graefe has said about baringdorf, because david byrne will be commenting on that at the end of the debate. i would like to make a statement on the question of the so-called protein gap. the commission was invited by the agriculture council on 4 december last year to analyse the situation on the market for high-protein crops and to draw the appropriate conclusions from this analysis. in addition, the invitation made it clear that any commission proposals had to be in line with the financial perspective agreed in berlin. the european council meeting in nice a few days later gave further details of this commitment and asked the commission to carry out a detailed analysis of the supply and demand of oil and protein crops, in strict compliance with the financial provisions of berlin. the commission has gladly accepted this invitation, has studied the issues raised in depth and has summarized the results in a working paper and a communication to the council and parliament. what's the matter? in 2000, the european union produced about 3 million tonnes of animal meal. of this, about half a million tonnes were exported to third countries and about another half a million tonnes were used for the production of pet food. the remaining 2 million tonnes were used for pig and poultry feed. the council decision of 4 december last year prohibited the use of such animal protein in animal feed for all farmed animals. until then, it was known to be forbidden only to the ruminants. the key question in this matter is whether there is a problem in replacing the waste of these quantities of animal meal with plant protein and how best to do this. in order to estimate the change in demand for feed, however, we must first look at the evolution of meat consumption and production. the analysis in the working paper is based on the assumption that, following the experience of the 1996 bse crisis, beef consumption per capita will only recover over the next three to four years or so. but this should mean an increase in the consumption and also in the production of pigmeat and poultrymeat. there are therefore two factors determining the demand for feed in pig and poultry production - the lack of animal meal on the one hand and the expected increase in production on the other. in order to replace animal meal in pig and poultry feed, soybean meal is the main product to be considered, as are rapeseed and sunflower meal, fodder peas, field beans, sweet lupins, but also cereals, even though the egg protein content of cereals is relatively low. in practice, the composition of feed is determined by the prices of raw materials, their availability and technical constraints. the combined effect of all these variables is difficult to predict, and it is even more difficult to isolate the changes brought about by the ban from the normal market adjustments or the consequences of other policies. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not distorted by the excessive use of the cap. firstly, as the prices of oilseed scrap are relatively higher than those of cereals, the proportion of high-protein feed ingredients will be reduced to the physiologically necessary level. as a result, the total amount of crude protein in animal feed is expected to decrease somewhat compared to recent years, especially 1998 and 1999, when soybean prices were extremely low. secondly, the proportion of cereals in animal feed is likely to increase. although cereals are the main source of energy and less of protein, at an average protein content of 10 to 12%, the 5 million tonnes of cereals fed more than last year will also provide about half a million tonnes of raw protein. the commission has not received any comments from interested parties. the slight decrease in the total quantity used and the additional quantity from cereals is expected to result in a demand of between one and one and a half million tonnes of soya. what options have we considered to close this gap that we expect? first, we examined the possibility of raising the aid rate for oilseeds to eur 74 per tonne, rather than keeping it at the same level as cereals, namely eur 63 per tonne, as decided in agenda 2000. the disadvantage of this option is that it would reinstate the crop-specific aid for oilseeds and would subject production to the ceiling set by the blair house agreement. in addition, this option would require an additional extraction cost of approximately eur 1 270 per tonne of soya-bean equivalent, i.e. six times the extra extraction cost of the soya-bean equivalent currently. the budgetary cost of this option would be approximately eur 475 million per year. secondly, we have examined the possibility of increasing the aid rate for peas, beans and sweet lupins by eur 6. we have chosen the 6 euro rate because such an increase would be covered by the peace clause in the wto. the simulations show that, given the current price ratio between protein crops and cereals, this increase would only lead to a very limited increase in the area under cultivation and, of course, since the entire area under cultivation has to be paid for with this higher support, this would also lead to higher additional expenditure than the price of the additional imported soya. fourthly, we have assessed the impact of the cultivation of protein-rich crops on land which is being set aside. if land set aside were to be used for the production of products which would then compete with cereals and oilseeds on the market, this would have the effect of calling into question the bluebox nature of the area premium for cereals, and would also be the subject of strong international criticism. finally, we have examined the possibility of increasing the maximum guaranteed quantity for green flour and dried fodder in conjunction with a reduction in the aid per tonne. but you all know that dried fodder is primarily used for ruminants, not for pigs and poultry, and our problem is primarily a problem of pig and poultry farming. it is also questionable whether an increase of 10% in the maximum guaranteed quantity would actually lead to an increase in the quantity produced, when we have already established an estimated surplus of 12% in dry fodder in the 2000/2001 marketing year. it is very likely that the increase in the guaranteed quantity would be used mainly to cover existing surpluses. in view of this, there are no convincing reasons from an economic point of view for us to introduce new support measures for protein production or to extend the scope of existing support measures. the availability of soybean meal on the world market is not a problem, on the contrary, the additional demand will only increase current imports by around 3 to 5%. the expansion of soybean production in south america and the united states will bring far more soybean waste to the market than the european union can possibly need. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the financing of the common agricultural policy.

mr president, madam president-in-office of the council, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. at the beginning of the negotiations on the proposal for a regulation on public access to parliament, council and commission documents, the committee on budgetary control considered an opinion on the proposal and i myself drafted the opinion. i would like to repeat the principles which are still valid today. we had highlighted three main points, namely, first, transparency and openness, which are the basic prerequisites for any democratic control. these principles promote the legitimacy, efficiency, accountability and proximity of the administration to the citizen. they also provide protection against arbitrariness and abuse of power. they also help to detect, punish and prevent irregularities and fraud, which have been a particular burden for the commission in the past. the second main point is that the documents of the institutions are in principle made public. the necessary exceptions shall be justified. this is now anchored. in addition, i did not think it was appropriate at the time to draw up a comprehensive catalogue listing existing legal provisions, which would only create uncertainty and conflict. the third main point is the concern of the public to ensure the practical exercise of their rights through a clear register, as is now required, and with the help of the internet, as well as the rapid response to requests for documents and the justification for any rejection of the request, and finally to use the language of the applicant. i could have imagined a coordinating body to facilitate all this. i am pleased to note that the basic conditions are in place, although not yet fully. that is the purpose of the revision. i also believe that the framework agreement must be revised to bring it into line with the demands we are making on the public and on relations between the institutions.

commission. – before i turn to the question of the stabilisation and association agreement, let me place on record our condemnation of the attack on the kosovo foreign border at the weekend in which eight fyrom soldiers were killed. as commission patten said at the weekend, this was an attack against democracy, an attack designed to derail the interparty dialogue that has recently begun in fyrom on interethnic relations, a dialogue which the european union has strongly supported. we continue to stand four square for the values of tolerance and moderation and in support of those who seek to resolve differences through dialogue instead of the bomb and the bullet. that is why the signature of the stabilisation and association agreement between the european union and fyrom which took place in luxembourg on 9 april was such an important event. it is the first such agreement we have signed with a country in the region and it symbolises the strong ties that exist between the union and fyrom. it was signed in the presence of the european union's foreign ministers and representatives of nearly all the parties: opposition government, albanian, macedonian, slav, which are represented in the parliament in skopje. the message was one of unity, unity in the face of the threats to democracy that fyrom has recently faced and continues to face today. unity in a shared belief in fyrom's future as a key member of the european family. the negotiations were launched by the commission on 5 march 2000. thanks to excellent cooperation with the macedonian authorities, the negotiations were concluded within nine months and the agreement was initialled in the margins of the zagreb summit on 24 november. the main elements of the agreement are the establishment of a free trade area between the community and fyrom within a ten-year period after the entry into force of the agreement, the establishment of a political dialogue, provisions on regional cooperation provisions on the freedom of movement of workers, freedom of establishment, supply of services, a commitment by the fyrom authorities to approximate legislation to that of the european community especially in the internal market, cooperation in areas such as justice and home affairs, establishment of a stabilisation and association council that supervises the implementation of the agreement. the agreement makes clear that fyrom is a potential candidate for membership of the european union once it has implemented the agreement and subject to the copenhagen criteria. the interim agreement also signed on 9 april provides for the trade-related provisions of the agreement to enter into force from 1 june 2001, without having to wait for the formal ratification of the agreement by national parliaments. the commission invites the european parliament to give its assent to the agreement and we hope that national parliaments will ratify the agreement as quickly as possible. as honourable members are aware, this is a critical period in fyrom's history. this agreement and parliament's support for it underline the european union's commitment to fyrom's wellbeing and the confidence in our people. that is the context in which the presidency, commissioner patten and the high representative have been working hard in recent weeks to facilitate the dialogue between democratically elected political parties in fyrom, initiated by president trajkovski and which is designed to address legitimate grievances. that hard work will continue, but as with the agreement, while the european union will wish to be as supportive as possible, ultimately the main effort must be made by the people of fyrom and their political leaders. it is they who carry responsibility for their countries future which is why it is so important to press ahead now with the political dialogue. thank you all for your contributions and thank you also to mr swoboda.
commission. – mr president, honourable members, the chernobyl accident in 1986 was a tragedy on a global scale and we continue to feel strongly for the victims this tragedy has caused, both among those involved in the clean-up and plant workers, and among people not directly involved, including innocent children. we also recognise the huge economic burden this accident has put on belarus, russia and ukraine and other countries and the problems for the population in contaminated regions to restore normal living conditions. the consequences of the accident on eu territory were comparatively minor but nevertheless important efforts continue to be made for monitoring levels of radioactivity in the environment and in foodstuffs: controls on the import of foodstuffs were even recently strengthened. the commemoration of this event provides us with an opportunity to reflect upon nuclear safety in the region. on 15 december 2000, ukraine shut down definitively the chernobyl nuclear power plant. the commission welcomed this decision as a major contribution to the improvement of nuclear safety in europe. we also appreciate that by deciding to close the chernobyl plant before the end of 2000, ukraine lived up to the commitment it made under the international agreement signed with the governments of the of the g7 countries and with the european commission. the european union has provided considerable support to ukraine over the last few years in addressing and overcoming the consequences of the chernobyl accident, which had such devastating effects on the population and the environment. over eur 340 million have been granted in assistance today, not taking into account technical assistance provided for other nuclear installations in the ukraine. for chernobyl, important eu support is related to turning the sarcophagus into an environmentally acceptable system and addressing social needs. the commission will soon adopt the formal proposal for a council decision on a second contribution to the chernobyl shelter fund at the ebrd which will then be submitted to the council and to parliament for decision. nuclear safety is a priority for the european union. since the beginning of the political and economic reforms that took place in the former soviet union, the european union has actively assisted the countries of the region in improving the safety of their nuclear installations. the strategy followed by the eu was in line with the g7 multilateral programme of action. this included support for short-term measures for nuclear safety improvements as well as longer-term measures to replace unsafe reactors by alternative energy sources. in the particular case of the candidate countries of central and eastern europe, the phare programme has helped and continues to help improve nuclear safety there as well as to develop economically and environmentally sound energy strategies for the replacement of the less safe nuclear reactors. as requested by the council, the commission has given a high priority to nuclear safety in the accession partnerships and in using pre-accession funds to pursue these priorities. important landmarks are: the agreement to close non-upgradeable units in lithuania, slovakia and bulgaria; the support that the programme has given to the nuclear regulators; the short-term urgent safety improvements made to some reactors; the design and operational improvements in upgradeable reactors and also considerable assistance to tackle the problems related to radioactive waste and spent fuel. the case of the russian federation is particularly important. russia is the only state of the former soviet union involved in all aspects of nuclear power, from uranium mining to plant design, power generation and spent fuel reprocessing. some 15% of electricity in russia is generated by nuclear power. russia's civil nuclear industry is also a major source of employment accounting for approximately 300 000 people in direct jobs. given the limited size of the available eu budget, the large number of operating reactors and the special economic conditions in russia, it would be impossible for the european union to offer russia financial assistance equivalent to that made available to the candidate countries and to ukraine. nonetheless the basic policy orientation is the same: to use the technical and financial resources available to the european union to help the russian federation improve safety levels. with regard to russia, we also pursue an active cooperation in spent fuel and radio active waste management in north-west russia. an enormous quantity of spent fuel from nuclear submarines is stored under very poor conditions. this poses a major threat to the barents sea and the arctic environment. the community is not party to the arctic monitoring and assessment programme, but is nevertheless closely involved in the work related to environmental radioactivity in the arctic. we are at present involved in active negotiations on a specified multilateral agreement, the mnepr, which should allow us to set up and implement a large international effort. to conclude, the commission has undertaken an active policy in assisting our partner states in their efforts to increase nuclear safety. we are committed to continue this policy and hope very much that together we can ensure a secure and safe energy supply consistent with sustainable development and respect for the environment.

and this is particularly true of my group - was to create a stable currency for europe. we now have the report by mr katiforis on the implementation of the stability and growth pact. we must remember what this stability and growth pact demands. it calls for balanced budgets or surpluses in those countries which are still over-indebted. at that time, when we were discussing the stability and growth pact in the context of the maastricht treaty, we were still talking about a net new debt of 3%, which was the entry condition at that time. but today the question is: are we balancing budgets or are we running surpluses? the question is, what's the news? the first message is positive: in euroland - balanced budgets. that is a positive thing. on the other hand, you have to be aware of the risks. on the one hand, we have achieved this objective in a growth phase which we cannot or will not achieve again next year, namely with a growth rate of 3.4%, a fat year in the sense of economic policy. the bible recommends that you save for the lean years in the fat years. secondly, there were the umts licences which have poured money into the coffers of our finance ministers. thirdly, we have to consider that the age pyramid is coming and that we have to take care of the expenses that will come to us in this context. i am convinced that this opportunity has not been sufficiently exploited, that this positive environment has not been sufficiently exploited. i am particularly concerned about the fact that some countries still have very high levels of overall debt, and in some cases a somewhat short-term structure of this debt. we need to see these risks. we must therefore also call for the consolidation efforts which have been initiated and which are impressive in some countries but insufficient in others to be continued. i must also tell you that i am concerned about my home country germany, because our growth is below the average of the eurozone. we have not achieved a balanced budget, although the umts licences have brought considerable financial benefits, particularly in germany. the commission has already made a number of proposals. we can agree with him as he stands now. we are concerned, however, about two amendments which have the same content, namely that investment should be excluded from the calculation of the margins of the stability and growth pact. we also believe that investment is necessary, that budgets must be restructured with a view to more investment, but within the framework of the stability and growth pact. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this.

stage in the history of european integration. twelve sovereign states will exchange their national currencies for a common european currency. the citizens of these 12 member states will henceforth use the same banknotes and coins. it seems appropriate to give a name to this new stage of integration of national economies, characterized by a common market and a common currency, which is probably unique in economic history. we propose to use the term 'european home market' as a synonym for the euro country or the euro zone. the european home market already has a single monetary policy. since the accession to the european economic and monetary union on 1 january 1999, it has been in the hands of the european central bank. the challenge today is to formulate common economic policies appropriate to the european home market. the committee on economic and monetary affairs has proposed, by a large majority, that these economic policies should be based on the principles of the social market economy. the main instrument for the coordination of economic policies at european level is the treaty procedure for the establishment of broad economic policy guidelines. the european parliament has so far played only a minor role in this procedure. i therefore believe that it is urgently necessary to provide for greater involvement of the european parliament in the future. another weakness of the procedure is its lack of flexibility. the recommendations are based on forecasts of economic developments. however, if economic data differ from the forecasts during the implementation expect to see a doubling of the amount of electronic waste in about ten years. the electronic waste is haunting europe, in fields, meadows, forests, ditches and everywhere. it is not only an environmental factor, but also a resource factor, because we all know that computers contain valuable components which should be collected and fed at a regular rate of reuse and recycling. i therefore believe that it is right that this directive should be published. this is particularly important because we have already taken the first steps on the altauto regulation, which differs from the electronic waste regulation in that we have hundreds of thousands of companies involved in the electronic waste regulation. in contrast, the altautoverordnung only has 50 or 60 companies involved. that is why it is very important that we find a common consensus on this directive in this house and also with the commission, because this directive has an impact. and if it has an impact, it must also have a controlling effect. environmental policy cannot be an end in itself, it must have an objective. a goal for the environment, but also for business, because business is part of this society, which is sometimes forgotten in my committee. we work in several categories, because we have, not least, ten different material streams, which have different levels of recycling rates that have to be reached. but first let me say something about the points on which the committee has followed my lead, for example on the question of the entry into force of this directive, which is not due to take place until 2005 or 2006. my children would ask me why i am going to brussels if my results are not available until 2006 or whenever. we have said that after 30 months, when the parliamentary process assume that the commission will follow it. the commission was a little weak on the question of the target: how many kilograms do we want to collect per year? we are basically calling for a ban on disposal. some participants in this discussion, particularly industry, argue that this is a crazy proposal. i'm saying the exact opposite. we have to make it illegal to throw a razor in the garbage can, because that's not where it belongs. although this is very common, many have not yet grasped it. the law of falling unit costs also prohibits us from having any vague quantities in the future. we need to concentrate them to reduce the cost of recycling. that is why we have introduced a ban on disposal and a binding quota of six kilos per head per year, rather than a non-binding quota as proposed by the commission. i think this is a real step in the right direction. we also developed a preference for trade. we all agree that when a retailer sells a product, it must also take it back. but we also know - at least those of us who have worked in a city parliament - that our trade is very tightly confined to the cities and does not have the capacity to build a small, possibly still blast-proof hall to store old tv sets. we propose that the end user can return his device at no cost. but the device doesn't have to automatically land at the trade. the retailers are responsible, but the consumer can also go directly to the general collection point. i think this is a good alternative to protect trade, because if we put a lot of construction on it, it will go green very quickly. but that is precisely where we do not want it to go, because we want to keep our cities attractive. this is an important point which is unfortunately all too often overlooked. we believe that, like the entry into force of the directive, manufacturers' liability should not start five years later, but thirty months after the entry into force of the directive, in conjunction with a voluntary cost allocation for historical equipment. the experts know what historical equipment is: these are devices which are already in circulation, some of them orphaned, and we do not know where they come from, whether the companies are bankrupt or whether some large companies have put them on the market just before christmas to make life difficult for small and mediumsized enterprises. ladies and gentlemen, individual funding for new equipment. of course, there may be exceptions in some areas where this is not possible. but i want to reward those who put in the effort and develop a product that can be recycled ecologically. these are the controls we have. so it's not about punishment, it's about reward. i would also like to make a request to the council sitting before me. i would ask you to take up three children, and my children have a moral responsibility to take a device, a computer, a radio, or whatever, when it's finished, to a certain place and dispose of it properly. i do not think we can have a policy where it is always someone else who is responsible, but never ourselves. the end consumer should be able to return the device to his dealer free of charge, even if he purchases it new. the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. the commission proposal is based on the council's common position on a water framework directive. the common position did not provide for the identification of priority hazardous substances or for the gradual elimination of pollution of waters by dangerous substances. we must emphasize once again: it is parliament's task to ensure that the ospar strategy is integrated. parliament has insisted that this should be a central point of the conciliation procedure. the objective is to gradually eliminate pollution of water by continuously reducing discharges, emissions and releases of priority hazardous substances with the aim of their complete elimination within 20 years. the water directive requires that the identification meet two criteria. the first is to take account of their inherent characteristics and the second is to use existing lists such as international, un, ospar, etc. of the 32 substances identified as priority, the proposal envisages that 11 will be classified as priority hazardous substances, another 11 as priority substances under review and the remaining 10 as regular priority substances. the committee on the environment proposes that the commission should include these 11 substances in the under review list as early as next year. the committee on the environment therefore wants to avoid the commission postponing the decision on whether these 11 substances are priority hazardous or only priority until 2004, when the list of priority substances is to be revised in accordance with article 16 of the water framework directive. the committee on the environment also wants to ensure that article 16 is implemented and that this decision is not put on hold because of industrial or other interests in the classification of substances on the under review list. i think it will be very important for us as the european parliament to put the appropriate pressure on the commission. we must always bear in mind that this report is only a preparatory report and that the water framework directive provides for 20 years to achieve the environmental objectives in the field of water protection. the committee on the environment also wants to have the commps procedure changed. it is to be continuously developed and improved. it is not intended to be limited to certain substances in future. for example, only substances for which data from community monitoring programmes were not available at community level have been used so far. this applies to 60% of pesticides available today, for example. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the task of drawing up a report on the implementation of the directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. many gaps are currently due to the lack of data in the chemicals policy. if we are to successfully protect water against dangerous chemicals, we also need to change our chemicals policy. the commission has now taken steps to do so. so you see, we are trying to reach a mutually agreeable solution with the council and the commission. the main focus of this discussion will be on the classification of the substances included in the under review list. the committee wants to achieve this classification as soon as possible, as i have already said. the commission and the council see a problem of feasibility. i have therefore tried once again as rapporteur to provide a solution in amendment no 27. the proposal is that the measures should not be jeopardised by this under review list which the commission is introducing. that is, i think, our common objective. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. in view of the discussions which have taken place between the council, the commission and parliament, i hope that we have now reached a good compromise which will allow a conclusion at first reading. it is therefore up to the council and the commission to decide whether they accept the vote of parliament so that we can get started here as soon as possible and take real action to protect water.

the council. - mr. speaker, i have to go. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. in late february, albanian extremists seized the village of tanusevci on the border between kosovo and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia (fyrom), which resulted in violent clashes between extremists and the army and police forces of fyrom. in mid-march, unrest spread to the town of tetovo in western fyrom as uniformed men took the villages north of the town and from there fired on the town ruthlessly. fyrom's army launched a motor offensive against the occupied villages that was completed on 1 april. later that month, however, the extremists resumed fighting in villages northwest of the city of kumanovo, and the fighting is still ongoing. it is therefore clear that the risk of outright civil war is imminent and the european union has made great efforts to prevent such a development. the european union reacted almost immediately to the fighting around tanusevci and tetovo by issuing declarations condemning the violent attacks and calling on all parties involved to put an end to the violence immediately. intensive diplomatic activity was initiated in skopje to support the government of fyrom, the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity. the eu presidency at local level established close contacts with the main actors. it called on the government of fyrom to act with restraint against the extremists, and urged the leaders of the main albanian parties to openly distance themselves from and isolate the extremists, and the slavonic-macedonian opposition parties not to take advantage of the situation to whip up nationalist sentiments against the albanian minority. from the outset, a major effort was also made to reach the general public through the media in the country with the union's message of distancing itself from the extremists. now, too, intense shuttle diplomacy was under way. foreign minister kerim was invited to hold discussions with the eu presidency and high representative solana on the occasion of the general affairs council meeting on 19 march. the next day, a polish troika headed with solana to skopje, and at the end of the same week, the troika of foreign ministers with solana went to skopje and pristina to mark their support for the government and their condemnation of the actions of the extremists. the visits resulted, inter alia, in the troika getting the albanian leaders in fyrom and kosovo to sign declarations publicly denouncing the violent methods of the extremists and instead calling on them to put forward their demands in political forums and in accordance with democratic rules of the game. as a further sign of eu support for fyrom's political leadership, president trajkovski was invited to the european council meeting in stockholm on 23 march. he was able to present his view of the vulnerable situation in the country to the entire european council. in order to provide financial support for the policy, a review of the union's assistance to fyrom for the current year was carried out. intensive efforts were made by both the commission and the eu member states to, inter alia, cover the funding gap for the new university with teaching in albanian in tetovo and to try to take rapid action to rebuild destroyed houses in the villages north of tetovo and to try to support other projects that can strengthen the inter-ethnic cohesion in the country. as you all know, on 9 april fyrom was the first country in the western balkans to sign a stabilisation and association agreement with the union after almost a year of negotiations. the agreement is a key step in fyrom's approach to the union, and the signing was also an important symbolic act of eu support to the country. fyrom is now considered as well as the other countries of the western balkans as potential candidates for membership of the union. however, the unrest in fyrom has made it clear that there is a real need to improve the status and rights of the albanian and other minorities in the country. in the context of the signing of the stabilisation and association agreement, the fyrom government launched a reform action plan to accelerate the overall adjustment required by this agreement, but also to intensify inter-ethnic dialogue and strengthen the position of minorities. we regret to say that the actual work on reform has been slow. the only thing that has been achieved so far is to prevent the declaration of martial law, postpone the general census until october and set the date for the new parliamentary elections for 27 january 2002. but above all, after intense negotiations and pressure from the international community, a broad coalition government has been successfully established to serve as the political base and platform for the necessary but difficult decisions that must be taken in the near future. there are, in the council's view, measures which the government should and could implement immediately. these include, firstly, the launch of a third state television channel for minority languages, secondly, the adoption of the long overdue law on the strengthening of local self-government and, thirdly, the ratification of the council of europe's charter on minority languages. in the medium term, and before next year's elections, the government must also implement the necessary constitutional changes to balance the differences between the status of the slav macedonian population and the status of other minorities in the country, as well as take the necessary measures to strengthen the representation of minorities in the administration. today, the troika of union foreign ministers is visiting skopje again to convey this message. foreign minister lindh went directly from this chamber to skopje. the new coalition government will be invited to report on its progress and its further action plan to the general affairs council on 25 and 26 june. in other words, fyrom faces a difficult but necessary reform process. time is short to avoid another civil war. it is important to point out that the primary responsibility lies with the management of fyrom. the union has an important supporting role to play and the council, together with the high representative, ms solana, and not least the presidency at central and local level, intends to continue its support for this process. we also believe that parliament and its political groups have an important role to play. in the period up to the end of june, the coalition government will need support and encouragement, but also pressure, to carry out the necessary reforms while holding together the fragile governing coalition. the council considers it of great value if the parliament's political groups could get in touch with their partners in fyrom and support them through this process, to the extent that this is not already happening. there is still a chance to avoid a full-scale civil war in fyrom. we must make sure that we take advantage of this opportunity.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteurs on behalf of the commission for their excellent work. we are talking about an area which is not only very important for the regions, but also very important for the european budget. the budget for this year, after all, has allocated eur 2.4 billion to the olive oil sector. in this respect, it is of course also a very important area for the audit activities of the european court of auditors. mr casaca has studied the special report of the court of auditors. mr jové peres chaired the debate on the commission proposal. strictly speaking, these two areas are not linked, since the court's special report deals with the measures and aid applied during a transitional period of three years of the scheme prior to the council's decision of 1998, whereas the commission's proposal relates to the measures to be taken from november 2001. first of all, the report by mr casaca. the commission can agree with mr casaca's motion for a resolution on the court of auditors' report on most points. we would like to make a detailed comment on two points. the commission, in its examination of the court of auditors' report in the middle of last year, stated that the improvement of the control system will of course be an important issue in the next reform of the common organization of the market. after a thorough examination of this issue, it became clear that fundamental reform is necessary if significant improvements are to be achieved. in any case, a geographical information system is required. since the conditions for such a reform were not yet in place in 2001, the commission proposed at the end of last year to postpone the date for the reform by two years, citing the crucial importance of the geographical information system. the court's proposals also pointed to further improvements in this area. following very constructive discussions with the member states, these improvements were then made the subject of commission regulation (ec) no 648/2000 at the end of march 2001. the present motion for a resolution expresses surprise at the commission's doubts about the reliability of the statistical data of the international olive council. these doubts, however, are not surprising. they were expressed at every council meeting between 1995 and 1998. the commission has examined the data in question and has discussed the details with the member states on several occasions. the international olive oil council's 1999 statistics had to be revised to bring the data together. this resulted in a 30% reduction in the calculated stocks. it was also found that the national data had a margin of uncertainty of between 10% and 12%. the following is to be said about the report by mr jové peres: the report on the commission proposal for the future common organization of the market in olive oil is divided into two thematic areas: firstly, postponement of the decision on the reform of the olive oil sector for two years until more precise data and a more reliable control system are available, and secondly, the introduction of a new system for the classification of olive oil and the quality strategy for olive oil. the amendments relate to four main issues: market measures and the final reform, the control of the current system, the classification and labelling of olive oil and the activities of the organisations of market operators. i want to answer all these questions. as regards the general market aspects, the commission supports amendment no 2, which points out the need to evaluate the results of the measures during the transitional period. the commission takes note of amendments nos 4, 5 and 9, but cannot formally accept them because they anticipate the decision on the final reform, which the commission intends to leave open at this stage. amendments nos 3, 6 and 26 on automatic private storage, even if the market situation does not require it, cannot be accepted. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 1 and 46 concerning aid for the actual production of oil shale, because they would make controls more difficult. the commission also cannot accept amendment no 27, which seeks to extend production refunds to products which are not subject to international competition with cheap olive oil. the commission is of the opinion that the implementation of amendment no 37, which concerns the prohibition in principle of new plantings of olive groves, and the legal consequences of this would raise major problems in terms of land use. over the years, many provisions have been adopted on control measures. but the remaining problems are related to the marketing structures. the commission has also proposed that the geographical information system, which will be introduced as a condition for granting aid from 2003, should be introduced. the amendments proposed in this connection are already largely incorporated in the commission's regulations. amendments nos 7, 11 and 14 call for greater involvement of the commission and further research. the commission is already working closely with the member states on checks, without overstepping their final competence. in the areas you have mentioned, research programmes have already been funded under the general procedure. amendments nos 8, 10, 22, 23, 24 and 36 concern the improvement of checks at the mills. this is particularly the case with the use of electronic data transmission. the commission regulation (ec) no 2366/98 already legally established the priority control of mills. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to apply the same rules to the various types of waste. in addition, mills must submit their stock records at the end of each month. these have already been compared with the information available on olive oil production and marketing. the proposal for a computer-based system for daily monitoring will be examined. if it proves to be sensible and practicable, the commission could adopt a corresponding regulation. it is important to bear in mind that the computer tools provided for the member states are unfortunately not yet fully operational. as regards classification and labelling in accordance with amendments nos 16, 18 and 45 and 19 and 35, we have taken note of their requests, and in particular of their demand that the place of harvest be considered as the place of origin. however, since these issues fall within the commission's competence, the commission cannot accept that these provisions be incorporated into the basic council regulation. the commission has already proposed that the use of olive oil as an ingredient be banned. these proposals are commercially questionable. the commission therefore considers that the labelling of foodstuffs should be in accordance with directive 2000/13 (ec). the commission is, of course, aware that the olive oil sector is calling for a ban on the marketing of mixtures of olive oil and other fats. the commission cannot, however, ban healthy and properly labelled products for which there is demand, simply to protect the sale of another product. we therefore reject amendments nos 17, 20 and 32. the commission will, however, ensure that appropriate labelling rules are drawn up and, of course, olive oil sold under one of the four compulsory names must remain pure olive oil and must have all the characteristics that distinguish this product. the commission has already proposed that the term 'natural olive oil' be used instead of 'raw olive oil' in amendment no 47 and that the term 'ordinary olive oil' be added to the term 'standard olive oil' in amendment no 48. the commission cannot accept this at the moment, as it prefers to look again for terms which better reflect the ideas of the whole sector. the commission will, however, bring its suggestion to the council's subsequent discussions. amendment no 21 proposes that the new classification should come into force on 1 november 2002, i.e. one year before the date envisaged by the commission. the commission has not yet been able to conclude the necessary implementing measures, the market adjustments and the international negotiations, and therefore cannot accept this proposal. finally, as regards the operators' organisations, the commission supports amendments nos 12 with the somewhat more general formulation of the objectives, 25 with the proposal to include table olives in the current provisions for the quality improvement programmes and 30 subject to legal examination and with the definition of 'recognised inter-branch organisations'. the very specific amendment no 13 could be of interest for measures to be promoted in the environmental programmes, but not for the basic regulation of the sector. as regards the measures for which operators' organisations could receive a grant, the commission is prepared to examine the inclusion of table olives and the guarantee of origin. the commission will, however, have to decide on the details of the possible measures. the various forms of promotion must remain within the harmonised framework applicable to all agricultural products. amendments nos 39, 40 and 43 must therefore be rejected. in order to be approved, an operator organisation must meet certain criteria which are yet to be defined by the commission. the restructuring of the olive oil sector has been less extensive than that of the other sectors, so that new discussions and conditions seem necessary. the commission notes its wish to give priority to producer organisations and inter-branch associations involving producers. however, at the present time, it does not seem to make much sense to restrict the measures which can help to improve the quality and thus the sale of olive oil. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the organisation of operators are applied as soon as possible. this is certainly desirable. however, it will take two years to develop the detailed rules for the sector, the operators' organisations and their programmes, the examination of the programmes, the examination and authorisation of the organisations by the member states and the development of the necessary control instruments. if we rush things, we will jeopardize the success of the quality strategy. the commission cannot therefore accept amendments nos 15, 28, 29, 31, 38, 41, 42 and 44. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. the remaining provisions are mostly within the commission's own competence and will be developed and amended in the coming months in the light of its recommendations.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the challenge facing the commission in preparing the preliminary draft budget for 2002 was to ensure that the rapporteur. the commission is not prepared to accept this. i regret that a number of sessions are being held at the same time, although this is a matter which concerns the whole of parliament. parties are the foundation of democracies. democracy is unthinkable without parties ideally competing for the best concept for the welfare of the state and society. all 15 member states of the european union are now governed by democratic forms of government, i.e. governments of varying party compositions. we have a right to be proud of this as citizens of democratically governed member states and as europeans. many people ask whether we need a european party statute. the european parliament is the only institution of the european union legitimated by direct free elections. the european parliament is also considered to be the cradle of european political parties. the cooperation within the political groups required increasingly close contacts between them and with the home parties. the new international party structures and european parties gradually developed. i would just like to point out that the european people's party has existed since 1976, the party of european socialists since 1992, the european liberal, democratic and reformist party since 1993 and finally the european federation of green parties since 1993. if i am correctly informed, two more european parties have been founded in the meantime, which means that we now have at least six european parties. the political landscape is not very clear. the number of parties represented in national parliaments varies widely between member states. the 626 members of the european parliament come from 130 different national parties. italy has the most parties in the european parliament with 21 parties. these different national parties have joined together in eight groups in the european parliament, in addition to the 14 non-attached parties. the european parliament has been calling for a legal basis for european political parties since the 1980s, based on these different approaches. ten years ago, the european parliament achieved a breakthrough in article 191 with the maastricht treaty, which was unanimously adopted by the governments of the member states. this article reads as follows: 'political parties at european level are important as a factor of integration in the union. they help to build european awareness and to express the political will of the citizens of the union. the treaty of nice extends article 191 to form its own legal basis. the council, acting in accordance with the procedure referred to in article 251, shall lay down the rules applicable to political parties at european level, and in particular the rules on their financing. european parties thus make a valuable and not to be underestimated contribution to european integration. this is a task which no national party can do. to continue this work, european parties, for example, need premises and staff, in other words money. the european parties have so far been supported by their groups in the european parliament. but it is precisely this indirect funding by the political groups that the european court of auditors has criticised for lack of transparency and incorrect use of parliament's funds, and it will not tolerate this any longer. the budget of the european union already provides for the current financial year for line b3-500 with 7 million euro for all parties. this is not a horn as the unfortunate see it. the allocation of funds is also regulated in the regulation. the commission has thankfully submitted a proposal for a regulation in february to lay down the conditions to be met. this includes the presentation of a statute proving that a european party is committed to the principles of democracy, respect for fundamental rights and control of expenditure and revenue enshrined in the treaty on european union. this goes beyond what is required by national party laws. in addition, a european party must prove, inter alia, that it has been successful in elections in at least five member states or that it is represented in the european parliament by members from at least five member states. in addition, there are detailed rules for the implementation of the regulation and for control. european parties are prohibited from using their funds to finance national parties. this prohibition also applies to the financing of electoral campaigns. the constitutional committee has added a number of items in its deliberations, including the reference to the charter of fundamental rights, a definition of the party as a legal entity in order to be able to operate, and further proposals for control, including over donations. i would also like to thank the committee on budgets and the committee on legal affairs and internal market for the good proposals. i would like to add 40 amendments which i would like to classify in three categories: clarification of the text of the regulation, detailed rules and motions rejecting the proposal. you will understand that as rapporteur i cannot support the rejection of the regulation, because it is parliament itself that has been calling for a regulation for a long time. i cannot understand a rejection for another reason. it is suspected of seeking to prevent the transparency of party financing at european level. i cannot recommend detailed rules at this time. this regulation is a transitional solution until we are able to work out comprehensive legislation with the council when the treaty of nice comes into force. we are taking the first step today and unfortunately we can only give an opinion before the council's unanimous decision. it is in the european parliament's interest that the criticism of the european court of auditors be met as quickly as possible by a clean solution. i would like to make one further point: the council was present yesterday and i was given the president-in-office's speech on behalf of the council presidency. i would like to hand it over to the president of parliament. because here the council says it's interested in us coming to a conclusion today if possible. the council is willing to do everything possible to ensure that this dossier is concluded under the swedish presidency. i would therefore like to thank the swedish presidency for its great commitment to trying to make the work of european parties stand on its own feet by giving them legal status and transparent funding. this is a very difficult task which, in the interests of our democracy, we hope will be crowned with success. i hereby turn this speech over to the president of the parliament. the commission has already made a number of proposals. it has been one and a half years since the tampere council decided to set up eurojust as the european coordination centre for law enforcement and prosecution. this is a relatively short period of time when compared with developments in other areas of european policy. we in parliament have welcomed and accompanied this rapid development. according to europol, the establishment of eurojust is another important step towards a more effective fight against organised crossborder crime in europe. the first step in the judicial field, namely the establishment of the european judicial network, has already been a success. for example, with the help of this network, the public prosecutor's office in the german town of celle was able to organise the deployment of an undercover customs investigator in belgium within a few hours, and to carry out an observation in a third country in collaboration with public prosecutors from another country within a few hours. the commission has also been able to provide legal aid to the victims of the violence. however, problems remained, such as in the interpretation of legal aid conventions, criminal and procedural law and in the area of jurisdiction. adding to the difficulties were problems of comprehension due to natural language barriers. eurojust is designed to overcome these obstacles. eurojust has a clearing function. the officials are to draw up legal comparisons, settle bilateral disputes on the application and interpretation of legal assistance conventions, set priorities in the european fight against crime and provide timely follow-up to transnational law enforcement actions. in future, eurojust will also have to be able to prepare and transmit lists of crossborder investigations, act as a registry for information on serious crime and plan, coordinate and implement training and education. eurojust will enable national law enforcement authorities to obtain reliable legal information while overcoming language barriers and resolving transnational disputes. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs gebhardt, for the preparation of the opinion of parliament which is now before us for a vote and for the good cooperation. i would like to add one amendment to your amendments. the judicial network has been a body without a head. if we are to create eurojust as this missing head, we are also required to provide common neural fibres, without which the head and body cannot function. eurojust and the european judicial network must not stand side by side or be in loose contact, but must be linked together as one. this can be done by using the existing contact points of the european judicial network instead of the planned national contact points for eurojust. this is the only way to permanently prevent the need for two systems with the same area of responsibility to be placed side by side. this is one of the points of our proposals. i would ask the council to take them into account in its deliberations. then eurojust will really be a success and will contribute to the security of the people of europe. refugees, human rights institutions, judicial reform and the development of free media. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the encouraging the process and expressing its concerns where appropriate . the commission considers this to be the best way of supporting the efforts of the un. the commission expressly welcomes the premature. as regards the situation in cameroon, i would like to say that the commission is closely following the human rights situation in cameroon and is aware that the country has begun to democratize its society and its institutions. we are also seeing positive developments in the field of human rights and civil liberties. but it is clear that the various actors do not have sufficient knowledge of and respect for these new rights and freedoms. cameroon has ratified the convention against torture and was the subject of a report by the committee against torture submitted in november 2000. in addition, a national committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms has been set up in cameroon, albeit with limited functions. in addition, a regional centre for the promotion of human rights has been set up in cooperation with the united nations. the european community has supported cameroon under the lomé convention by allocating eur 6 million for institutional reform in the field of the rule of law, democratization and respect for human rights. in addition, a programme of assistance in the field of the organisation of the criminal justice system in cameroon was examined. a special allocation from the provisional financial envelope of the 9th european development fund will support judicial reform and the strengthening of good governance in coordination with the bretton woods institutions. specific funding from the 9th european development fund will also be provided to support non-state actors, in particular associations and non-governmental organisations active in the fields of governance, promotion of human rights and strengthening the rule of law. in this context, the commission is pursuing a positive approach based on dialogue, in line with the cotonou agreement. it therefore considers that there is no justification for initiating consultations under article 96 of the cotonou agreement. the situation will be monitored on the ground together with the member states. the government has set up a commission of inquiry, whose findings will be carefully analysed by the commission and the member states. on the last point of this human rights debate, i would like to say that there can be no doubt that freedom of expression and freedom of the press are absolutely constitutive of a democratic society and that freedom of the press and freedom of expression can only be exercised if there is media diversity. where this is not the case, there is either no democracy at all or democracy is in danger. the threats to freedom of the press and of expression throughout the world are one of the saddest chapters in our international work. like parliament, the commission takes the widespread persecution and suppression of freedom of expression and the press very seriously. it starts with the media situation, as some members of this house have described it in relation to russia, and ends with terrorist attacks on journalists, as we heard yesterday from the basque country. i am happy to inform the house, however, that the basque journalist landaburu, the younger brother of the commission's director-general for enlargement, was not a victim of this attack. he's badly injured, but thank god he'll live. but it's a very clear sign that terrorism is targeting journalists, because it's precisely the freedom of the media and freedom of expression that is rightly considered by all extremist organizations around the world as their most serious threat. let me briefly mention that the eu has taken a position on freedom of expression, freedom of religion and freedom of belief at the 57th session of the un commission on human rights. the eu not only expresses its views on the international stage, but also provides practical assistance from the community budget. the european initiative for democracy and human rights, for example, provides substantial funding to support independent media around the world. the assistance training of journalists. a major project in asia and africa, carried out in cooperation with reporters without borders, addresses some of the main risks faced by journalists as identified in awareness-raising campaigns. the support under the european initiative will be continued. the call for proposals of january 2001 explicitly mentions freedom of expression as one of the priorities. trafficking in west and central africa. according to unicef, more than 200,000 children are victims of cross-border trafficking in west and central africa. we call on the governments of these on its measures to reduce poverty in africa. this is the main objective of the cotonou partnership agreement. i would also like to emphasize that the commission is pursuing a strategy to promote food the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. the commission thanks the member for his sympathy with the floods in france. the commission regrets the problems and damage caused by the storms, which were particularly severe in the department of somme in the picardy region. the commission expressed its readiness to use all the measures at its disposal to enable the affected areas to recover and restore their economic viability. these are measures under regional policy, agricultural policy, rural development policy and state aid policy. under regional and rural policy, a large part of the department concerned is eligible for objective 2 of the structural funds for the 2000-2006 programming period. the programme for the picardy region, which has a community contribution of chf 1.7 billion for the period 2000-06, already includes measures to deal with natural disasters. the commission is awaiting proposals from the french authorities and invites them to submit these proposals so that the funds provided for in the programme can be used for the economic rehabilitation of the areas concerned. as far as agricultural policy is concerned, the commission has already taken the initiative to allow producers a great deal of flexibility as regards the eligibility of aid for large-scale farming and for set-aside. the commission also approved certain interpretations of the current legislation by the french authorities. the commission has also taken measures to extend the sowing season beyond 15 june. as regards state aid to the regions concerned, the commission will do everything in its power to ensure that notifications and authorizations of any state aid to remedy the damage caused are dealt with promptly, in compliance with the legal provisions. some members of the house have raised the question of emergency aid for families in the affected areas. the commission regrets that it is not in a position to comply with this request. as you know, there has been no dedicated budget line in the european union budget for disasters and emergency aid in the member states for a number of years, and i do not in itself. it is further complicated by the very heterogeneous national criminal law. definitions and sanctions differ widely, and in the criminal law of several member states the offence of 'trafficking in human beings' does not even exist. the european union has therefore been working for some years to develop a comprehensive approach to combating trafficking in human beings. the palermo protocol, signed at the end of 2000, agreed for the first time on concrete, common definitions. the commission proposal aims to establish, by means of a framework decision, minimum rules on the elements of the offences and minimum maximum penalties. the establishment of a minimum maximum sentence of 6 years and 10 years in aggravated circumstances should be sufficient to include trafficking in human beings in union-wide police and judicial cooperation in the fight against organised crime. i think that the commission's proposal is to be welcomed. i particularly welcome the fact that not only the offence of trafficking in human beings for the purpose of sexual exploitation is covered, but also the offence of trafficking in human beings for the purpose of labour
