commission. - mr president, i will try to answer mr posselt in some detail. first of all, i would point out that the commission is not responsible for the introduction of coins and banknotes. as he knows, banknotes are the responsibility of the central bank and the central banking system, and as far as currencies are concerned, the national authorities are responsible. however, as regards the changeover process, a distinction must be made between activities within the euro area and those outside it. in the euro area it is the central banks and the money factories, or the finance ministries, that have decided the exchange rate plans. outside the euro area, it is basically seen as a commercial activity and left to the market. this means that national banks are not, therefore, involved in the logistics and existing means of distributing the new currency or repatriating the old currency, and must maintain the systems they have traditionally used for these types of operations. however, it is true that there is a concern in the european central bank and in some national banks, specifically in the german central bank, as a result of the enormous amount of deutsche mark abroad to take any action to support this changeover situation in countries outside the euro area. in this connection, the european central bank decided on 14 december to allow the frontloading or pre-feeding in euro of those financial institutions which are branches or subsidiaries of european banks in countries outside the euro area. obviously, if the central bank is working on the possibility of pre-feeding, the first step has been taken so that this type of financial institution can go ahead with the subsequent process of currency exchange. in the former yugoslavia there are three distinct cases: bosnia herzegovina, kosovo and montenegro. in the case of bosnia herzegovina, we are talking about a currency board with a national currency linked to the framework with an exchange rate of 1 to 1. it is true, however, that this currency is specific to bosnia-herzegovina and will not undergo any change in itself. it will no longer have a relationship with the framework, but a fixed relationship with the euro and will be approximately half of the euro, which is the same framework-euro relationship. as far as kosovo is concerned, there is a significant possession of physical currency. it is an economy where currency circulation is based on notes that are not normally from the zone and, especially, from the framework zone. the yugoslav dinar still has legal tender status, but it is also true that the mark is in circulation and has been recognised as a currency that can function, and obviously the circulation of the euro will not change this situation. there is a specific problem of how to change these frames which are circulating on euro coins and banknotes. i have been informed that the german central bank, which was aware of this operation at the time, is considering what solution to adopt in such situations. the problem in montenegro is similar. in november 1999 it decided unilaterally to establish a dual currency system between the framework and a parallel currency; on 1 december the government of montenegro declared the framework the only legal currency in the territory of the republic and, as in kosovo, the commission has no capacity to act and, in our opinion, it will also be up to the german central bank of the federal republic to take the relevant decisions to make other operations than frontloading which, as i said before, will be made with branches or subsidiaries of european banks working in that area.

commission. – the proposal to set up the ‘.eu’ top-level domain was first tabled by the commission last december after public consultation over the whole year. in internet terms, it is a lifetime. european internet users are becoming increasingly impatient to have a ‘.eu’ top-level domain where they can register pan-european names. it is becoming imperative, therefore, that the eu takes the necessary steps to implement ‘.eu’ as soon as possible. in this respect, i am pleased to note the common orientation agreed last week in the council, which was a major step forward. with regard to agreement between the institutions, which would enable implementation of the ‘.eu’ top-level domain soon. i am extremely happy about the high quality discussion we have here today in this plenary. as far as the amendments are concerned, the rapporteurs in particular have proposed a number of amendments, which will significantly improve the text of the regulation. this includes reinforcement of the key principles of internet management, clarification of conformity with the community data protection rules, and more precise definitions relating to the role and the functions of the registry. the commission also welcomes the support given by the rapporteurs to the commission's proposals for an advisory committee. there are also a number of proposed amendments which the commission can accept in principle, subject to further clarification. these include the proposal that the commission would be authorised to levy a management charge on the registry for services provided. if the intention is to ensure that the registry remains cost-neutral to the commission, this is acceptable, although the commission would welcome a clearer reference to avoid any suggestion that a standing charge of any sort is imposed on the registry. with respect to the proposals for a policy advisory board to the registry, the commission agrees that broad consultation with the european internet community will be a prerequisite for the proper functioning of the registry. at the same time, it will be important to clarify how such a body would interact with the commission and the member states committee. the 'first-come-first-served' approach for registrations is supported by the commission, as it is one of the underlying principles for the registration process proposed by the commission. we would, however, point out that this general principle must be subject to the rules and principles adopted as public policies in relation to the registration of the ‘.eu’, just to avoid the problems which have been mentioned by a few speakers tonight. similarly, the commission has no objections to the requirement for registrants to respect a code of conduct, although care needs to be taken to avoid confusion and any suggestion of a priori controls. mr carraro also made comments which i endorse. the commission is fully committed to transparency principles and supports the publication of a call for expression of interest in the official journal, as was also mentioned by mr martin. however, the procedure of publication of the conditions of implementation of the registry and of the policy framework in the official journal may prove a very cumbersome procedure and alternative publication may be more efficient. why not this time a website? when talking about ‘.eu’; why not go to the public on the website? there are however, some proposed amendments which the commission cannot agree with. in relation to the proposed amendments on the preventive measures to be adopted by the member states on the geographical and geo-political basis, i would like to point out that should the member states impose individually such measures to the registry, this could lead to conflicting measures or various incompatible approaches. the issue of geographical and geopolitical names is, however, an important political issue for some member states and is fully recognised by the commission. i am convinced that the compromise which was reached at the council, introducing a new paragraph for article 4.1a may offer an alternative which parliament may wish to consider further. the proposal to require the registry to ensure that companies registering a name are legally established in the community is also problematic. given the automated nature of the registry process, it is not practical for the registry to carry out a priori checks on registrants. apart from questions of technical feasibility, the commission would view such a requirement to be an excessive burden on the registry and an unnecessary barrier to registrants. the proposal that the registry should be obliged to supply information to third parties with a "legitimate interest" is also unacceptable as such to the commission. it is not clear exactly how such a provision could apply, and we suggest that the registry will, in any case, be subject to existing legal provisions for disclosure. there also seems to be a linguistic problem surrounding the concepts of "public policy" and "public order" in the french and english versions. here the commission must reiterate its position that the public authorities must only be involved in those areas of registry policy where matters of genuine interest to the public at large are involved and not in the day-to-day operational decisions of the registry. mr crowley raised the question about ‘.eu’ and i also received an e-mail at the end of june, talking about the creation of 'www.eu' and a welcome to use our services. of course, it was slightly embarrassing, but we must make it clear that, after verification, we are aware of the existence of so-called alternate routes outside the domain-named system; top level domains coordinated by icann and of the recent introduction of the alternative route www.eu by the organisation called 'the universal registry'. the future ‘.eu’ top-level domain will, however, operate within the icann-approved named system, partly because of the need to ensure that most eu users can access addresses under ‘.eu’, but also because the commission supports the principle of a single authoritative rule for the domain-named system. alternate rules operate quite legally within the internet, but have relatively limited visibility and can be difficult to access, because the majority of browsers, quite naturally, point at names servers related to icann-authorised top-level domains. to mr cappato, the commission has just accepted a communication on e-commission and that is a big challenge to guarantee that all the activities of the commission will be online, that we will be able to give access to all citizens, but also in the medium and long-term, to interact with our partners and citizens. of the 40 amendments proposed by the rapporteurs the commission can accept in full amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 16, 17, 19, 21, 22, 25, 26, 28, 31, 35, 38, 39 and 40. the commission can accept, in part successful registry.

- the next item is the report (a5-0232/2001) by mrs niebler, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council decision (com (2000) 407 - c5-0449/2000 - 2000/0187 (cod)) on a regulatory framework for electricity spectrum policy in the european community.
the committee on budgets i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the future of the community. i would like to begin by thanking all of you for your support of my report. we have had a very intensive and fruitful debate on the subject of frequency policy in the committee on industry, and i have received good amendments not only from my colleagues in the committee on industry but also from my colleagues in the committee on transport and the committee on culture, which i was happy to include in my report. the amendments were finally incorporated very well in a compromise which was adopted in committee by 49 votes to 50, with one abstention. the subject of my report is the commission proposal for a decision on a legal framework for radio spectrum policy in the european community. the main aim is to determine which institutions are to take decisions on radio spectrum policy and by what procedure. the proposal expressly does not lay down any substantive requirements for the allocation of frequencies, i.e. it does not specify whether certain frequency bands should be made available for telecommunications, broadcasting, transport or the military, but is limited to institutional and procedural matters. the objective and purpose of the directive is to provide a reliable legal framework on the basis of which harmonisation of spectrum use, allocation procedures and conditions of use are decided at eu level whenever the implementation of union policy objectives requires frequencies. there are two types of questions. the first is to make political and strategic decisions. these policies must then be implemented. in this respect, they are technical implementation measures. we have already seen this distinction between political decisions on the one hand and technical implementation measures on the other hand in the lamfalussy report. the importance and scope of the proposal are evident from several points of view. the use of spectrum is becoming more and more a limited economic asset and a major factor in employment, as its use is increasing rapidly. the allocation of portions of spectrum for uses such as communications, broadcasting, transport, police, military, earth observation, etc. is becoming increasingly complex. strategic decisions must be made to reconcile the needs of commercial users with those of non-commercial users. the value of spectrum has been demonstrated by the results of the umts licensing auctions carried out by member states last year for a narrowly limited part of the spectrum. for example, in germany, the companies were willing to pay 50 billion euros for the area to be used, and in the uk, the auction reportedly raised 38.5 billion euros. the allocation and assignment of frequencies to the different user groups and users must therefore, as is currently the case, be carried out in the most transparent and democratic way possible, whether at member state level, at european level within the framework of cept and now also at eu level when decisions are to be taken on community activities related to frequency. it is basically self-evident that decisions on radio spectrum policy are to be taken at european level by the european parliament and the council. it is usually the task of politicians and in particular of elected representatives to decide on a matter as important to society and the economy as radio spectrum policy. the commission may be entrusted with the practical implementation of these decisions, i.e. with technical implementation. the commission should also be able to draw on the expertise of the cept by requesting it to propose solutions to technical problems, where appropriate. the amendments agreed by 49 out of 50 members in the committee on industry provide for this. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. these are amendments nos 22 and 23, which have been tabled in the plenary. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be given the right to vote in the council. the commission is to be the only body to consult the council on these matters. i cannot support that and therefore i can only urge you not to vote in favour of these amendments. i can, however, recommend the amendments tabled by the eldr group and my own group, which were tabled on legal grounds following a recommendation from the legal service. (applause from the centre)
draft opinion of the consultative committee on culture, youth, education, media and sport. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. mrs niebler has handled a very difficult subject which i had to deal with for the committee on culture with great skill. no one will be able to deny that in the light of technological developments a new legal framework for radio spectrum policy makes sense. but there are certain principles to be observed, because while technology is neutral, its use is not. the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, role in finding a peaceful solution to this conflict. the high representative for the cfsp, javier solana, made several visits to the country from april onwards and met with the political authorities instrument to put pressure on the parties in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. since the first demonstrations, the european union has strongly condemned the violence perpetrated by ethnic particular reforms relating to the law and the protection of minorities. this should also help to isolate the extremists by clearly opening up prospects of hope for all the populations concerned. in this spirit, the european union and the high representative welcomed the agreement reached on 11 may on the formation of a broad coalition government including the leaders of the main democratically elected slav and albanian political parties. it called on them to intensify their efforts to produce rapidly concrete and substantial results on the main issues under discussion. at the european council in gothenburg, the heads of state and government of the european union reaffirmed the need for a peaceful solution to the crisis. this implies, for the political side, the opening of a genuine political dialogue within the coalition of governments on all the issues under discussion, including constitutional reforms. the european council called on the local political forces to produce results as soon as possible. the deadline is the general affairs council on 27 june. on the security front, the european council condemned in very clear terms extremism and the use of violence. he stressed the imperative of reaching a durable ceasefire agreed by the parties, which could require a minimum of direct or indirect contacts between them. in this respect, the european union and nato have a possible role to play as intermediaries or facilitators. the disarmament plan proposed by president trajkovski is the other pillar of the security component. it gives nato a central role in this process, as its possible presence and that of eu observers on the ground are considered by the parties as an essential element of confidence. nato has already made the necessary arrangements to be able to respond. this intervention to disarm the albanian-speaking rebels is, however, subject to specific security conditions which, so far, have not been met by the parties. the conclusion of a lasting ceasefire on the basis of a political agreement to develop a negotiated solution to the crisis is the key element. in this respect, it should be noted that since the beginning of the crisis the european union has maintained close coordination with nato, which takes the form of regular and frequent joint meetings of the atlantic council and the political and security committee, regular liaison between secretariats, and direct contacts between high representative solana and the secretary-general of nato, lord robertson. the two officials also made joint visits to the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, during which a consistent and unambiguous message from the international community was conveyed to the parties. in order to ensure a permanent european union policy in skopje, the european council in gothenburg agreed to the appointment of a special representative of the union in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. the general affairs council of 25 june appointed the former french defence minister, françois léotard, who has been in skopje since thursday 28 june, to this post. mr léotard's mandate includes firstly the establishment and maintenance of contacts with the government of the former yugoslav republic of macedonia and with the parties concerned in the political process. it also provides for the european union to provide advice and support to the ongoing dialogue, close liaison with the representative of the presidency and the commission on the ground, with the heads of mission of the member states and with the european observers. it also provides for establishing and maintaining contacts with other relevant international and regional actors, including nato, the osce and the united nations, with a view of course to ensuring the necessary coordination. it also plans to contribute, where appropriate, to the implementation of any agreements and to follow closely all developments and initiatives in the field of safety in liaison with the competent bodies. the way forward for the belgian presidency has therefore been clearly marked by the decisions and approach adopted by the european union in recent months, by the use of the instruments mentioned, by the considerable commitment of the high representative solana, and by the action taken on the spot by mr léotard. the european union is demonstrating its active commitment to this crisis. this effort to contribute to rapid and tangible progress is also being made in cooperation with other relevant actors, notably the us envoy, mr pardew, and with the international organisations involved on the ground. the new presidency must now continue and encourage the political dialogue in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia with consistency and determination. in this connection, it is to be welcomed that, under the auspices of president trajkovski, an agreement was reached last night to relaunch political dialogue between the political parties of the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. following this agreement, intensive meetings are planned over the next few days. the commission will be presenting a report on the implementation of the new rules on the protection of the environment. at the same time, and in close coordination with nato, the security component will be pursued with the same determination, as the two aspects of the crisis are inseparable and will have to progress in parallel.
commission. – mr president, the situation in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia remains, as the minister has just said, a matter of intense concern to all of us. in the three months since i last discussed this matter with honourable members, there has been a steady deterioration in the security situation, a growing polarisation of political opinion and an exponential rise in the number of refugees and internally displaced persons. the violence in front of the parliament in skopje just over a week ago, without exaggeration, brought matters to the very brink of the abyss. it is welcome that in the last week there has not been a further serious deterioration in the security situation, and it is welcome, as minister michel has just said, that the political dialogue pioneered by president trajkovski has been resumed. i want to pay tribute to the president’s efforts, i want to pay tribute to the president’s calm decency in the face of this crisis. as honourable members will know, the european union has been intensively involved, from the outset, in efforts to contain and extinguish this conflict. all of us who have some responsibility for this region are acutely conscious of the danger that a descent into civil war in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia would pose, not just for the community there, that would be bad enough, but for the region as a whole. working with nato, working with the osce, working with the united states, we will leave no stone unturned in the search for an end to this conflict and an agreed way forward based on dialogue and political settlement. one feature of this crisis, has been the very close cooperation between the relevant international organisations and bodies involved, not drawn from any manual or textbook, but because we know how vital it is that we tackle this problem in a united and coherent fashion. we have not yet succeeded in bringing the conflict to an end, but we are absolutely clear that it is only by working together and working with the democratically elected government in skopje that we will succeed in doing so. the leading role on behalf of the european has, of course, rightly been taken by my friend and colleague, high representative javier solana. he has been to skopje on countless occasions and i have accompanied him on a number of those visits as well as making visits on my own. he has worked, and is working, tirelessly for a peaceful solution, ably supported on the ground in skopje by the outgoing presidency ambassador, mark dickinson, and by the head of the commission delegation, josé pinto texeira. i want to pay a particularly warm tribute to him for his courage and steadfastness and wise advice. a week ago, as the minister has said, the general affairs council appointed mr léotard as the european union’s resident envoy, in skopje, under the authority of mr solana. i met mr léotard last week and promised him the full support of the european commission in his work. we stand ready to do all we can, anywhere and at any time. mr léotard is initially locating himself in the commission’s delegation office in skopje. as honourable members know, in april the former yugoslav republic of macedonia signed a stabilisation and association agreement with the european union. that agreement includes important commitments by the government in skopje about respect for human rights, including the rights of minorities. it is essential that those commitments should be honoured, and we all want to see early results in the inter-ethnic dialogue. that is the only route to a lasting political solution. the european commission is providing very substantial support, eur 42 million under cards in 2001. much of it will specifically help with the implementation of projects which will assist the albanian as well as the macedonian slav community. for example, the eur 5 million we have delivered for the south-east europe albanian language university at tetovo, funds for the census and funds for local government reform and the implementation of small-scale local infrastructure projects, which make a visible difference to people’s lives and communities. we have made it very clear, and i want to repeat this point today, that we will be ready to come forward with substantial assistance for the former yugoslav republic of macedonia as soon as a political agreement is reached between the parties. i hope that all involved will regard that as a serious incentive to work intensively and constructively with mr léotard and mr pardew, the united states representative, in the coming days. let it also be an incentive to extend the cease-fire and to halt the military activities on both sides which are costing so much politically, financially and in human lives. i just want to underline this point. this parliament would not take kindly to proposals from the commission, or from anyone, to spend more money supporting reconstruction and development, supporting the budget in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, if at the same time money was being spent, which frankly no one really has, on more bombs and more rockets, and if there was not a clear prospect of a political settlement and continuing cease-fire. when the foreign minister of fyrom reports to the political and security committee of the council in brussels on friday, she will be in a position to speak about substantial progress, because the alternative is frankly too awful to contemplate. it is not too late to avoid catastrophe, but it requires the courage of every citizen of the former yugoslav republic of macedonia to pull back from the brink. it requires those with influence in kosovo over the rebels to pull them back from the brink and it requires the continued stand for moderation exemplified by the government in tirana to whom i pay unreserved tribute for their contribution. there cannot be a solely military solution. there has to be a political settlement and it cannot come soon enough.

counsel. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour for me to address this house as i begin this presidency. human rights are, as i think you know, a subject of concern which carries a large part of my personal political commitment. i shall therefore take this happy opportunity to tell you how the presidency intends to promote in practice the universal values on which our union is founded. i would like to take this opportunity to express, as president, the need to defend these values first at home, but also throughout the world. the european union is barely over forty years old. i mean, she's still very young. in reality, europe still has its whole future ahead of it. i am convinced that the future of europe will be determined primarily by its ability to preserve and spread its humanistic values. the european model is based more than ever on three fundamental values: freedom, progress and equality. these values have proved very fruitful whenever they have been combined to initiate dialogue and exchange. unfortunately, too often they have been misused and used for sectarian and sometimes totalitarian purposes. freedom is an ideal that is never satisfied. the history of europe could be written as a long struggle against any arbitrary power. the advancement of freedoms, civil, political and social rights, the assertion of the people, democracy and the rule of law remain the most motivating objectives of european integration. these objectives have been largely and substantially achieved. and yet, we know that there are still many struggles to be fought, even in our old democracies, to achieve them in their fullness, and nothing is ever achieved. freedom can also infringe the rights of minorities or the rights of the weakest. when freedom justifies selfishness, it always leads to intolerance and exclusion. among the freedoms, there is one to which the union is particularly attached, and that is freedom of expression. freedom of the media remains the guarantee of the existence of a public debate which is indispensable to democracy and which allows citizens to exercise control at least as strong as that of our parliaments. this freedom of the press is still violated where regimes do not feel blameless enough to dare to face criticism, where lying is the only way for a power to survive. the protection and promotion of media freedom is the primary responsibility of the state. it is the public authority's responsibility to guarantee everyone's freedom of expression. which makes it all the more difficult to win that freedom, and sometimes to preserve it. let us admit that even democratic governments are sometimes tempted to curtail this right and are often reluctant to accept controversy and criticism. it is equally intolerable that democracy should be held hostage by the press. freedom of the press is a vital, existential right for the rule of law. this right also corresponds to a duty, that of honest information, which seeks to explain or to learn, or to convince, not to mislead. that is why freedom of expression must be a wake-up call to the problems facing the opinion press. the second european ideal is progress. this value has given a powerful impetus to the development of science, technology and economics in the service of man. this ideal has enabled the european project to move forward with confidence, and no doubt irreversibly. it is he who is the origin of the rigorous process of thought and action. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. when uncontrolled progress takes on its own dynamic, it generates fear and confusion. the third ideal: equality. equality is a great lever in europe. it is in its name that the european countries try to ensure equal rights, the equitable distribution of the fruits of economic activity and the democratic representation of everyone's interests. in western europe, it has led to the adoption of extensive social legislation which fosters the concept of equal opportunities and justice. in communist europe, the extreme equality movement has sacrificed the right to personal identity on the altar of collectivism. freedom, progress, equality are not just theoretical values. they are at the heart of the european construction. they give it its most specific and strongest meaning. these values, which are embodied in the founding texts of the union, permanently anchor humanism in european identity. last year, the 15 eu member states adopted this key text of the charter of fundamental rights. this charter sets out the rights and duties of european citizens, both towards each other and towards the human community and future generations. the notions of freedom, progress and equality are prominently featured in the preamble to the charter. the question now arises as to whether this text will become a genuine european constitution. the fact that a contradictory debate can animate reflection on this question must be seen as a way for europe to ask itself about its own future. it is also an opportunity to offer citizens the opportunity to take a stand, because to take a stand is already to taste freedom. it's allowing him to re-appropriate his power of free choice. but too often the citizen feels that he has lost this right to various powers, which are becoming less and less identified, such as technocracy. article 7 of the treaty provides for a mechanism to respond to serious and persistent breaches of european values. in a united europe, the respect of fundamental values by each member state has become the concern of all. each country is now concerned with what is happening in the whole of europe. if it is to convince third countries of the validity of its humanist values, the european union must set an example before it teaches lessons. the core values are not only in the texts, they are also put into practice in the policies of the european union. a prime example of the application of european values in everyday life is the enlargement policy of the union. as you know, the enlargement of the european union is a huge challenge. i think that our public opinion is wrongly concerned about the imbalance between the development of the member states of the union and that of the applicant countries. the consequences for security, social rights, immigration and agriculture, for example, cannot be overlooked. if we are not careful, this enlargement could lead to the end of the progress that has been patiently achieved over the last 40 years. why, then, some might ask, take the risk? the answer lies in the generous political audacity of the founders of europe who enshrined the notion of international solidarity alongside the national interest. furthermore, enlarging the european union is a historic task, one of reuniting peoples who have been separated by history for too long. these two good reasons, which were the basis of the most beautiful political idea of the 20th century, are still very much alive. enlarging the european union is in keeping with the open and generous vision of the original european project. the second example concerns the foreign policy of the european union. in the last two years, this european policy has undergone a spectacular development. at the end of the belgian presidency, the european union should be declared capable of managing international crises, which means clearly that it would be able to mount humanitarian missions, evacuation missions and peacekeeping missions to stabilise regional conflicts. beyond the defence of its economic and commercial interests, europe must also ensure that its values are defended through concrete action. europe cannot remain passive in the face of the intolerable. freedom, progress and equality are only possible in a context of peace. europe exists because of peace. i would even dare to say that europe is peace. the reconciliation of former enemies, the unification of different countries by peaceful means, is a political innovation which is an example for third countries. it is not for nothing that the need for europeanization of the balkans is often mentioned. the process is already under way. these are the values on which our great european enterprise is based. to question these values is also to discover one's european identity.
commission. – mr president, may i start by commending mr wuori for a challenging and focussed report, which has attracted overwhelming support from this parliament. i also enjoyed listening to the minister’s speech: parliament knows his personal commitment to the enhancement and protection of human rights. the year since parliament’s last report on human rights has been punctuated with important institutional and policy developments. the reform of external aid has taken root and europe aid is tackling the avalanche of responses to the two recent calls for proposals on human rights, some 1 400 proposals for a total of eur 1.6 billion. the charter of fundamental rights has been solemnly proclaimed and it is an important element in the european union’s efforts to ensure coherence between internal and external human rights policy. the adoption by the council of guidelines on torture has provided a clear framework for policy and action in that area and the communication on human rights and democratisation, which was long in gestation, but strong in delivery, was adopted on 8 may and it sets out a clear strategy for the short term and the medium term. we now have to focus on the implementation of its proposals. it is evident from mr wuori’s report that parliament and commission are thinking along similar lines when it comes to human rights. this is my first opportunity to present the communication to parliament in a plenary session. boiled down to its essence, the communication seeks to promote coherent and consistent human rights policies in the european union’s relations with third countries, to maximise the leverage afforded by political dialogue, trade and external assistance, and to set out a more strategic and focussed approach for the european initiative, for democracy and human rights. several issues raised in mr wuori’s report dovetail with points in our communication. for example, we make clear that parliament will be consulted on the programming of the european initiative for democracy and human rights for 2002 and the years beyond. on reporting and evaluation, the commission is committed to publishing regular reports on the activities that we fund. the latest report was released on 22 may and it provides a thorough analysis of projects supported under the 2000 budget. the promotion of human rights is, as the honourable member’s report makes clear, an indispensable element in the prevention of conflict. the communication on conflict prevention issued in april confirms the high priority given by the commission to developing the union’s capacities. more systematic use of country-strategy papers will help to ensure the cogent use of community instruments to address both the root causes of conflict and other human rights problems. as regards the rapid reaction mechanism, the commission will provide parliament in due course with an evaluation of activities undertaken. the central theme of the honourable member’s report, freedom of expression, finds an echo in the communication, which makes clear that this will fall under the first of the four priority areas for the european initiative for democracy and human rights programme for 2002 and beyond, and that theme is indeed of pivotal importance. the right to express one’s opinions without fear or consequence is to borrow a phrase from the great english judge lord devlin, –a lamp that shows that freedom lives.’ when state authorities start to close down newspapers, when they start to harass or imprison journalists, it is a sure sign that human rights and freedom are crumbling. the european union makes its views plain on this subject in its contacts with third countries, and in international fora such as the un commission on human rights. moreover, the rhetoric is matched with hard support. under the european initiative alone, over eur 5.4 million was allocated in 2000 to projects in support of freedom of expression, free media and the protection and training of journalists. a large project in africa and asia undertaken by ‘rapporteurs sans frontières’, offers a good example. fact-finding on imprisoned journalists, and the provision of practical assistance to journalists and their families, is coupled with education and media campaigns. i would like to look now at another thread running through the honourable member’s report, the relationship between our two institutions. parliament has cultivated a high profile with respect to human rights. as i mentioned when i presented the communication to the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy on 15 may, the reports and resolutions of parliament on the commission’s previous performance on human rights were of great use in drawing up the communication. the commission is keen to reinforce its dialogue on human rights with parliament, and this is reflected in the consultations which will take place on programming the european initiative in 2002. in cooperation with the presidency, the commission would also seek to ensure that the timing and location of the human rights discussion forum with non-governmental organisations, and with others, takes full account of the need for systematic participation by members of this house. moreover, we want to enhance the potential of the forum. we will begin by evaluating the events held so far, in consultation with parliament, the council and ngos. on human rights clauses, i note parliament’s concern about the lack of implementing rules on suspension in many agreements. as we know, the most recent version of the essential elements clause, as contained, for example, in the cotonou agreement, makes provision for a consultation procedure prior to any suspension of an agreement. it is state-of-the-art in that respect, but changes to existing agreements would require individual renegotiations with partners, which is an undoubtedly lengthy process. nonetheless, the commission stands ready to discuss the future shape and use of the clause, an issue that i raised at the informal foreign ministers’ meeting last month, and it will continue to attach importance to parliament’s views. a final word on police and security equipment, a point which is not directly addressed to the commission in the report. the commission intends to submit to the council before the end of summer a proposal for controlling and, where necessary, prohibiting exports of equipment that may be used for the purposes of torture and cruel inhumane or degrading treatment. the commission will examine with member states whether there is a need for community action in respect of manufacturing, promoting or using such equipment. i know this is of concern both to members and to ngos such as amnesty international, and i am glad that we are close to taking such a significant step. i congratulate the honourable member once again on the excellent report and look forward to working with him and with the house in taking forward our shared concern in human rights.
the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. i would like to join commission. – i very much welcome the fact that all the european union institutions are united in working towards the abolition of the death penalty and am pleased that once again the european parliament is in the forefront of these efforts. as the house knows, both the council and the commission have made abolition a priority. the council is pursuing implementation of the european union guidelines where the death penalty still exists. the european union calls for its use to be progressively restricted and insists that it be carried out according to minimum standards. the european union also presses, where relevant, for moratoria to be introduced. it might just be helpful if i set out in detail the guidelines of our policy towards third countries on the death penalty. those guidelines stipulate that the subject should be mentioned, if appropriate, during political dialogue with those countries. it was mentioned, for example, in our recent meetings with the united states. the guidelines stipulate that démarches should be made when there is a threat that the death penalty will be restored or that an official or de facto moratorium will cease. the guidelines make it clear that supportive démarches or public statements should be made when a country takes steps towards abolition. we indicate, in the guidelines, that individual démarches should be made when it seems that minimum standards in this area are being violated. for example: when there is a lack of legal safeguards; when the death penalty is to be applied to those who were minors when the offence was committed; to pregnant women or to the mother of a young child or to the mentally ill and the application of the death penalty for non-violent crimes or offences such as crimes of opinion and conscience and financial crimes. in the recently adopted communication on human rights and democratisation, the commission identified the campaign for the abolition of the death penalty as one of the four priorities that we would pursue over coming years under the european initiative for democracy and human rights. we have already funded a number of projects in this area by mobilising public opinion worldwide against capital punishment. we hope to consign the death penalty to the history books as a form of punishment which has no place in the modern world. to take an example, and i follow what an honourable member said a moment or two ago, i find it almost impossible to believe that i am reading a newspaper published in 2001 when i read reports that women in iran are once again being sentenced to death by stoning. i agree with honourable members that the first world congress to abolish the death penalty in strasbourg on 21 and 22 june 2001 was a very important gathering. while i was not able to attend in person, the commission services represented me and delivered an address. i understand that the presence of those individuals who came to the congress to testify about the years they had spent awaiting execution before being declared innocent was particularly moving and particularly valuable. also, i believe that the congress proved useful in highlighting both the difficult problems related to the abolition of the death penalty and in gathering suggestions of a number of innovative policy strategies, in particular, from the american participants. it was interesting to hear the honourable member's remarks about recent converts on this issue. i also take this opportunity to thank the president for her initiative to invite a number of presidents of parliaments as well as the congress participants to attend the solemn appeal that took place in the european parliament in strasbourg on 22 june last. this was an important part of the congress highlighting the important role of parliaments in eliminating the death penalty. the strasbourg appeal that was adopted at this event will serve as an important reference document for our continued efforts to abolish the death penalty. i am sure that as long as it is required, this parliament along with the other european institutions, will continue to give this issue the priority and the importance which it deserves. commission. – the decision on which country will stage the 2008 olympics will be decided by the international olympic committee when it meets in moscow on 13 july. i have some knowledge of the way the international olympic committee does its work. i appeared in front of it in 1990 in support of the magnificent bid by manchester to host the olympic games. it was one of the examples in my life of tilting at windmills, but i know a little about how the ioc works. the european union, as a whole and the commission do not take a position on whether the games should be held in china or elsewhere. the decision is one for the international olympic committee, though i understand why honourable members have such strong views on the subject. i do not have to explain to parliament that i share the concerns which have been expressed about the human rights situation in china – and i will return to that in a moment. just as i have always been doubtful about mixing the pursuit of trade objectives and the pursuit of human rights objectives, however, so i have doubts about mixing up sport and human rights. my worry on both scores is that very often you do not achieve your objective, you simply muddle your objectives. when i was the governor of hong kong, much involved in the debate and the argument about human rights and democratisation, i still every year went to washington to plead for china to have most-favoured-nation status and i certainly did not criticise the earlier bid by china to host the olympic games. i concede that at the margins, it can be helpful occasionally to take measures in regard to sport. for example, one could not argue that taking those measures in relation to south africa during the years of apartheid was anything other than helpful, largely because of the emphasis which the white community in south africa placed on sporting links. if you take the issue of the olympics, while i accept that there are some horrendous examples of the olympic spirit being abused – and one speaker mentioned the 1936 olympics in which my late father-in-law ran – one should also take account of the olympic games in seoul. you would not find many democrats in seoul who argued that holding the olympic games there had set back the pursuit of democracy and human rights, rather the reverse, so the argument is perhaps a little more complex than some honourable members suggested. while these are matters of rather subjective judgment, when i argue this case, i am not doing so out of – to borrow a phrase from the honourable member – supine complicity. i am doing so out of moderate, but not complete, conviction. if beijing is selected to host the games, it will require certainly both welcome and necessary steps on the part of the chinese authorities if they are to have any chance at all of matching the outstanding performance as host, of sydney last year. for example, it would be inconceivable that a country hosting the olympics would or could prevent both its citizens and its visitors from having access to the news on the internet about the games themselves. on a visit i paid to china a few weeks ago, an extremely interesting visit, it was curious that both the bbc and cnn website were inaccessible. i do not think that would be possible at the time of an olympic games. i have spoken on many occasions to this parliament about the european union/china human rights dialogue. i accept what the honourable member said, that we have to be very careful that the dialogue actually produces some progress and it does not turn into, as he said, an act of complicity with the abuse of human rights. our dialogue with china is undoubtedly the most complex and multi-faceted dialogue on human rights which we have with any country, as befits discussions with a country in which so many abuses continue, alas, to occur. the european union is constantly seeking to work with china to make it more effective and to have more tangible impact on the human rights situation on the ground. we are encouraging and supporting china in early ratification and implementation of the un covenants and we continue to urge cooperation with the un high commissioner for human rights. we welcome the memorandum of understanding, which china has signed with mary robinson, but we hope that they will now implement it. within this dialogue, we will continue to press for action in the areas of most concern to us, such as the repression of political dissidents, the suppression of religious freedom, the appalling and excessive use of the death penalty under the strike-hard campaign, the treatment of ethnic minorities, including those in tibet, and the arbitrary detention conditions. i also raised during my last visit to china, the reports of torture and ill-treatment of the followers of the falun gong movement and there are other issues which we must address. there is increasing concern about the abuse of psychiatry in dealing with dissidents and members of religious groups in china. i commend to the house's attention an article written recently in the asian wall street journal, which summarised the academic research of robin monroe, a very distinguished china-watcher, the author of probably the best book on tiananmen, black hands of beijing. i recommend it to the house. i share parliament's concerns for the environment in beijing and in china more widely and for the effects which preparation for the games could have on the city. during my visit in may, i met some of the handful of genuine chinese non-governmental organisations working on environmental issues. i was left with the strong impression that china will find it impossible to meet the objectives it has set itself for environmental protection without the assistance of a civil society, which has mobilised itself voluntarily. a relaxation of the rules governing the establishment and operation of genuine grassroots ngos is essential, so as to harness the energy and commitment of a population of over a billion. the same is true for any country or city which hosts the olympic games. sydney's success derived from the whole-hearted commitment of its citizens to hosting the games and making them a success in the eyes of the world. any country which hosts the olympic games will have a problem if it does not enlist the support of its citizens. i do not believe that i am being naive. i know the appalling problems that exist, but it seems to me at the very least inconceivable that any country like china, although there is no country really like china, but any country with the sort of authoritarian repressive government that china has, would find it impossible to host the olympic games without that having a considerable impact on the development of civil society within that country. - mr president, the un convention on the rights of the child has so far been adopted by 191 countries. the aim of the un special session in new york in september must be to ensure that this convention is not only ratified by all countries but also implemented thereafter. the fight against child labour is an essential element. too often, children are seen as an investment in the survival of the family. parents who have never had an education like their children are bound to fall into the poverty and debt trap. children who are exposed to the most intense physical stress from an early age lose not only their ease and identity but often their entire childhood. i've seen it happen that kids can't live past 14. unicef estimates that 200,000 children are sold into plantation work in west and central africa each year. worldwide, 2 million children - mostly girls - between the ages of 5 and 15 are exploited by sex traffickers. but there is reason for hope. i have seen positive examples on the ground in india and nepal. the rugmark foundation, for example, provides a qualified education for children whose parents work in carpet factories. this ngo was founded jointly by german development aid organizations and carpet manufacturers. these carpets rightly bear the quality label "not made by children". 10% of indian exporters have now successfully applied for a rugmark licence. this is a first step in the right direction. but sustainable success will only come when consumers' awareness changes and they demand these products. another example that gives hope comes from brazil. 11 million children from the poorest families have been introduced into school on a tuition basis. this special programme is designed to last for ten years and, with 850 million euros per year, children will finally be able to benefit from paid education. examples such as these few i have been able to give should be taught in schools all over the world for the sake of children! the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the idea of creating a european society that follows the same supranational rules in all member states is almost as old as the european union itself. the societas europaea - se - is regarded as the flagship of european company law. the scientific foundations were laid in the late 1950s. in 1970 the commission proposed a statute for an se in the form of a regulation. it contained a uniform law governing all its facets. in 1989 the commission presented a completely new proposal for a regulation. social and labour law, taxation and competition law, industrial property protection law, insolvency law and company constitutional law were excluded. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. the 1989 proposal was based on what is now article 95. this meant co-decision. the nice proposals are based on article 308, so parliament is only consulted. the legal basis for the regulation is article 95 as well as article 308. in the interests of democratic legitimacy and in accordance with the constant case law of the court of justice, the legal basis to be chosen in such a case should be the one which grants parliament greater powers of participation. parliament therefore reserves the right to seek a procedure before the court of justice to review the legal basis once the council has adopted it. the regulation: articles 2 and 3 provide for different types of incorporation. the capital must be at least eur 120 000. the laws of the member states on companies have two different systems for administering public limited liability companies. the monist system, as in the uk, has only one administrative body. the dualist system applicable in germany, for example, provides for a supervisory body and a management body. the european union now requires that both systems be available for free choice in each country. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to adopt the same rules for the transfer of companies and the transfer of their registered offices. in the case of an se, the transfer of its registered office does not lead to the dissolution of the company or the creation of a new legal person. the convergence of formerly separate markets requires that we finally create legal forms of organization that correspond to the new situation in europe. however, the se's structure shows considerable weaknesses. the se will be different from one member state to another. it will not be a european type se, but one with, for example, french, spanish or german characteristics. there's more to it. within a single member state, too, a variety of ses will be formed, ranging from social characteristics to co-determination. i think it is absolutely essential that the regulation should be accompanied by additional tax provisions. the reality of the se will of course also be determined by tax law. in this context, a number of amendments tabled by the eldr group are to be welcomed. i am therefore in favour of sending the se on her maiden voyage. then it will show where it needs repairs so that it can one day be built into the expected flagship!

by the heads of state or government is more than a negotiating roadmap. it is essentially a self-imposed commitment by the 15 member states to find common positions within certain time limits, even in areas where there is a wide divergence of interests. it also tells the candidates that their efforts are worthwhile and that nothing is put on the back burner. after almost a year, we can say that the nice strategy has given the candidates enormous motivation and that the adoption of community law is proceeding more quickly and smoothly. at the same time, the candidates have shown more flexibility in adjusting their positions, allowing real breakthroughs to be achieved in the negotiations. the treatment of the subject of the free movement of workers is an instructive example of this. the timeframe for the first accessions was then clearly defined in gothenburg. it came at the right time. on the one hand, the progress made in the negotiations has made it possible to define the target for the candidate countries which are sufficiently prepared, and on the other hand, the decision taken in gothenburg gives the parliaments and governments of the candidate countries the political back-wind they need to mobilise all their forces and to counter the existing doubters. the idea of using the 2004 european elections as a reference point for accession was born here in the european parliament a year ago. we reached agreement on this in our debate last year. i am very pleased that we have succeeded in actually implementing this policy of the european parliament in relation to the nice and gothenburg councils. i believe that it was a wise decision not to set specific accession dates for individual countries or define accession groups in gothenburg. the basic principles of the process - namely individual merit, differentiation and the chance to catch up - work. if we adhere to these principles, we will have a natural, real accession scenario, justified only by the outcome of the negotiations. the commission will remain firmly committed to this line. i say this also to counter the notion that in the end there will be purely political decisions, political in the bad sense of the word. the commission will propose the conclusion of an accession treaty for each applicant only after it is satisfied that the applicant is sufficiently prepared and meets all the conditions. i shall therefore not speculate today on how many and which new members will be represented in the next european parliament. i can only say that today, out of the 12 countries with which we are negotiating, 10 have decided to use the gothenburg window. it would be a serious breach of trust if we now said to individual candidates: 'you are definitely in' or 'you will definitely have to wait a little longer'. we must therefore prepare ourselves internally for the possibility that we will have to accept an initial group of up to 10 applicants. this is more dramatic than it sounds, conceivable that countries which have completed fewer chapters than others may nevertheless have made more progress in preparation.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. the european parliament has set up a special committee to investigate whether there is a system of interception of communications, operated by american intelligence, which has the following characteristics: it operates globally, with the ability to intercept every phone call, every fax, every e-mail in europe. it is run by a group of countries, including the uk, which is a member of the eu, and it is primarily used for economic espionage at the end of the cold war. this system is allegedly codenamed echelon. this, mr president, was a difficult task of enlightenment, because the european parliament has no access - under any circumstances - to files of eu member states' intelligence services, and certainly no access to detailed information on the activities of american services. nevertheless, after a year of careful research, we can say to the house without any doubt what follows: firstly, there is no defence system operated by any intelligence service of any state which can intercept any communication in europe. this claim must be relegated to the realm of creative journalism! the fact that it is unfortunately found in a study commissioned by the european parliament, which has been awarded a kind of quality seal, does not make this statement any closer to reality. it's not about what you believe. telecommunications obey the laws of physics, and where there is no access to communication media, there is no eavesdropping, and there is no special magic physics for intelligence! secondly, there is a very good system of interception which has the following characteristics: it operates globally and is implemented with a listening network of the so-called uk-usa states - that is america, the uk, canada, australia and new zealand. this is not a random mix, this defense alliance has its historical roots in the second world war. it has access essentially only to intercontinental communications, which are either transmitted by communications satellites or run by underwater cables that land in the above-mentioned countries. communication within europe is therefore hardly affected, while communication to african countries, arab countries and latin america is very much affected. we don't know how many messages can be intercepted on radio traffic in their vicinity, but it's clear that it's not the main part of the defense business. unlike police surveillance, which is always directed at a single person or a well-defined group of people, the surveillance system we are dealing with works differently. it intercepts any communications it can access and feeds them to a computer search engine. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be consulted on the draft directive. so the system works like a vacuum cleaner, and the intelligence agencies set the filter. technically, it's called strategic telecommunications control. the search engine can collect phone numbers, voices of top targets, the content of e-mails and of typed telefax messages. handwritten faxes or spoken messages cannot be detected by this search engine for the foreseeable future, and are therefore not accessible to intelligence analysis. otherwise, we have indications that the system is code-named echelon. it doesn't matter what it's called. it can be called rumplestiltskin, but we care what it does! these are the findings, and i'd like to add that we're not just saying that. we can prove it with a chain of evidence strong enough to stand up to a jury trial. if you want to know more, you can't miss the report. i would like to make one point: if we had written something wrong, you can be sure that the intelligence services of the countries mentioned would have been happy to publicly dismantle us! but you didn't, and that speaks for itself. how do we evaluate these findings? one of the criteria for evaluating this must be: what are our own services actually doing? it is not the only criterion, but it is also one if you want to have an honest debate. most intelligence services in the majority of eu countries use strategic remote sensing. only belgium, greece, ireland, austria, portugal and luxembourg do not use this technique. secondly, the purpose for which it is used is of course also important in the evaluation. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. if it is used to spy on companies in order to benefit the economy, then it must be evaluated differently. thirdly, the end does not justify the means. so it's not just about the purpose, because every wiretap, every individual case is a violation of privacy. this is not a problem of quantity. human rights are individual rights, not a matter of statistics. such a breach of privacy is permissible only under certain conditions. the european court of human rights is crystal clear in its case law on this. these conditions are summarised as follows: intervention must have a legal basis, it must not be arbitrary. so there has to be a trade-off between the invasion of privacy and the purpose at hand. it must be predictable, i.e. citizens must know that such a system exists. and wiretaps should only be used when there's no other way. so it is an ultima ratio. there are colleagues here in the house who say that when it comes to law enforcement, if the police do it on the orders of a judge, then that's fine. the intelligence community says it's a violation of human rights. i have a great deal of sympathy for people who say, politically, i don't want services to do this. i can relate to that. i'm not in that position, but i can relate to that. but if anyone says that this is illegal, then he is not taking into account the case law of the european court of human rights here. economic espionage is certainly not a legitimate purpose. now all news services also cover economic issues, for example developments in financial or commodity markets. in this sense, most services are engaged in economic espionage. that is not the point being criticized either. the problem arises when, instead of clarifying general facts, details are leaked to the industry of one's own country in order to give it a competitive advantage. moreover, such behaviour between eu countries would be incompatible with eu law, as it is a form of prohibited state aid. it is more than an unfriendly act on the international stage, and between allies it is a scandal! moreover, wiretapping is not the method of choice in economic espionage, which is usually done with the classic means. but there are cases where this instrument can be used successfully. the united states was now the main target of criticism. the us has always denied that it provides intelligence directly to us companies. but you admitted that you've been listening in on the details of major international contracts. the argument and justification is that european companies are bribing and that we should fight against it. this behaviour must be - i say this now very politely and carefully - questioned. first, we know that american companies also pay bribes. in the analysis of corruption worldwide, they are in the middle of the bribery activity. secondly, this is now prohibited by convention within the oecd and the member states of the european union have transposed it into national law. if the united states of america still insists on a right of first refusal with a cowboy mentality, then that is incompatible with the idea that such things are regulated by international legal agreements. commission - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission is actively preparing for the european council meeting next friday, which is fully in line with the meeting of the eu troika in the united states of america tomorrow. that is why my colleague, chris patten, who wanted to speak in particular on external relations in the fight against terrorism, was not able to attend this debate. i would like to stress, on behalf of the commission, that we support the principle that the union must make an extra effort to speak with one voice on the fight against terrorism and that we need a european agenda on this subject which recognises the central role that must be given to the united nations in the fight against terrorism on a global scale. we therefore welcome the initiative of the belgian presidency to convene an extraordinary and informal council next friday and we are pleased to take part in this debate today in the european parliament. we must show the solidarity of the whole union with the american people and the american authorities. but if the union is to influence the direction of the fight against terrorism, it must speak with one voice. terrorism is not a new phenomenon. but the threats are new, and the tools used by terrorists are new and more sophisticated. the tragic events in the united states of america painfully demonstrate the timeliness of the two proposals which the commission has approved today, which are closely linked and which also respond to a request from this parliament approved at the september plenary session in strasbourg. i would like to make it clear that our proposals are not a response to what has happened in the united states of america. they are mainly in response to the fact that we have, even in our member states, problems of terrorism which we must deal with. the commission has been working on these proposals for over a year in close liaison with the european parliament and we would like to stress that these proposals are a contribution to europe being able to cooperate more effectively within itself in the fight against terrorism and thus to cooperate in the fight against it at international level. terrorism is one of the greatest threats to democracy, the free exercise of human rights and free economic and social development. in recent years, it should be stressed, we have seen an increase in terrorist activities, both within the union's borders and at the global level. this increase in terrorism is characterized by a profound change in the nature of terrorist offences. the actual or potential effects of armed attacks are increasingly devastating and deadly. the increasing dependence of our society on technological development is giving rise to new forms of terrorism. increasingly, terrorism is carried out by networks operating at international level with very close links to other types of organised crime based in several countries, exploiting legal loopholes resulting from the geographical limitations of investigations and sometimes benefiting from significant financial and logistical support. therefore, action is needed now more than ever to combat this scourge. the treaty on european union expressly provides that the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice shall include the progressive adoption of measures establishing rules on the constituent elements of criminal offences and on sanctions applicable in the field of terrorism. the european parliament recently adopted a resolution which shows the determination of the representatives of the european citizens to ensure that the fight against terrorism is conducted with vigour and efficiency. at this stage, the commission's response is twofold: firstly, we propose a common definition of terrorist acts and the setting of levels of sanctions which reflect the seriousness of such acts in all member states. terrorists take advantage of any differences in legal treatment between states, especially when the offence is not covered by national law in one of them. the situation is, it must be admitted, very different from one member state to another. in most of our member states there is no specific rule on terrorism and terrorist acts are punishable as common law offences. six member states, on the other hand, have specific laws or legal instruments on terrorism in which the terms 'terrorism' or 'terrorist' appear explicitly. the commission's proposal for a framework decision on terrorism aims at harmonisation in this area. it includes a list of offences ranging from murder to other forms of action which may be equally devastating, even if more insidious, and which are termed terrorist when committed intentionally by individuals or groups against one or more countries, their institutions or their populations, with a view to threatening them and seriously damaging or destroying the political, economic or social structures of a country. it is envisaged that these acts will be punished by particularly severe custodial sentences of up to 2 or 20 years' imprisonment depending on the offence committed. secondly, the commission is putting forward a proposal which is, i admit, quite ambitious in nature, and which is to replace the traditional extradition procedures with a system of surrender to the judicial authorities based on a european arrest warrant. this proposal, which is complementary to the proposal on terrorism, although its scope is wider, is based on the principle of mutual recognition of judicial decisions, which the tampere european council wanted to become the cornerstone of european judicial cooperation. the basic idea is that when the judicial authority of a member state requests the surrender of a person, whether on the basis of a final conviction or because that person is the subject of criminal proceedings, its decision must be recognised and enforced throughout the territory of the union in order to simplify and speed up the procedures as much as possible. it is intended to set a time limit of three months and to restrict the refusal to execute to a limited number of cases. in particular, the principle of double criminality should be abolished. the exception for nationals should also not be maintained. the most relevant criterion in the union is not nationality but the place of residence of the person. the proposal aims to facilitate, as far as possible, the execution of the sentence in the country of arrest, where the person is most likely to be reintegrated into society. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as you know, i shall have the opportunity to present these proposals to the ministers tomorrow at the extraordinary council convened by the belgian presidency to discuss the union's contribution to the fight against the terrorist threat. the interest of this meeting is to provide us with an opportunity to put the questions of principle to the ministers at the political level and to try to decide them. this concerns both our legislative proposals and a whole series of measures which should be taken to strengthen our action at operational level and to improve and make more effective our collaboration with our partners. on the operational level, as you know, the commission has no powers, but it believes that the union should take a number of measures at internal level, including ensuring that europol becomes an operational instrument in the fight against the various forms of crime, including terrorism. this requires the implementation of the provisions of the amsterdam treaty on europol which provide for its participation in joint investigation teams and the possibility of inviting member states to launch investigations, which also requires a major revision of the content of the europol convention, including the issues of judicial and democratic control. a strong commitment by member states is needed now to establish real and effective cooperation between their intelligence services and thus demonstrate the existence of mutual trust between them. this is also necessary to significantly improve the conditions under which the police and intelligence services of the member states provide europol with the information necessary for the performance of these tasks, of which i consider the most important to be the prevention of terrorist acts. in addition, it is important for the union to strengthen cooperation at international level and this will include taking all necessary measures in the fields of judicial assistance, extradition, police and judicial cooperation to improve the capacity to prevent and combat terrorism at international level. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, these are some of the ideas that the commission has put forward and which are being proposed to the european parliament and the european council. in these difficult times, when i am sure that the citizens of our member states are looking to the future with uncertainty and a feeling of insecurity, i believe that the best political message we can send them is that we have here a unique opportunity to demonstrate that there is a real added value in the european venture to guarantee them a future of freedom, security and justice.
