mr president, commissioner, madam president of the council! i consider the economic and social cohesion policy to be one of the most positive achievements of the european union, because it documents the principle of solidarity between the more developed and the weaker regions. of course, if we analyse the way the structural funds policy has worked so far, we must clearly say that there are a lot of shortcomings. firstly, while divergence between member states has decreased, differences within member states between highly developed and weak regions have increased. secondly, the unemployment rate in the weak regions has not decreased significantly. thirdly, the average per capita income of the richest regions, which account for 10% of the union's population, is still 2.6 times higher than that of the regions where the poorest 10% of the population live. fourthly, the underdeveloped regions still lack self-sustaining economic and social cycles. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the matter. fifthly, look at the commitment appropriations still to be disbursed at the end of 1999: they amounted to almost 42 billion euro, which means that the use of the structural funds for certain projects is inefficient! - the next item is the report (a5-0233/2001) by mr coelho, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the crossing of external borders and the development of cooperation within the framework of schengen [10846/1999 - c5-0042/2000 + (11329/3/1999 - c5-0043/2000) + (schac 2533/1/2000 - c5-0729/2000) + (sek2000) 1439 - c5-0730/2000 - 2000/2015/cos) ].
the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. this report on the crossing of borders and the development of schengen cooperation touches on a subject which is central to the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice. schengen has a special characteristic. on the one hand it ensures freedom of movement, which is a key element of the treaty, and on the other hand it makes effective the need to surround this freedom with a sound policy of coherent external border control and other compensatory measures. but the integration of schengen into the union has, in fact, signed the death of this agreement, but it still remains alive by the symbolism surrounding the term. schengen was conceived as a laboratory to ensure the implementation of a result obligation under the single european act. and then schengen was split up and integrated into the union, and little by little community and union legislation replaces and develops the schengen convention and the other decisions relating to it. for example, the common consular instruction and the common manual have become regulations, and new proposals based on the third pillar supplement or replace equivalent provisions of the convention that have been broken down towards this pillar. in july last year the commission submitted to the council and parliament a proposal to bring together in a single legal instrument five categories of persons who may move freely within an area without control, thus fulfilling the wish expressed by the european parliament to bring together all the fragmented elements governing the movement of persons. the commission also intends to present a proposal on article 2 of schengen, in order to better encompass the safeguard clause on the reintroduction of internal border controls. the work is not finished, but the aim is to arrive at 'amsterdamiser' schengen in the near future. that is why i think it would be problematic and difficult, mr president, to start an exercise which would consist in making a regular report on schengen, because it would end up being a report on the various instruments which have replaced or are in the process of replacing schengen. but i can engage the commission to continue to inform parliament regularly of developments in this area, which for the sake of simplicity of the term we shall call the schengen area. parliament is also kept informed of all legislative and practical activities by the scoreboard which was set up following the tampere council and is regularly updated. the commission has considered that conversion of the acquis should be done on the basis of priority needs which depend on developments and the political situation and indications of the council and parliament. these priorities naturally include the development of the schengen information system and of course - and you are very interested in this - questions relating to the applicant countries. the rapporteur has made these concerns his own, and the commission can only share them. as regards the schengen information system, sis ii, i would like to give some information on the latest developments. as you know, the justice and home affairs council of 28 and 29 may did not reach a unanimous decision in favour of intergovernmental funding. the decision was therefore taken to finance the project from the community budget. in addition, the belgian and swedish presidencies presented two initiatives, one on the first pillar and the other on the third pillar, aimed at giving the commission, assisted by a committee, the responsibility for the development of sis ii, between 2002 and 2006 therefore, to be launched. the main objective of these two proposals, which are currently being analysed by the council, is first of all to provide a legal basis for the financing of this development phase. but secondly, legislative proposals will have to be made on the various essential aspects of sis ii, in particular the question of management and functionalities. as part of its responsibilities for financing, the commission will also present a communication which will cover various aspects of sis ii: legal, technical and financial issues, but also the various preparatory steps to be considered, as well as the general method to be established until sis ii is finally established. in conclusion, mr president, mr rapporteur, i can assure you that your resolution will be taken into account by the commission in assessing the efforts made and those still to be made, and in defining its priorities for action in the schengen area.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us. i think the committee which adopted this report by a majority is sadly on the wrong track. i would like to explain why i am doing this. we have tried to find a compromise on this very sensitive and difficult subject when the commission's working document on this subject was presented about a year ago. we have agreed to divide asylum seekers into three groups: first, those who seek asylum, secondly those who come to us temporarily from crisis regions and thirdly those who want to immigrate to the member states with the intention of establishing their future livelihood here. we were also clear that we could only manage the last pillar of immigration sensibly if we also made sure that the number of - i will not deliberately use harsh words - unjustified asylum applications could be reduced, or at least that we could deal with them consistently. we know that at most 10% or 15% of the applications submitted are genuinely eligible applications under the geneva convention and are recognised as such. i therefore believe that the committee, with its majority, has made two mistakes: firstly, because it has abandoned this consensus which we have tried so hard to find, and secondly, because it has not done a good service to those who are really entitled, to those who are really politically persecuted, by treating those who have entered germany or other member states unlawfully in the same way, so to speak, and thereby damaging the reputation of those who are really entitled. the way in which the reasons for flight are extended to non-state persecution, the way in which the possibilities of member states, at any rate those member states which have to cope with large flows, to have effective recourse to the safe country of origin institution are restricted, but also the question of how to deal with manifestly unfounded requests, all that is now in this report, means that there is no longer any really effective means of acting, even in the area where unjustified requests are made in large numbers. i must appeal to them again and again. i know how difficult this subject is. i also know how sensitive this issue is. but let us try to maintain in detail these common pillars which we discussed with great consensus a year ago. i hope that the german social democrats, who talk very differently to their minister of the interior in germany, will perhaps change their voting behaviour today. i also hope that we will find a way back to consensus and that we will give the people who are really affected, the politically persecuted, the respect they deserve in our member states.

the commission has already done so. in a situation where the terrible events in the united states are also used by some as a pretext to create anti-asylum sentiment, it is all the more important that the european union formulate minimum standards for the granting or withdrawal of refugee status, which are oriented towards the respect of human rights. the commission proposal fulfils this condition. i expressly welcome two regulations proposed by her. article 3 (3) refers to the possibility for member states to extend the protection granted to persons other than those who can rely on the geneva convention relating to the status of refugees. it would also enable people seeking refuge from violent fundamentalists - in algeria, for example - or victims of rape to find refuge, a demand which the united nations high commissioner for refugees has long made and which, unfortunately, is not currently being put into practice in my country. annex 1 lists the three conditions which must be met for a country to be a so-called safe third country. if this condition is applied in the future, some deportations from eu countries may no longer be possible. i am glad that the acceptable commission proposal has been improved in the committee responsible and not deteriorated, as the original rapporteur, mr schmitt, intended. the proposed directive is therefore an important step towards a more humane asylum policy in the european union.

president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, on 4 september i presented to this house the white paper on european governance. i have already had some of the reactions of members of parliament. the committee on constitutional affairs and the committee on legal affairs have also begun to examine our proposals. today's debate is therefore taking place in the context of a debate which has already begun. i shall therefore make a few preliminary remarks to clear up some of the misunderstandings which have emerged in this debate, while remaining unwaveringly ready to respond to further remarks which will emerge in the course of this morning's debate. as is well known, the main purpose of the white paper on governance is to renew and reinvigorate the functioning of the institutional triangle, which operates according to the community method under the treaty currently in force. this complements and reinforces the constant policy pursued by the commission and its presidency in favour of institutional changes aimed at consolidating the role of the european parliament. the commission has always maintained that, in the institutional triangle, the body which is the expression of the people must play a central role, in balance with the representative body of the states, the council, and the body which represents the european public interest, the commission. the commission also supports the role of the court of justice in the european union based on the rule of law and human rights. this is a commitment we are pursuing consistently and steadily. our aim is to consolidate the legitimacy of this assembly and, with it, representative democracy. the white paper is inspired by this choice to strengthen representative democracy and to ensure that it functions properly and swiftly. the criticisms which have been voiced in recent weeks against that part of our proposals which seeks to clarify the distinction between legislative and executive functions are, in my view, based on a misunderstanding. i have heard, for example, that the commission would ask for a blank cheque in respect of the executive function, outside the legitimate control of parliament. that is not true, and the reading of the white paper clearly shows that. the commission suggests that parliament, the council and the commission all take a step back and return to their institutional tasks. the commission must therefore present fewer proposals, more targeted proposals, focusing on the executive function. the council must play its role as legislator and not as executor. finally, parliament has primary responsibilities in monitoring the implementation of policies and in the budgetary field. it therefore goes far beyond its simple role as a co-legislator. the white paper's proposals are therefore ambitious: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the callback option is in fact flawed in that it merely partially modifies the system currently in force, which we all know is seriously flawed, without, however, addressing its fundamental shortcomings. as the white paper shows, what is needed is structural change that clarifies who is responsible for implementing policies. this is essential to know who will be held accountable, in accordance with the principle of accountability which is a fundamental part of the functioning of democratic institutions. the white paper calls for the commission to play a policy-implementing role and questions the need for the current system of regulatory and management committees. the prospect of enlargement also makes it urgent to review comitology. but the white paper also makes it very clear that the new legislation which you will be discussing on the basis of the commission's final proposal will have to define the conditions and limits of this executive role. it also added that a simple legal arrangement was needed to enable the council and parliament placed on an equal footing to monitor and control the actions of the executive. we are already considering the various possible ways in which this mechanism could work, but at this stage it seems more appropriate to precede this proposal by a hearing phase. we therefore expect to receive an important contribution in this respect from the consultative committees of the member states, as well as from the work of this house. in the white paper, the commission also committed itself to improving its consultation methods in the preparation of its policy proposals. it has been suggested by some that these proposals would jeopardise the role of parliament. i sincerely believe that this does not correspond to reality and, in any case, does not correspond to our intentions. it is clear that we have never proposed and will never propose replacing the role of parliament or other democratically elected institutions with forms of spontaneous aggregation of organised civil society, which we call 'non-governmental organisations'. these associations play an important role in raising awareness and integrating our society and we therefore want to benefit from a relationship with them. this relationship, which - i repeat - has nothing to do with the role of democratically elected institutions, is now being carried out in an opaque and confused way. we must therefore put our present practices in order. we need guidelines in particular to make this process more transparent and structured than it is at present. and we need guidance on how we use experts in policy-making. all these elements will improve the way in which the commission exercises its right of initiative. having a targeted and comprehensible system for interacting with both democratically elected structures at local level and, albeit in a markedly different form, with civil society, will ensure greater transparency and efficiency than current consultation practices. in any event, the treaty remains unchanged and all decisions will continue to be taken by the appropriate institutions, in accordance with the democratic rules in force. the white paper thus opens the way to an interinstitutional debate on how to improve consultation of all the institutions. we do not consider these proposals to be definitive, however, and are therefore open to suggestions and alternative proposals, provided they are aimed at achieving the same results. i also understand that there are some concerns about the new forms of regulation that the white paper proposes. some fear that they could weaken the role of parliament. a closer examination of the white paper should, however, convince you that the commission is, like you, determined not to diminish but to increase the role of parliament. the white paper therefore proposes to place new forms of regulation, such as self-regulation, within the framework of principles and practices which ensure democratic control. as for the creation of regulatory agencies which will only be able to take technical and case-by-case decisions such a creation will obviously require a legislative act. parliament will therefore be fully involved in the elaboration of the rules and the necessary guarantees accompanying the adoption of this act. we must therefore strike the right balance between the need to set the objectives and the essential elements of european legislation and the need to remain flexible and able to react to rapid social and economic changes. in this spirit, the white paper therefore proposes, for the first time, to involve parliament in the complex process of implementing the open method of coordination. these forms of intergovernmental cooperation in the frontier areas of community law must necessarily be based on a logic compatible with the functioning of the institutional triangle. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the main challenge facing europe today is a political one. the laeken summit is just around the corner, and it should set the stage for the next intergovernmental conference. governance is already part of that debate. changing the way the institutions operate - the purpose of the white paper - and changing the institutions themselves - the purpose of future treaty amendments - are obviously two different but closely linked issues. that is why i said that the debate on the options presented in the white paper on governance is a first step in the debate on the future of the union. this phase, although it operates as a permanent right and therefore with the limitations that this entails, cannot be reduced to a mere academic debate but must be concretized in precise operational proposals. this will increase the trust of european citizens in the way the union works. this is essential. we must immediately win back the confidence of our fellow citizens by using the existing rules correctly and efficiently. this will then give us greater legitimacy to call for the necessary amendments to the treaty. however, acting quickly must not mean acting without waiting for the necessary maturation of the options and reflections, especially those taking place within this house. it is therefore clear that i do not intend to make any proposals until you have worked out your views on the matter. the commission is aware that the renewal process set out in the white paper can only be successful if the european parliament and the council have the political will to make a joint effort and begin to change the way we operate within the framework of the existing treaty. i am therefore in favour of forms of dialogue between the union institutions - if necessary also through a joint working group of the commission, parliament and council - to examine in depth our proposals on governance. i thank you sincerely in advance for your commitment and your help. - madam president, mr president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, the european union has had a great success story in the 51 years of its existence, since the beginning of the european unification process, since the declaration of robert schuman. the common market, the common currency, the approaches of european foreign and security policy have made us a zone of peace, law and security, and we are here to set an example for many regions of the world. but why is it that the action of the various institutions of the european union is not perceived by our citizens as it should be, as it should be expected? why is there so little positive response? the question then immediately arises: what is wrong with the european union in its external appearance, but also in the way we design and implement our policies? the commission has already taken a number of decisions on the subject, and i am sure that the council will be able to take them into account in its decision on the transeuropean transport networks. the transeuropean transport network has been the backbone of our internal market since its conception in the maastricht treaty and, thanks to the guidelines we adopted jointly in 1996, the european union has a network of european interest that allows the interconnection of all our regions and facilitates the mobility of people and goods. these transeuropean networks are the first attempt since roman times to really look at europe's infrastructures in a global and integrated way. the revision we are proposing today is intended to bring the development of this system up to date and to add new priority projects which respond to the problems of the challenges which our common transport policy has posed in recent years. the liberalisation of transport systems and the increase in demand for mobility have led to an imbalance between the different modes of transport and have contributed to the creation of bottlenecks in some areas of our infrastructure. both the gothenburg summit and the white paper on transport adopted on 12 september have identified these pathologies and have called on the commission to take urgent measures to alleviate them. in today's proposal the commission recommends that eight new rail, combined transport, inland waterway and intelligent transport networks, namely the galileo project, be included among the priority projects in addition to the so-called essen projects, and that three of the initial projects already completed be withdrawn. the new projects would be: first, a railway crossing of the pyrenees which will allow the natural barrier separating the iberian peninsula from the rest of the continent to be overcome. the second is the high-speed train, combined east-west transport, from paris to vienna, which will later be extended to budapest and which will complete our network, opening the door to enlargement. the third is the navigability of the danube between straubing and vilshofen, which will connect the north sea with the black sea, thus improving the interconnection between the danube and the rhine. the fourth is the galileo satellite positioning system, whose priority has been recognized by successive european councils and by this house. the fifth is the firm connection between germany and denmark via fehmarn on the orensund model, which will improve the interconnection of the nordic countries with the rest of the continent. the sixth is the interoperability of the high-speed rail network in the iberian peninsula, adapting it to the track gauge of the rest of the european continent, which will reduce congestion both on land and in the air. the seventh is the extension of the brenner project from munich to verona, up to naples, by adding the bologna-milan section. and the eighth is the extension of the southern high speed train to nîmes, which will enable the connection between the south and the north of europe. the overall investment required for these projects, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, will amount to more than 66 billion euros, which should obviously be financed mainly through national, regional, private, public and also, possibly, community funds. its geographical scope covers the whole of our territory and will have a decisive impact on the competitiveness of our economy. we also took advantage of this review to include in the transeuropean networks some minor technical adaptations of existing projects which were left outstanding after the conciliation on the 1996 package of guidelines. we have committed ourselves in the transport white paper to this most urgent and priority review being followed in 2004 by another which will include in greater detail the projects of the new countries of the union. it would be premature, ladies and gentlemen, to do so now, because, despite the preparatory work, which is well advanced, important information is still missing which we can only obtain in the last phase of enlargement. the next revision will therefore the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, i would like to thank you for your reply. we're late for the meeting. we are running out of time, and galileo in particular. the longer the european union hesitates to launch the european satellite navigation system, the less interested the industry and the public will be in reacting. the last danger is that galileo will be buried one day. i am particularly concerned about the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. the opinion of the european parliament on the commission's communication is not a legislative one, but it is an important guideline. the european parliament will adopt my report tomorrow - and i hope by a large majority - and thereby support the position that a european satellite navigation system of its own is urgently needed, not least in view of the particular situation in which the world and europe have found themselves since 11 september. this is the basic view of the council, as was reaffirmed in the stockholm conclusions. but how can we dispel the doubts which arise again and again, even in the amendments before us? the basic question remains: why do we need a european satellite navigation system of our own when the americans have already supplied a working model with gps? let me give you some of the main arguments. firstly, the american system is military in design, with its corresponding disadvantages in terms of continuous availability, accuracy and also legal certainty. we are talking about reliability, and that must be guaranteed even in times of crisis. we must all be clear that the sovereignty and security of europe would be seriously threatened if the navigation systems were to escape european control. we need a civil system of our own, but one which is open to all - and i stress all - potential users. i am sorry, therefore, that i cannot support the amendments tabled by the gue/ngl group, which call for a purely civilian application. secondly, we are in favour of free competition within the union, but also in the world. it is therefore not surprising that we should be willing to accept a monopoly of a foreign state and expose our users to what may not be optimal services. we must be involved here in the interests of our citizens and users. thirdly, the european union would be falling far behind in the high-tech sector if it did not have its own system. this can't be intentional. no, we want europe to be at the forefront, and that is what galileo is for. fourthly, galileo is creating jobs in europe. these jobs are highly skilled and are being created in a field with a future - high technology. the development of the infrastructure and the various applications can create up to 100 000 jobs in the coming years and generate a high return on the market. so why is galileo important for europe? in my report i have detailed the advantages and positive aspects of the different fields of application. these benefits become even more convincing when other countries are involved. for example, china has recently expressed itself positively at the brussels meeting. europe is capable of creating its own system. we will not hold back the galileo praline, but we will offer it to the partners if they so wish, and we will share the great benefits with the partners. from the beginning, we have placed a great deal of emphasis on compatibility with other systems, because we want to offer the best possible benefits. the industry is showing interest. this is not only evident from the letters of intent for eur 200 million which the commission has received, but we must not overtax our industry. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the preparatory work carried out by the commission and the european space agency deserves the highest praise. i am, however, looking forward to the commission's approach to financing and administration, as called for in the report. this concept will be another building block and a solid pillar for the construction of the satellite navigation system. galileo is a community project. the first community project in this field! so a vision for the future! let us get started here, instead of waiting for st. nicholas day, because galileo will revolutionize transport and mobility - as the internet has done. success stories - and we already have some in europe - require thought, courage and decisiveness. let us seize this historic moment in the vote tomorrow.

the commission is aware of the fact that the council has not yet adopted the budget for the financial year, and that the council has not yet adopted the budget for the financial year. the council meeting in liège on 22 and 23 september 2001 focused its discussion on the economic impact of terrorist attacks in the united states. i would like to point out three aspects of this impact which were discussed at ecofin: firstly, the economic situation, and the opportunity was also taken to discuss the stability and growth pact. secondly, the financing of terrorism. and thirdly, the airline's insurance problems. i would also like to make a few comments on two other important issues that were discussed at liège: preparations for the changeover to the euro and issues related to globalisation. on the first point, i would like to point out that the terrorist attacks in the united states have reinforced our conviction that international cooperation in economic and financial matters is indispensable and that there is a need to strengthen the coordination of economic policies in the european union. the european union has been affected, already since last year, more than we originally anticipated, by the slowdown in economic activity in the united states and the rest of the world. the tragic events in the united states have increased uncertainty and also negative risks to overall growth expectations. we cannot pretend that nothing has happened, but at the same time it is very difficult to estimate precisely the potential impact of these acts. growth in the european union this year will be clearly below 2%, but we still expect a gradual recovery in domestic demand in the coming quarters as a result of a number of factors: lower inflation, recent tax cuts and more favourable monetary conditions. the risks, therefore, should be manageable. of course, we must monitor economic developments very closely in order to be able to adjust economic policies as necessary, both in the union and in each of the member states. after the events of 11 september, policy makers have shown their determination to act quickly and appropriately in order to eliminate the risks of a longer-term slowdown, for which it is also necessary to maintain our medium-term objectives, to accelerate our agenda and, in particular, i am thinking of the lisbon agenda, to rapidly modernise our economies to get out of the slowdown as soon as possible and to increase our capacity for growth. as i noted above, the informal ecofin declaration confirmed the commitment of the member states to the framework, rules and implementation of the stability and growth pact. it is true that the lower growth will affect, as the presidency has pointed out, the nominal value of budgetary positions, but the deviation from the objectives must be measured. the stability and growth pact is an appropriate framework for budgetary policy both in good economic times and in less good times. in this sense it allows the right budgetary policy to be implemented at any given time. the covenant offers every possibility. the automatic stabilisers will have a greater effect if the deceleration is more significant than expected. the way and extent to which these stabilizers can be used depends on the situation in each member state, and those closer to budgetary equilibrium will naturally have more room for manoeuvre. the current budgetary positions, which result from respect for the existing budgetary rules, have enabled the european central bank to pursue an accommodative monetary policy and, in particular, have enabled the bank to take the appropriate and rapid decision to reduce interest rates by 50 basis points on 17 september. a rise in deficits beyond what can justify the use of stabilizers would reduce the margin of the central bank for possible rate cuts in the future. the european council asked the commission to present to the next european council in ghent on 19 october an analysis of possible developments in the economic situation and possible recommendations. the report should be regarded as a continuous and systematic exercise which allows the assessment of the evolution of risks and their possible consequences to be adjusted. a second comment on the measures to combat the financing of terrorism. the ecofin declaration underlines a number of specific actions. firstly, the revision of the money laundering directive which is - as you know very well - under way. i would like to stress again, on behalf of the commission and in line with the ecofin declaration of liège, the political importance we attach to its being able to be concluded quickly. it will be an unmistakable sign of the union's commitment to eradicating criminal activities that find their instrument of support in money laundering activities. i would also like to highlight the commission's approval of the proposal for a regulation on specific measures to freeze the assets of persons and entities linked to the financing of terrorist activities, which we hope the council and parliament will be able to deal with urgently with a view to its immediate entry into force. it is a clear demonstration of our political determination not to give breathing space to those who attack political coexistence and the freedoms of all citizens. the ecofin council also agreed on general guidelines to guide the action of governments on insurance problems faced by airlines. the ecofin declaration calls on the commission to extend the scope of the ad hoc group set up within the transport council to include insurance issues. the declaration also states that any measures taken by governments, including financial amounts, must be notified to the commission. this allows the commission to exercise its responsibility for ensuring the compatibility of these measures with community legislation and for organising consistency in the member states' response. the commission is preparing a report on the impact of the 11 september attacks on the air transport industry. the informal ecofin also had the opportunity to discuss, as has been done regularly, the preparations for the introduction of the euro. the commission is preparing a report on this for the european council in ghent on 19 october. in liege i asked the member states to pay particular attention to three aspects which i believe are crucial at the moment. firstly, the problem of pre-feeding the small traders. it is important that they are informed and convinced of the commercial advantages of pre-feeding, but it is also important to find ways of helping them to work together with the banks and that they offer fair debit conditions for the amounts of euro that small traders receive before 31 december 2001. it is also essential to provide specific training for small traders and for all those responsible for cash handling in any business. finally, the third problem of concern is the monitoring of the prices of goods and services around the euro changeover period. we cannot, and it is not sensible, reproduce the calculation of the harmonised consumer price index every week, but we objectivity, and that the sample chosen is appropriate. the informal ecofin also agreed with the commission's proposal to set up a common european network to organise the exchange of information during the introduction period of coins and banknotes. this network will start operating at the beginning of december in close coordination with the european central bank's cash changeover committee. the last point i would like to make is the debate on globalisation. the commission has followed closely the public debate on globalisation, including the debate on the so-called tobin tax. we have noted the interest of ecofin in having a report on these issues. this discussion reflects two objectives which are clearly relevant and about which we share the concern of many of the participants in the debate on globalisation. firstly, to avoid excessive exchange rate volatility which can block the desired economic development of developing countries and, secondly, to find sources of additional financing to combat poverty. we cannot respond to these objectives with a single instrument. the union, together with other countries, international institutions and other groups, has developed a number of instruments and policies to try to meet these objectives. of course, more and better can and should be done, and the commission is ready to explore new possibilities. the idea of professor tobin of a tax on foreign currency transactions was, by his definition, to put a grain of sand on the international money markets. it was proposed as a second best solution to curb short-term speculative movements. the commission has already expressed its views on several occasions. a tax on monetary transactions cannot effectively address the problems caused by excessive volatility of financial flows or inequality between countries. a wide range of instruments must be mobilised: the tobin tax is not the miracle instrument to meet all these challenges. we must consider a set of instruments to achieve financial and monetary stability. a comprehensive approach to the financial architecture is needed, both at the internal level of the european union and at the international level, including regulatory frameworks, institutions and the problem of money laundering. a broad approach is also needed to development finance. poverty, debt management, provision of international public goods and environmental protection can be addressed through different instruments. the commission - and i am sure that parliament and the council can be counted on to do so - is ready to contribute actively to the debate on the instruments which will ensure coherence between globalisation, sustainable development and global governance. of course, these issues go beyond the strict sphere of the union and we have to address them with the other countries and institutions. the commission is ready to respond to the council's invitation to continue working on how to respond to the key objectives i have mentioned. in any case, some of the work is already under way in the commission, as we are preparing a report by january next year on the external dimension of sustainable development for the rio+10 conference to be held in johannesburg next year. these are the fundamental elements that i wanted to share with you. - the next item is the report (a5-0299/2001) by mr agag longo, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the xxxth report of the commission (sec2001) 0694 - c5-0312/2001 - 2001/ 2130 (cos)) on competition policy (2000).
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. recently, especially after the stockholm european council, there has been a change in competition policy in the european union. this can be seen in the increasing conservation of structures. the agag longo report rightly addresses this. after the success of liberalisation in the 1990s, the postal, electricity and gas sectors are now trying to escape from the sticky competition. first liberalization, then regulation, and the headline for this scenario is: welfare. the agenda of the heads of government for laeken expressly provides for a discussion of the tension between competition and welfare. it is a question of whether the competition can hold its own there. if you ask what the difference is between our modern open society and another society, which is characterized by classes and castes, the answer is clear: in our open society, competition has become the culture-bearing order, the culture-bearing principle. the breakthrough in the competition principle is therefore a great cultural achievement. the state has never been able to meet this principle. it has always protected its education system, its banks, its railways, its airlines, its mail, its telephone networks and its housing associations from the fierce winds of competition. some industries also argue that competition cannot work in their case or that they have to pursue objectives that could harm competition. there are plenty of examples. coal is valued for its security of supply. in health care, it is claimed that the market is harmful because patients are unable to judge the services. in agriculture, the market is said to be unsuitable because farmers are said to produce more at lower prices. the postal services cannot be excluded from competition - at least not completely - because they have social responsibilities. that's the way to go. but all these lazy excuses have one thing in common: they all recognise competition as a principle; it is merely claimed that the principle is not applicable in this particular case. the european environment has certainly become more difficult for competition policy again. it is therefore important - and the committee on economic and monetary affairs calls for this - that the eu's competition policy should finally be extended to the energy, transport and pharmaceutical sectors. let us therefore continue to plan, promote and advocate freedom together in the future.

i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i am not talking about the cause, but about the institutional issues. parliament has already refused - or at least refrained - from lodging an objection with the european patent office. that's right. parliament is the legislator and a legislator cannot interfere in a process that is in progress. you can't do that! this is, so to speak, the basic principle of a democracy based on the rule of law! the legislator adopts a law - in this case, the directive - which will be confirmed by the european court of justice next week. it is then the authorities who apply the directive and grant or refuse to grant a patent, and then it is the courts who decide whether or not that grant or refusal was justified. that is the procedure, and otherwise there is no procedure in a democracy governed by the rule of law! the legislator - in this case the european parliament - cannot therefore interfere in an ongoing procedure. the european parliament has no more competence in this matter than, for example, the commission or a green party congress or a greenpeace assembly. the commission does not decide how a directive is to be applied, nor does the european parliament, nor the greens, nor greenpeace, but the authorities who are responsible. they decide that, the courts decide that, and no one else! and that's a good thing! i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this.

a heavy machine gun, for example, is enough - were to be released and spread over the city, the city would simply burn up if it mixed with the surrounding air. we've had accidents like this in the past. thank god we've avoided them for the last ten years. the same is true of the water supply. poisoning water is relatively easy. the consequences, as we can all imagine, would be unpredictable. i accept that in our countries there are some who are against nuclear energy, in some countries it may even be the majority. i respect that, even though i don't share that opinion. but with the argument of terrorist attacks, we could also say goodbye to the gas industry or stop drinking water, and i think that is absurd. my conclusion simply follows the line laid down by the commission. it is admittedly not very effective, but it has the advantage of being reasonable. we should identify the hazardous installations, improve the security of the object, perhaps take further safety measures. these safety measures should also be taken without delay. we don't need studies. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is only at the cost of total surveillance, which is incompatible with a free state based on the rule of law.
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. i have a small dream which is coming true today: i have ten minutes to speak, which is the usual time for a group chairman. but that's because two reports were merged that don't belong together. i would therefore like to separate them in my speech. first, the area of civil law. with the entry into force of the maastricht treaty in 1993, judicial cooperation in civil matters became a matter for the member states. the treaty of amsterdam then transferred this cooperation from the third pillar to the first pillar by means of article 65 of the treaty. since its entry into force, there has been a flurry of european legislation on this subject. the council adopted a regulation on the insolvency procedure and on the service of documents in civil and commercial matters, and proposals for regulations on the taking of evidence and on the rights of access were submitted to the council. finally, with the entry into force of the current treaty of nice, future decisions in the field of judicial cooperation in civil matters will be taken by the council by qualified majority under the codecision procedure. you see, there's really a rapid development in this area. however, the content and design of vocational training in civil justice remain the sole responsibility of the member states. the community's role is to assist the member states, whether in removing obstacles to the application of community law or in cooperation between judicial authorities. in no area of european law is the continuing training of the professions so essential as in the already well-advanced field of harmonized civil law. criminal and administrative law, on the other hand, are still at the beginning of european development. in the past, the union has supported this training with two programmes. grotius, the joint support and exchange programme for the legal professions, ended in 2000. the support was maintained only by a temporary one-year successor programme, grotius-civil law. the three-year action programme robert schuman, which was designed to increase the awareness of lawyers of community law, also came to an end in the same year. the commission proposal before us today now provides the legal basis for further funding of activities in the field of judicial cooperation in civil matters. this will promote judicial cooperation and mutual knowledge of the legal order, as well as measures to implement and apply community legislation in this field and to improve public information. in addition to financing specific projects, financial support for the running costs of non-governmental european bodies is also envisaged for the first time. i can only support this very strongly. the fact that the accession countries are also allowed to participate is also particularly welcome. in addition to the general satisfaction with the direction of this proposal, which is also enhanced by a generous financial framework of eur 14.5 million until 2006, some critical points remain. the requirement that non-governmental organisations only apply for funding if two thirds of the member states participate is already almost unenforceable. in view of the forthcoming enlargement, it therefore seems urgently appropriate to reduce this threshold to one third. otherwise the good approach of the regulation on this point would be immediately stifled. i also wonder why the commission, contrary to its usual practice, fails to define precisely the applicants - in this case the legal professions - as was the case in the grotius programmes. the debate on the money laundering directive has shown us how necessary definitions are in this area. the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council at the next meeting of the european council. i therefore proposed adopting the old definition from the grotius programme on civil law. i would like to make one further comment on this matter: i would have liked the union to continue to finance projects up to 80% of the cost and not reduce this to 50%. unfortunately, that was not the wish of the committee responsible. i think, however, that the european union still has a great responsibility for the further development of judicial cooperation. this responsibility will be greater in the future than it will be smaller. we must continue to be the engine here. that was the first part of the explanation, the civil law area. the european union has a duty to help the countries of central and eastern europe. the schengen information system was established in 1995 on the basis of the 1990 schengen implementing convention. as a transnational computerised police tracing system, it now provides online access to more than 8 million tracing data, making it the most comprehensive database in europe. in addition to 13 member states of the european union, it is also used by iceland and norway. the sis is thus a successful component of a new european internal security policy, the need for which arises from the dismantling of internal borders and the consequent loss of control. two problems are on our minds today. first, the technical development. the schengen information system as we know it today was originally designed for 18 member states. since all the current applicant countries will also participate in sis upon accession, it is urgent to start thinking about a successor system today. the technological development has also made progress. the initiative of the kingdoms of belgium and sweden to develop sis ii is therefore very welcome. as the preparatory work for the development of sis ii will take more than three years, these initiatives will provide the necessary budgetary legal basis. however, the initiators also went a little over the top. in order to ensure the greatest possible influence on technical developments, the participation of the member states in the comitology procedure should be carried out by a combination of management and regulatory committees. the commission has also proposed a number of measures to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states. i do not see why, at a stage of development when only technical aspects are to be discussed, the member states should be consulted and involved in every detail. the proposal to set up a regulatory committee for all matters relating to the architecture of the system and the technical aspects of data protection is also contrary to council decision 468/99. the regulatory procedure is therefore to be used only for measures of general scope intended to implement essential provisions of basic acts. but this is clearly not the case here. i would also like to draw the attention of the council representatives to the fact that, for example, the establishment of eurodac has deliberately avoided a formal participation procedure and that the member states ensure their influence only through an informal network of technicians. this has saved us all a lot of time and money, and yet it has led to an efficient outcome. at the same time, i am confident in the commission's expertise in this area, which is the lead agency for development. my proposal to the member states is therefore: replace the unnecessary bureaucratic combination of administrative and regulatory procedures with a combination of administrative and consultative procedures. less is sometimes more! the second problem is the legal development. although the member states decided at the intergovernmental conference in amsterdam to integrate the schengen acquis into the eu legal area, the schengen information system was assigned to the third pillar due to a lack of agreement. the collection of data on persons who have been issued an alert for refusal of entry is, however, clearly covered by the first pillar. this is why we have two initiatives today from the belgian and swedish presidencies. as the european parliament, we are trying to integrate schengen and the schengen information system as a whole into the first pillar as far as possible. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. as a step in this direction, i therefore expressly welcome the fact that the development of schengen ii will be financed from 2002 onwards from community funds. unfortunately, the initiative forgets to submit the commission's semiannual progress reports to parliament. it is hardly conceivable to apply the budgetary procedure of the european community to the financing of schengen ii without wanting to inform the budgetary legislator, namely parliament, of developments. the commission has already made a number of proposals, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. i apologize if i have to leave in about 15 minutes - this also concerns other colleagues - but then the committee on the interior is meeting. we must also take part in votes there. in that sense, it's not disrespectful to the house! them. we have not yet succeeded in developing a working system of early warning indicators, in moving towards transparency of information and in developing a code of conduct that works for everyone, still have to go further, because monetary union is only a contribution to stability in europe and the world.

- the report (a5-0360/2001) by mrs weiler, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the proposal for a council decision (com (2001) 511 - c5-0498/2001 - 2001/0208 (cns)) on guidelines for the employment policies of the member states in 2002; the commission's communication (com (2001) 438 - c5-0423/2001 - 2001/2168) on the draft joint report on employment in 2001 is intended to provide a framework for the implementation of the european employment strategy.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. employment policy in the european union has been successful in the past year, although not all of our ambitious targets have been achieved. but the course is set. there are few areas where you have to think as long term as in employment policy. i have the impression that the member states have not only understood this, but are also acting on it. my report is in line with the line taken by the parliamentary committee in recent years. we have always been critical and constructive in our support of the employment process in the member states. this year, therefore, i have focused on some new priorities. it is the new issue of quality of work for the first time. on this point we in parliament agree with the initiative of the commission and the belgian presidency, which have also placed the quality of work as a very high priority on the agenda. we would like to see this issue mainstreamed into all policy areas. the second point is equality between women and men in the labour market. here too, according to the commission figures, we have made progress: women's employment rates have increased by at least 2%. it is not enough, of course, but it is the right way forward and it also shows that the member states are rethinking their approach. this change of thinking - which was not so easy - means that at least in some member states, such as germany, greece and ireland, there has also been a change of consciousness. the third point which is of great importance to me is the integration of disadvantaged groups into the labour market. this has been an important issue for parliament for many years. i have advocated in my report that immigrants should also be included in labour market policies. i think that is an important aspect for the future, particularly in view of the fact that we are creating new social focal points. the commission has already made a number of proposals. there has been some debate in our committee about whether it makes sense to demand a right to continuing training and to instruct national governments to implement it. i think that at a time when we are already facing bottlenecks in certain sectors, which are due to a lack of training and continuing training, such a national right to continuing training would be the need of the hour. i'm convinced, by the way, that we'll have that in four or five years. why should parliament not even be a pioneer? the implementation of these policy objectives requires national and european targets. in addition, i believe that more collaboration between business and academia is needed than has been the case so far to enable efficient knowledge transfer and to initiate entrepreneurial innovation at a faster rate than has been the case in the past. i also appeal to the member states, the council and the belgian presidency to have the courage to launch a public debate on employment policy in europe. we find that there is still little or no discussion of employment policy in europe in national parliaments - with the possible exception of denmark - and also in regional and national parliaments. the social partners at regional level also do not know what meaningful debates and decisions we take in the european parliament. the commission's proposals are not only a means of improving the quality of life of the citizens of the community but also a means of ensuring that the quality of life of the citizens of the community is not undermined. i would like to say that we in parliament are not yet satisfied with the objectives and the debates in the council on this point. i think that a little more courage will be needed here on the part of the finance ministers in the ecofin council to guarantee here too the appropriate balanced objective for a meaningful european employment policy, because only then can an offensive for growth and employment in europe be realised. the council. - madam president, mr president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, as is a good tradition, i have come here today, a few days after the european council meeting in ghent, to report on the discussions we had there. and rest assured i'll be concise and businesslike. the european council in ghent was in fact the second under the belgian presidency and, like the previous meeting in brussels on 21 september, it was strongly influenced by the aftermath of the attacks in new york and washington. of course, how could it be otherwise? the events of 11 september will forever be etched in our memory, and the international community and the international alliance against terrorism have now taken action. as you know, the ghent summit was originally conceived as an informal exchange of views on the enlargement of the union and, in particular, on the laeken declaration, which is to structure and launch the debate on the future of europe later in the year. and it was also our initial intention to make a final evaluation of the introduction of the euro. i did indeed think that the council should, as a kind of good steward, check whether all the preparations had finally been made for a successful introduction of the european single currency. but as often happens - at least i have heard it from those who have much more experience as president of the council - the current situation has thrown that agenda into a bit of a tailspin, and i would say that rightly so. the events of september 11 have an unprecedented immense significance, and i think it becomes clearer every day that the world after september 11 will never be the same again. a new world order is emerging, a new multipolar world in which the european union will have to play a more prominent role. i had the opportunity yesterday to give a first view of this in poland at the beginning of the academic year of the college of europe. but of course, the big considerations are one thing, but to make the union act as a whole in this crisis is quite another matter. a month ago, on 21 september, the union succeeded in adopting a clear, unambiguous and common position. and we also approved a far-reaching and detailed action plan against terrorism. the final declaration of the council of ministers last friday in ghent shows that we have been able to maintain this united approach without any shortcomings. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. we unequivocally support the military action which began on 7 october. they are legitimized by un security council resolution 1368, and we attach the utmost importance to saving the civilian population. we also want to see a normal government in afghanistan after the conflict, a stable government, a representative government that respects human rights. such a government will be able to count on full european help in rebuilding the country. in the meantime, we will work with the union to increase our efforts in humanitarian aid to the many millions of afghan refugees. our commitment is that no country in the region should be made the victim of this conflict by the influx of displaced persons. the council also gave the presidency a mandate to visit the region in order to obtain political support for the replacement of the taliban regime. the second element i would like to stress is the rapid and full implementation of the action plan against terrorism. i would like to say that the introduction of a european arrest warrant is a breakthrough. the abolition of double criminalization was now accepted by everyone in the council, not only for terrorist acts but also for all other serious crimes. the list of terrorist organisations was decided to be finalized and adopted at least by the end of the year. we also discussed in the council the proposals put forward by our american partners and it was agreed in the council to strengthen our action plan if necessary. the commission and the council were also instructed to draw up a programme of cooperation between member states to combat terrorism involving biological and chemical weapons. the programme will include the appointment of a european civil protection coordinator. thirdly, there is the more active role of the union in preventing and combating sources of conflict. the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force. the council clearly conveyed the message on friday that peace is only possible on the basis of two states. we have also warned the council once again not to allow an amalgamation between terrorism and the islamic world. on the contrary, dialogue between europe and the arab and islamic world must be intensified. i would like to say, madam president, that the clear decisions taken last friday also immediately put into perspective the 'incident' surrounding the previous meeting between the french president, the british prime minister and the german chancellor. the impression of a directory in the making, an impression which might not have been there had that meeting been held in another place or at another time, was reduced to its true proportions after the three confirmed to me that it was a consultation on purely technical-military matters. i accepted that explanation, also to prevent this issue from dominating the european council in ghent, and i reiterated in the council that it is the fifteen who jointly decide positions in the european union. president of the commission. - madam president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to say that the commission has welcomed with great satisfaction the good news that the irish republican army has begun to surrender its arms in accordance with the good friday agreement. the commission will be following closely the consolidation of the reconciliation process in northern ireland, also through our peace programme. (applause) i would like to thank following the attacks of 11 september 2001 on the united states of america, our historic allies, the european union has publicly committed itself to cooperating fully with the efforts being made to bring to justice the perpetrators, organisers and instigators of these acts, and to hold to account those who have sheltered, supported and hosted them. we have thus assured the government and the people of the united states of our full solidarity. in the days that followed, i was very pleased to see these declarations of solidarity translate into rapid and concerted action at european level. chris patten, belgian foreign minister louis michel and javier solana went first to washington and then to pakistan, iran, saudi arabia, egypt and syria to participate in the building of a global coalition against terrorism. the european authorities have rapidly started to strengthen cooperation between police and intelligence services, both within the union and with third countries, in particular the united states. on the basis of emergency legislation agreed at community level, we have frozen assets belonging to suspected terrorists worth more than 100 million euros. we have developed uniform standards applicable throughout the union to make air travel safer. the commission also put forward proposals for a common definition of terrorism, a system of penalties applicable throughout the european union for related offences and a european arrest warrant. these proposals were strongly supported by the european council at its extraordinary meeting on 21 september. on that occasion, the council called on the countries of the european union to contribute, each according to its own means, to the new global campaign against terrorism. so it was: some countries have mobilized or offered their armed forces, while others have provided information or made their air bases available. despite the importance and success of this joint action, it is a fact that media attention has focused mainly on the initiatives taken by individual countries. this has somewhat clouded and polluted the debate on the actual role of europe as a whole in the international arena. that is what i would like to focus on today. since the beginning of my commission's mandate, one of the commission's own objectives has been to strengthen europe's presence in the world. the new world situation has made this objective even more urgent. to be a leading actor on the world stage, the european union must speak with one voice - a clear and strong one - and must follow its words with united action. the union has taken steps in this direction, there is no denying that. it is enough to compare, for example, the variety of attitudes adopted by member states at the time of the gulf war ten years ago with our recent position on the situation in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia and the coherence of our current response to terrorism. i take this opportunity to highlight the excellent work done in this respect by the belgian presidency, which has always been careful to support the shared and common objectives of the european union with courage and intelligence. however, we are still far from having the effective common foreign and security policy we so badly need. i am therefore pleased that in the european union declaration of 14 september we publicly committed ourselves to developing our common foreign and security policy and to ensuring that the union can really make itself heard and can really speak with one voice. a common policy is not, of course, a single policy, uniformly adopted by each individual member state, as each has specific roles. a common policy is a policy which multiplies the strength of individual countries around shared objectives and with shared instruments. has there been an 'absence of europe' on this point, as some claim? my answer is no, although we have to distinguish. wherever integration is possible and real, europe is responding with specific initiatives and appropriate responses. this is not surprising, since the community method has been ensuring for 50 years that the union is able to act effectively, quickly and visibly in all areas where it is possible. it is in the less integrated areas, where the community method is almost absent or absent, that the real problem of the effectiveness of the european union's action arises. this fact should serve as an incentive to prepare with even greater determination for the next major political events in the union. a common policy ensures the coordination of the various national policies in a community context, according to the community method, in order to serve the general interests of the union. and in the field of the common foreign and security policy we have not yet reached that point, because the necessary consensus has not yet been reached: we are, as they say, in a transition phase. but this is the objective which must be pursued by building up a policy from the outset, drawing inspiration from the experience gained in the community and making the best use of the instruments at our disposal. firstly, the unity of action. that is why i believe that the separate action of a few is not in the common interest or in the interest of individual countries, whether small or large. i noted at ghent that no member state wants to go in this direction, but the commission has an obligation to remain vigilant, for the sake of all. secondly, the concrete institutional mechanisms for decision-making. this is the kind of common foreign and security policy we must develop, and we must develop it quickly, taking into account the positive things that have already been achieved, if we are to have a real impact on the world emerging from the tragedy of 9/11. i am pleased to note that the committee on constitutional affairs of the european parliament has discussed at length and with great attention the implications of the common foreign and security policy for the functioning of the institutions and in particular of the council. i welcome the proposals in the poos report and i congratulate mr poos on the results achieved in dealing with such complex and sensitive issues. i hope that this house will approve them in full today and that the council will commit itself to making them operational as soon as possible. the commission is ready to cooperate fully in this direction. the declarations of 14 september have important implications for the union's foreign policy priorities. in the short and medium term we must pay even greater attention to our dialogue with the arab and islamic worlds; to the middle east peace process, which is at the heart of the tragedies we are experiencing; to the full exploitation - and this is our task - of all the potential that the barcelona process has to offer us. the time has come to open a new phase in mediterranean policy. the results achieved so far - though not always, and often not because of us - have not been satisfactory. now we must make the most of every opportunity at our disposal to make a qualitative leap. the euro-mediterranean area must have concrete prospects for economic integration and the establishment of institutional mechanisms for joint decision-making. we are all expecting a revival of our role in the middle east. we must act concretely and jointly to meet this difficult challenge, which is within our reach today. in broadening our horizons, we must review our policies on trade and cooperation with pakistan, india and iran, as well as with saudi arabia and the gulf countries. we have already made some concrete progress with pakistan in the past few days. i also believe that we should be prepared to respond to renewed signs of interest and concrete action towards common objectives - such as the fight against diseases such as aids - from countries such as libya. this is a completely new development. once again, europe is in the best position to respond to these political signals and to help these countries join our coalition. at the same time, we must work vigorously to build a coherent and active policy with all our neighbours: a partnership with objectives, institutions and means, in particular in our relations with russia and ukraine; the european union is committed to a partnership that chance for sustainable development. i've said it before and i'll say it again: we need to govern globalization, make it work for everyone, rich and poor alike. we europeans should be proud of the
