council. - mr president, mr rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, i am in a perilous position because i have to speak as president of the institution which, according to the rapporteur, is the worst-functioning of all the institutions of the union. so exercise is definitely dangerous. you will agree that the presidency has read with great interest mr poos' report on the reform of the council. mr poos has a very distinguished political career, which he has led in various european forums, which he knows well, both from within, for having participated in them, and from outside, for having observed them with critical interest. however, let me say that the presidency broadly shares the analysis, perhaps not the qualification, but the analysis that there is a need to improve the functioning of the council. the european council in helsinki in june 1999 had already recognised that important changes were needed in the council's working methods and indicated that these changes should be introduced gradually so that by the time of enlargement the council could smoothly take on the increase in its membership. the same council also approved operational recommendations to this effect. the main thrust of these recommendations is broadly in line with some of the concerns expressed in mr poos' report. i will mention only a few. the recommendations thus stressed that the european council's priority task should be to give the union the impetus it needs for its development and to define its general political guidelines. they emphasized the general coordination role of the general affairs council. the committee also called for better coordination of european policy in the member states. the recommendations stressed that it is ultimately up to coreper to prepare and present to the council all items on the agenda. they also called for a reduction in the number of council configurations. these recommendations, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, have been partially implemented. for example, the general affairs council followed the practice recommended in helsinki, which consisted in dividing the council's agenda systematically into two parts: external relations and horizontal issues, including overall policy coordination. the general affairs council also reduced the number of council configurations to sixteen, in order to improve the coherence of its work and to prevent fragmentation of the union's activities. the role of coreper has been specified in the council's rules of procedure. public debates are now being held on new important legislative proposals, as well as on the agenda of the general affairs council and the ecofin council. a first review of the implementation of the helsinki recommendations was presented by the secretary-general of the council at the european council in gothenburg in june this year. it shows that progress has been made, but that it is still insufficient.
commission - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam president, i too would like to say that the commission very much shares the analysis made in this excellent report on the council's dysfunction. i am not surprised by the quality of this analysis, given the experience and expertise acquired over the last few years and now put at the service of the european parliament by you, mr poos. i would like to say, after this first overall assessment, that the commission also supports the reforms you propose for the council. the restructuring of the european parliament into a structured and efficient body is in the interest of the whole european union. your report takes up many of the suggestions and observations that we have made in the past, including in our recent white paper on european governance. these reforms are all the more interesting because they can be introduced - as you have said - at the same time. in speaking here about the council, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would of course like to say that, from my point of view, each of our institutions has its own autonomy and is first and foremost responsible for its own reforms. but we also know that each institution is interested in the proper functioning of the whole: that is the spirit and the limits with which i wish to give you the european commission's opinion of the other institution, the council of ministers. it is true that in the debate on the future of the union we must fundamentally examine this institutional architecture, the role of each institution and the changes to be made to the treaty if our union is to have a truly more democratic and effective institutional framework. that is why i think, mr poos, that your report is a very important element in the great debate which is about to begin on the institutional framework of the union, its effectiveness and its democratic legitimacy. nevertheless, the debate on these most fundamental reforms in the run-up to 2004 cannot be an alibi for refusing to adopt today the reforms which the council can already implement in accordance with the treaty. the white paper also sets out the objective of making the council's work as efficient as possible. beyond the differences that can be expressed on some particular point, there is a certain convergence in the analysis of the malfunctions we see - and therefore the reforms that must be carried out - in the framework of the report you are presenting, mr poos, the white paper and also - as you have reminded, madam minister - the trumpf-piris report, drawn up by the general secretariat of the council itself, the operational conclusions of which were widely accepted in helsinki by the european council and which has also been largely implemented in the council's rules of procedure. it is the responsibility and duty of each institution - i repeat - to keep under constant review the efficiency of its own operation. the commission has done so by adopting the white paper and proposing the administrative reform advocated by my colleague neil kinnock. it seems to me that the council will have to do the same someday, as will the european parliament, and the commission will certainly support these two institutions in this exercise. i would remind you that the european council in gothenburg has already instructed the secretary-general of the council to make detailed proposals to that effect for its meeting in laeken. i would like to stress, without going into the details of each of the proposals in your report, mr poos, that the completion of this work of evaluation and improvement is first and foremost a simple matter of political will. it is clear that this will must be expressed as much by the governments of the member states as by our own institutions. at least two points deserve special attention: the concept of the legislative council and the role of the general affairs council. we are well aware, ladies and gentlemen, that mr poos' report distinguishes between three functions of the council, namely a legislative function, a governmental function and a policy coordination function. it is very clear from this - and the commission supports you on this point too - that the council will have to organise itself differently depending on whether it is acting in the context of one or other of these three functions. the legislative council should therefore act in a transparent manner, with open debates and public votes. the number of sectoral councils is probably too high, but it is above all the lack of coordination between these sectoral councils that makes it so that, unlike the european parliament, where all final decisions are taken by the plenary assembly, the 'council' branch of the legislator probably has, by its very nature, much more difficulty in coordinating its various decisions. this situation calls for special reflection on the desire - mentioned in your report - to promote consensus between parliament and the council in the co-decision procedure from the first reading. mr poos, while the commission fully shares this desire to obtain rapid agreements, we must avoid that they are made at the expense of the coherence of the texts it has proposed. the treaties have given the commission the exclusive right of initiative and the duty to safeguard the common interest. the commission is therefore hoping that parliament and the council will ensure that the commission is fully involved in all substantive and procedural aspects of the first reading, in order to ensure that the texts adopted are consistent.

i have to say that i am not in favour of this. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been a great help to us in the past. this second directive on combating money laundering in europe has a long history. you know that the money laundering legislation in the member states of the european union has its origin less in the will of the national legislators than in the fact that in 1991 the european union had already launched a first money laundering directive, which then was the initial trigger for the vote and decision on a number of national money laundering laws. however, this 1991 directive had only a minimum standard. this minimum standard required drug offences to be recorded in the criminal records catalogue and, with regard to the professions that were required to participate in the fight against money laundering, only banks and financial service providers were obliged to do so. this has led to wide variations in implementation across europe. there have been member states which have gone far beyond this minimum standard, and there have been member states which have only implemented this minimum standard. we have already held a major hearing on this subject in the european parliament's committee on internal affairs back in 1995. the result of this consultation was that this different standard of implementation leads to major problems in the fight against money laundering in europe, because cooperation between member states also did not work sufficiently. the consequence for us in this house was already then - and there have been two reports on this, one in 1996 and another in 1998 - that we asked the commission to come forward with a proposal for a second directive with the aim of raising the standard in europe, in particular by extending the register of criminal records and also by making other occupational groups subject to the obligation. we have already mentioned the professions of luxury goods dealers, gambling casinos, auctioneers, but also lawyers, notaries and other legal professions. the commission then made its proposal in 1999, but in our view it was not sensitive enough, at least as regards the legal profession. you know that since the charter of nice at the latest, but also in national constitutional systems, there has been a right of citizens to legal advice and representation. this can only be effectively ensured if those citizens are also able to share all information with their legal adviser and can be sure that he will then keep it confidential and not call the prosecutor the next day and pass on the information. the european parliament therefore wanted to maintain this right at first reading, but at the same time to combat money laundering in europe effectively. this has continued until the conciliation procedure and i think the compromise that has been reached is a good compromise. the council has made concessions in order to allow member states, in accordance with their legal traditions, to continue to subject legal advice to the obligation of professional secrecy. the european parliament, on the other hand, has also given in by not requiring this regulation but leaving it to the discretion of the national legislators. article 6 (3) therefore provides for an option allowing all member states to ensure that the obligation of professional secrecy in the field of legal advice is maintained in accordance with their national legal traditions. the same procedure was followed for the other points in dispute. there too, good compromises have been found. the issue of tip-off, i.e. the prohibition on passing on information to one's own clients, was also resolved by a compromise within the meaning of article 6 (3) - i.e. an option scheme. the question of what to do with the information provided there and now in the possession of the national law enforcement authorities has been left to the national legislator. to sum up, all the groups involved said at the end that they were not 100% satisfied with this compromise and that it was not ideal, but that they could live with it. that is precisely the nature of a good compromise, and that is why i would recommend mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr meijer, you are right. let me say in advance that i do want to say a word of thanks to you, because i know how committed you have been to trying to bring this issue up and how many conversations you have had to put forward a proposal, so to speak. i must say, however, that i cannot accept most of what you propose. all that we are discussing today is not new in principle. when the regulation finally came from the commission in the summer of 2000, when it reached parliament and when the first talks with trade unions, representatives of local transport operators and representatives of associations began, it was clear to everyone that there would be controlled competition. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. the question was also which exemptions from the obligation to tender should apply. all this played a role, as did the recurrent question of social dumping, i.e. the danger that tenders could recruit particularly cheap labour. there was a consensus. we want controlled competition, which is not privatization, by the way. it's always confused. it is not automatically privatisation. the only consequence is that it is no longer automatic that municipal transport companies continue to benefit from substantial subsidies from the land, the federal government or the local authorities without having to face competition, but that in future there should be a tendering obligation. we all know that the local transport companies - and they know this too - are in principle offering their product at too high a price. the reason for this is that in recent decades, trade unions have always been very successful in collective bargaining, particularly in the public service. it is a given that in the private bus sector - commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr meijer, for the work he has done; it is a complex and complicated work, a proposal which has given rise to many amendments and positions. the good work of mr meijer and all the honourable members has enabled a very important debate to take place in this house. in many ways, this debate has helped to generate another broad public debate. the analyses in this dossier, both within and outside the institutions, help the commission to improve its own ideas. the debate has highlighted the controversy surrounding these issues, although there have been times when the feelings have not revealed the real substance of the proposal we are dealing with. firstly, there is legal uncertainty in this sector today and what we want to do with this proposal, ladies and gentlemen - and this must be made very clear - is to resolve a situation of legal uncertainty which can create serious problems in public transport. the first aim of this initiative is precisely - as mr jarzembowski has said - to promote public transport; we all agree that the european union must promote quality public transport at the best possible price. the commission considers that many existing contracts and agreements, which confer exclusive rights or financial compensation, risk being challenged under the competition rules of the treaty. this is the risk we face and which we intend to solve with this proposal. secondly, if the problem of legal uncertainty is already very serious in itself, it is also clear that regulated competition in public transport must benefit both users and society at large. the facts have shown that systems open to competition controlled and regulated by the public sector have experienced faster growth in the number of travellers during the 1990s than systems not subject to any competitive pressure. the reality is that we do not want private monopolies either. i am sure you will understand that it would take hours to present the commission's position on each of the 130 amendments to this dossier. i shall therefore refer to the fundamental questions raised by the honourable members and, as regards the specification of the amendment numbers, i am at your disposal. as far as what we can accept, we welcome first of all the proposals to strengthen the quality criteria which the authorities must take into account when assessing transport needs and when awarding contracts. when markets are opened up, the authorities will have to address all employment, environmental, consumer and possibly even more issues if services remain closed to competitive pressures. we must therefore facilitate the opening up of the market, precisely to guarantee those standards and levels of employment, the environment and consumers that we all want. secondly, the commission may also accept a longer maximum duration of contracts. we find the time limits proposed in amendments nos 15 and 54 (8 years for buses and 15 years for railways) acceptable. thirdly, as regards the exceptions to the competition principle, only those amendments which do not go against our initial proposal are accepted, and not those which seek to limit the scope of the regulation even further. we can also accept those amendments which raise the de minimis thresholds for direct awards. and, after attending the debate, we accept that emergency situations may arise where it is impossible to organise the competition in time, and in a way that allows the service to be maintained. the amendments in this direction are therefore acceptable in principle, although they may need to be reworded. we believe that they should be combined in a single emergency clause covering other similar circumstances as well. the commission could also accept those which help to give the authorities responsible for compensation more flexibility in relation to the general rules for all operators, such as those setting maximum rates, which in some cases should be applied with nuance. finally, ladies and gentlemen, the commission can accept the idea of a transitional period ending at eight years, as proposed in amendment no 90. however, instead of a big bang at that date, we think that the regulation should provide for a gradual opening up of the market by the authorities, with a first step being taken after four years. it is also acceptable that existing contracts, awarded in accordance with competition, can continue their natural course, provided that their duration is fixed (i.e. they are not unlimited contracts) and reasonable. however, ladies and gentlemen, there are things we cannot accept, because they would distort the meaning of the commission's proposal. for example, we cannot support the exclusion of entire sectors from the scope of the regulation; we cannot accept amendments nos 23, 28 and 128, which would exclude all long distance services. parliament may be in favour of widening competition in long distance rail passenger transport, but it would prefer that this issue be dealt with in the second railway package. the draft report raises legal problems in certain cases. amendment no 24 would give priority to the regulation on directives on public procurement. ladies and gentlemen, the commission is of the opinion that this could lead to the european union breaching commitments under the world trade organisation's public procurement agreement. for this reason, we cannot accept this amendment either. the second legal problem concerns reciprocity. permanent and structural reciprocity clauses are contrary to the non-discrimination requirements of the treaties. we cannot therefore accept amendments which simply propose structural reciprocity clauses. however, we believe that, until certain exceptions are introduced, it is necessary to be able to accept, on a transitional and exceptional basis, some type of clause restricting access to a market. it is important that the transition to controlled competition be accompanied by appropriate safeguards, including in the area of social protection, as has been pointed out by several honourable members. we cannot therefore accept amendments which would leave the competent authorities with no room for manoeuvre in this respect. i have presented the commission's views on most of the major issues raised in mr meijer's report, but - i assume you have not missed them - there are still some crucial issues. for example, the report includes a group of amendments (3, 12, 14, 61, 100, 126 and 129) which seek to safeguard the ability of public operators to continue to exist without their ability to compete and to provide services in an appropriate and good service to citizens being regularly challenged, through public tenders. in legal terms, there is no fundamental problem with the principle that public authorities decide to provide the transport service themselves. it's in the initiative. the main legal problem arises when the public authority continues to deny all other undertakings the possibility of providing these services in the same area, in transparent and fair competition. we are talking about transport at a certain level, not small-scale transport between two towns, which is excluded from the scope of this directive by the de minimis rule, as is clearly stated. we are talking about important transport markets. we cannot therefore accept these amendments as they stand. we believe that they do not benefit the citizens, because they go too far, isolating operators from the market pressures to maintain and improve the situation. however, we believe that the option of self-production provided for in those amendments could be maintained, subject to certain strict and clearly stated conditions. it is clear that this approach should be accompanied by provisions to ensure that all operators maintain quality and integration standards and that the authorities remain able to control competition for the benefit of the users of services. the final part of amendment no 112, which proposes the direct award of up to 10% of public services to a private sector operator, is also acceptable, provided that the authority cannot invoke this and other exceptions in the simultaneous tendering for a single mode of transport. finally, ladies and gentlemen, if parliament votes on this report as it stands, i fear that the text, the spirit and the objective of the commission's proposal would be seriously affected. in this sense, it would be necessary to re-examine overall what this change would actually bring to community legislation. the commission still believes that the current regulation (which has been in force for several decades) needs to be modernised and updated in order to provide public transport with sufficient legal certainty to guarantee the highest level of quality, greater competitiveness, better prices and legal certainty to enable public authorities to subsidize and financially support certain routes or certain requirements, such as those of pensioners or other groups, without having to argue before the courts. we need efficient public transport, at the service of the citizens, which will help to rebalance transport systems and avoid a future situation of collapse within the european transport system, which would cause damage to the productive, economic and competitive capacity, to job creation and, above all, to the quality of life of our citizens.

chairman of the committee on economic and monetary affairs. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. the report on the proposal for a council regulation introducing temporary safeguard measures for shipbuilding is of particular importance because shipbuilding in the european union is a sector of strategic importance. i should like to take this opportunity to express the opinion of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, which unfortunately does not agree with the rapporteur's opinion. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs riis-jørgensen, for her excellent work, especially in the very short time available. i would therefore like to thank her, even though she has difficulty in accepting the legality of this proposal. we have of course examined this as a committee and have come to the conclusion that the legal basis has been chosen correctly and that the concerns about the legality of the proposal have been wrongly expressed. i would therefore like to say a few words about the content of the proposal and the report. i would like to stress the good cooperation with the committee on industry, trade, research and energy. i think we have made a good proposal. i very much hope that the commission will accept parliament's amendments. in its conclusions of 5 december 2000, the industry/energy council confirmed the end of operating aid to shipbuilding from 1 january 2001, in accordance with the council decision of 1998. however, it was already indicated at that time that the commission might change its position following a review in the event of a failure of the negotiations with korea. we must note that korea has not complied with the 2000 agreement on price and subsidy discipline. the commission therefore had to consider whether, in the event of the failure of the negotiations with korea, which continues to violate the existing trade agreements by granting state subsidies, a temporary aid mechanism for the european shipbuilding industry should be proposed. the proposal is now before us because the negotiations have failed and the proposed safeguard measures have to be evaluated. the committee considers that the proposal is inadequate because it is limited to container ships and tankers for the transport of petroleum products and to chemical tankers, except those made of stainless steel. the proposal allows for an operating aid of 6% and, in special cases, up to 14%. the commission also proposes to open a dispute settlement procedure at the wto. the aid is to be granted only until the procedure is closed, at the latest by 31 december 2002. we believe that the european parliament should stick to its position of initiating a dispute settlement procedure. the proposal for temporary safeguard measures presented needs to be improved, however, since the three market segments it covers account for only 20% of european shipbuilding. in contrast, virtually all market segments in the european union are affected by unfair competition from korea. in particular, the categories of vessels which will also be the subject of the complaint to the wto must be included. only then will our message to korea be clear and convincing. i think that your agreement to amendments nos 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 is of the utmost importance. we also consider that the duration of the agreement is insufficient. we therefore propose that the safeguard measures should be applied at least for the duration of the current regulation 1540/98 on aid to shipbuilding, which expires on 31 december 2003, or possibly even until the wto procedure is concluded. as the european parliament, as the european union, we must not allow unfair trading practices to damage the european economy and put jobs at risk, otherwise such unfair trading practices will spread to other sectors and damage growth and jobs too. at the same time, however, we must also carefully weigh up the justified protectionist measures against the anti-market protection of certain sectors by state aid which prevents fair competition. i believe that the committee's proposal reflects this concern and i would ask that this report be accepted and that the commission declare its willingness to accept the amendments.

the council has not yet adopted the common position on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. my speech is intended to take stock of this and to inform you of the initiatives which have been taken and which will be developed by the council. i shall therefore concentrate on afghanistan, which is at the heart of the current crisis, but i shall also mention the situation in the middle east. the council has reacted with determination and clarity to the emergency situation in afghanistan. the european council, at its meetings on 21 september and 19 october, defined the framework for european union action, the main elements of which are as follows. firstly, solidarity with the united states and support for action taken in selfdefence and in accordance with un security council resolution 1368, on the understanding that it must be targeted action to spare civilian populations. secondly, a contribution to the anti-terrorist coalition formed under the auspices of the united nations. the troika visited pakistan, iran, saudi arabia, syria and egypt at the end of september, where it also met with the leaders of the arab league. recently, a tour of central asian countries was carried out. the eu-russia summit on 3 october and the european conference on 20 october provided an opportunity to discuss the efforts to be made at international level. the november session of the general assembly will be a further opportunity to strengthen this coalition. in concrete terms, the european union is articulating its strategy for afghanistan around five major axes: priority for emergency humanitarian aid, the central role of the un, the search for a just and lasting internal political solution, the importance of a reconstruction plan for the country and, finally, the need to give a regional dimension to the stabilisation plan. it should be noted that these five priorities were clearly endorsed by the general affairs council in luxembourg on 17 october and by the informal summit in ghent on 19 october. in terms of emergency humanitarian aid, some eur 320 million has been mobilised to date to address the refugee and displaced persons crisis and the effects of famine. the main difficulty is access to people in need, which requires the full cooperation of afghanistan's neighbouring states. the presidency has taken various steps to this end. in terms of mobilizing and distributing aid, close coordination is ensured between the cooperation agencies of the member states, echo and the various international humanitarian organizations, whether the unhcr or the world food programme, not to mention the icrc and the many ngos. secondly, the central role of the un. the european union recognises that the united nations alone has international legitimacy in the search for an internal political solution. the role of the united nations will also be crucial in the implementation of a reconstruction plan for the country. the european union therefore relies on the secretary-general and his representative for afghanistan in their efforts. it also pays particular attention to the plan which has just been presented by the special representative of the un secretary-general, mr brahimi. the council shall coordinate its action to determine the best way of contributing to the implementation of this plan. as regards the internal political solution, it is important for the european union that the future afghan authorities be elected by the afghans, that they be representative of the ethnic groups present and that they respect and promote human rights, humanitarian law and the rule of law in general; the european union is also committed to the principle of non-alignment, which is the basis for the european union's policy on the middle east. the european union prefers not to express itself openly in favour of one solution or another at the moment, leaving this role to the special representative of the un secretary-general and to the afghans themselves. as regards the reconstruction plan, the european union considers that, in view of the internal political developments in afghanistan, there is an urgent need to draw up a reconstruction plan for the country. it wishes to be associated with it, as do many other actors, including donor countries and international organisations. it also considers that this will be a long-term project, involving a long-term commitment from the participants in the plan. the european union is convinced that the peace process in afghanistan will be completed by the end of the year. in other words, it is a question of convincing afghanistan's neighbouring states, as well as certain other powers in the region, that pacification of afghanistan will also be to their advantage. the security concerns of these states must be legitimately taken into account to prevent the continuation of the foreign interference that has so often undermined afghanistan and fuelled its internal conflicts. the european union considers the following countries and international organisations to be essential elements of any regional strategy on the afghan issue. this is the case for pakistan, iran, india, uzbekistan, tajikistan, turkmenistan, china, russia and the organisation of the islamic conference. of course, we cannot help but mention the latest developments. events have accelerated in recent days with the capture of mazar-e-sharif and kabul. these events are evidence that the taliban regime and terrorist networks are gradually losing control of afghanistan. they are a further step towards achieving the objectives of the international coalition, namely the eradication of terrorist networks. at this crucial time for the future of afghanistan, the president-in-office of the european council, mr verhofstadt, yesterday reiterated the council's position that there will never be stability in afghanistan unless a stable, legitimate, democratic government is installed in the country, representative of all ethnic groups. it will also be necessary for this government to adhere fully to the principles of human rights. he also stressed that the united nations should play a central role in helping the afghans to form a government. the union intends to support the un plans in this direction and urges the northern alliance to contribute fully to these efforts. the union is also ready to help afghanistan to devise and implement a comprehensive reconstruction plan, which is an essential guarantee of peace. this project does not in any way alter the priority given to the urgent humanitarian aid that the afghan people need more than ever. the president-in-office of the european council also stressed the regional dimension of the afghan problem. while it is obvious that the afghans themselves will have to decide who will govern them in the future, the fact remains that all countries in the region must feel reassured by a new afghan government. it is in this spirit that the president of the european council will, together with the president of the commission, begin a visit to india and pakistan on 23 and 24 november. finally, as regards the middle east, the situation in the middle east remains a central concern of the european union. the violence and lack of confidence between the parties are preventing the resumption of political dialogue, which should begin with the implementation of the tenet plan and the recommendations of the mitchell report and should eventually lead to a just and lasting solution to the conflict, based on un security council resolutions 242 and 338 and the madrid and oslo principles. in the context of a strategy of relay diplomacy, the european union, whether representatives of the member states or the council, is constantly present on the ground. the action of the high representative mr solana, the special envoy mr moratinos and several european ministers made it possible, after many vicissitudes, to hold the peres-arafat meeting on 26 september. unfortunately, israelis and palestinians have failed to put into practice this new attempt to establish a ceasefire. the euromed conference, held in brussels on 5 and 6 november, provided an opportunity for a wide-ranging exchange of views on the question of stability and security in the mediterranean region. it has, among other things, enabled the parties to take a further step towards the re-establishment of a high-level dialogue which could, in the long run, restore the confidence necessary for a resumption of final status negotiations. the president of the european council and the president-in-office of the council will be visiting the middle east again this week. they will be accompanied by the president of the commission and the high representative, mr solana, whose important role is recognised by all parties. the mission, which falls within the mandate given to the belgian presidency by the informal council in ghent, will be an opportunity to remind the parties once again of the clear position of the european union on the objectives to be achieved by the final negotiations, namely the establishment of a viable and democratic state for the palestinians and the end of the occupation of their territory, and the right of the israelis to live in peace and security within internationally recognised borders. the european union will also recall that the search for a comprehensive and lasting peace in the region requires that due account be taken of the israeli-syrian and israeli-lebanese aspects of the conflict, the resolution of which must be based on the same principles. in conclusion, as you can see, the european union has not spared its efforts to try to bring the middle east closer together, and will continue to do so as long as necessary. the european union also continues to follow closely developments in afghanistan and the whole of the central asian region. it will continue to work within the framework of the anti-terrorist coalition to combat all forms of support for international terrorism. commission. - madam president, madam minister, ladies and gentlemen, as you know, the situation in afghanistan is changing very rapidly. almost every hour brings its share of fresh and dramatic news. the military strategy against the taliban is a success. nevertheless, it is important to emphasize that, despite the encouraging developments of these last days, the task is far from finished. the military component of the campaign has not yet achieved all its objectives and we have always made it clear that the humanitarian and diplomatic component is of vital importance. in the light of what has happened, it is appropriate to redouble efforts in this area. the european union must also make a stronger effort to establish a broad-based government for the afghan people. as mrs durant has also stressed, we strongly support the process being led by the united nations under the auspices of ambassador brahimi. in addition, we must take advantage of the new military situation to increase our humanitarian effort. the commission is playing an active role on both fronts. last week commissioner patten met with mr wolfensohn, president of the world bank, and this week he met with ambassador brahimi in new york. the commission will work closely with the world bank and other parties to assess needs and contribute to the reconstruction effort in afghanistan. the commission does not intend to speculate at this stage on the precise amounts involved. the first step will be for the international community to assess the urgent needs and define, in consultation with the afghan people, exactly what needs are. in the meantime, we are working to ensure that the €52 million of aid allocated under the echo programme for 2001 and the €22.5 million for displaced persons in 2001 reach those in need. in addition, we are providing €23.5 million in food aid, or about 36,300 tonnes, through the world food programme, and we are giving €4.5 million to ngos to provide the population with food, seeds and tools, for a total of about €100 million in aid this year. in addition, we have already planned to ensure that these levels are at least maintained in 2002. you know that the commission has not spared any effort since the events of 9/11. you also know that in the space of a few days we have presented new measures to combat terrorism in europe, including a common definition of terrorist acts, a european arrest warrant to replace the cumbersome extradition system in force between member states, a tightening of the rules on money laundering and, finally, a legislative mechanism to freeze quickly the assets of an individual or an organisation throughout europe, as soon as it is identified as a potential source of terrorist financing. the commission has also been quick to take measures to improve air safety, from access to cockpits to baggage surveillance. at the same time, european ministers collectively decided that member states should be able to protect airlines from the worst consequences of 9/11, for example by providing them with insurance cover against acts of terrorism, which commercial insurers no longer offered, while avoiding a war of subsidies that would distort competition. the european union is also providing massive humanitarian aid inside and outside afghanistan. the eu and its member states have already mobilised some eur 310 million to alleviate the suffering of the afghan people. this effort, second only to the united states, is largely unrecognized, but it has already saved lives. in addition, the echo humanitarian office has acted with impressive diligence in translating the commitments into action. under the leadership of president romano prodi, the commission is also involved in the crucial diplomatic effort, and minister durant has also mentioned the trips that mr prodi will have to make in the coming days and weeks. this is obviously a sign of the european will to achieve a balanced international diplomatic action. as you know, in the days following the attacks, mr patten, together with mr louis michel, belgian minister for foreign affairs, representing the belgian presidency of the council of the eu, and mr solana, visited pakistan, iran, egypt, saudi arabia and syria. everywhere they went, they heard the same message: all of humanity must unite in the fight against terrorism. they discussed the need to strengthen cooperation ties in the region. the union has already taken a major trade initiative by improving access for pakistani exports to europe, and we hope to be able to conclude a free trade agreement with the six gulf cooperation council states soon. we will also make proposals for a trade and cooperation agreement with iran. we are also playing our full part in the efforts to relaunch the middle east peace process, not only by providing financial support to a palestinian authority in enormous difficulty, but also by working to implement the mitchell report, to which the european union is a co-signatory. mr peres and mr arafat, as mrs durant has pointed out, both attended a euro-mediterranean conference in brussels this week. as you can see, the european union has a common foreign policy, but it is not a single policy. each country, each institution, is harnessing its own strengths and putting its own resources to work for the common cause. the determined action of individual member states strengthens the common effort, and vice versa. the fact that member states take independent initiatives, especially in a crisis, is not a sign of a failure of the union. it is the illustration of his very nature. in conclusion, i can say on behalf of the commission that we are all aware that the events of 11 september changed the game and we have recognised that the attacks on new york and washington were an attack not only on the united states but on all free and open societies. the threat is a common threat, which is why it requires a concerted response. the european union, and the european commission in particular, is making a full contribution to this common objective and we intend to continue along this path. commission. – mr president, the position taken by the committee on economic and monetary affairs on the proposal under discussion has surprised me. it diverges considerably from the position taken by this parliament in 1996. at that time, parliament urged the commission to make proposals for upward harmonisation of tobacco prices, based upon higher duty rates across the union for reasons including health protection, and to consider measures to reduce the scope for price manipulation by cigarette producers applying widely diverging pre-tax on the markets of each member state. the present commission proposal is consistent with that opinion. that is why i say that the advice of the economic and monetary affairs committee has greatly surprised me. the commission is doing what parliament wanted in 1996 and therefore it is odd that the report should not accept the commission's proposal. the changes proposed will bring about increased convergence in duty rates within the european union and, as such, improve the functioning of the internal market, both now and as it will be after enlargement. they will also reduce the incentive for excise fraud within the union. more surprisingly – and mr blokland has just drawn attention to this – the draft report does not set out the reasons for rejecting the commission proposal. that is the least that the commission would have expected. according to the working document presented by the rapporteur to emac in june, the main justification is that the introduction of a minimum amount of taxation of eur 70 for cigarettes constitutes a shift towards specific taxation, and would disadvantage small- and medium-sized producers in southern member states. i would like to emphasise that this is emphatically not the view of the commission. the introduction of a fixed amount in euro does not alter the structure of excise duties on cigarettes. member states affected by the introduction of the fixed amount will retain the flexibility they enjoy at present to determine the proportions of the specific and ad valorem components of cigarette taxation, as other rules remain unchanged. i would also like to point out that the commission proposal has received broad support in the council. last week in the ecofin council the member states unanimously agreed a compromise text produced by the belgian presidency, which is clearly in line with the commission's proposal. for cigarette taxation, the most significant element is the introduction of a minimum amount of duty of eur 60 at the initial stage and eur 64 at a later stage, rather than the eur 70 proposed by the commission. the adoption of the proposal is also extremely important in view of the forthcoming enlargement of the union eastwards. mr folias has quite rightly drawn our attention to that aspect of the proposal. the existing minimum taxation requirement – the so-called 57% rule – allows for a higher degree of price manipulation and would not in itself be sufficient to reduce to a sustainable level the gap between the tax and price levels of the present member states and the candidate countries. such a situation would result in substantial revenue loss for present member states, especially those having borders with candidate countries. the requirement for a minimum amount of duty will avoid this happening and ensure the proper functioning of the internal market after enlargement. the commission is aware that achieving the amounts in euro will require a significant effort from most candidate countries. therefore, it has proposed that the council grant limited transitional periods to candidate countries for reaching the minimum rate of taxation. next, i was pleased to see that the two parliament committees that have issued opinions on the proposal – the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, with mr maaten as draftsman, and the committee for legal affairs and the internal market, with mr wieland as draftsman – accepted the general thrust of the proposal, subject to a number of amendments. most of the amendments proposed in mr maaten's report have been re-tabled in this plenary. the commission broadly shares the concerns of mr maaten on the need to pay more attention to health policy and to combat fraud and smuggling. i do not see why mr katiforis cannot accept the arguments relating to health. it is a well known fact – and i am sure he is aware of it – that 75% of smokers started before the age of 18. report after report and study after study confirm that for young people under the age of 18, price clearly is a determining factor in terms of smoking. i was pleased to hear both mrs stihler and mr blokland support the view of the commission that there is a direct link between price and quantity consumed and that therefore the price very definitely has a bearing on health. mr folias said that if the price goes up then cheaper cigarettes will be purchased and smoked. according to that reasoning, if the price went down then more expensive cigarettes would also be purchased. that is something that, in reality, is not noticeable. therefore, with all due respect to mr folias, his reasoning is not in line with reality. while i am answering specific questions by parliament, i have to say that i do not understand the argument by mr wieland – referring to the legal aspects of the case – when he says that the interplay of vat and excise taxes would be illegal. of course they have a bearing on competition and smuggling, as we all know, but why should this be illegal, as he maintains? the point of view of his committee is based on the legal state of affairs. he says that there is a problem in that cigarillos of a certain dimension and character should be treated as cigars and not as cigarettes. well, i have some here. if you showed an average citizen of the european union this packet of cigarillos, took one of them out – of the same dimensions and weight as an ordinary cigarette – and asked them if it was more like a cigarette or more like a cigar, i would wager mr wieland 144 packets of cigarettes or cigarillos – whichever he prefers – that the average citizen of the european union would classify them as cigarettes. most of the amendments proposed in mr maaten's opinion have been retabled for this plenary. the commission broadly shares these concerns on the need to pay more attention to health policy. but the amendments require no change to the proposal. according to the existing review requirements, the commission already has the obligation to take into account the wider treaty objectives, including health. new developments, resulting for instance from the conclusion of a who framework convention on tobacco control, will thus automatically have to be taken into consideration in a subsequent review. the commission and the member states have also taken a number of initiatives to combat fraud and smuggling following the considers the proposals by the commission to be a direct reply to parliament's own opinion expressed in 1996. therefore the commission invites all members of parliament who have expressed an opinion contrary to that of the commission to reconsider their position on this issue very carefully before tomorrow's vote.

counsel. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as you know, the european council meeting in brussels-laeken on 14 and 15 december will deal with the following subjects: the future of the european union, the european security and defence policy, enlargement, the fight against terrorism, the area of freedom, security and justice, the general situation and prospects of the union, employment and social cohesion, the various institutions and agencies, and external relations. the future of the european union: the european council will adopt the text of a declaration to launch the debate on the future of europe. the text consists of a first part on the strengths and weaknesses of european integration, a second part which sets out the thematic issues that the convention could address, and a third part which lays down the arrangements for organising the debate. the general affairs council of 19 november confirmed the convergence of the member states as regards the procedure. the principle of convening a preparatory convention is an important step towards a union that is more comprehensible, stronger and more concerned with pursuing its essential objectives. the participation of representatives of governments, the commission, national parliaments and the european parliament in the convention is of course a given. the presidency's proposal for the candidate countries is based on the following principles: they shall be fully associated with the work of the convention and have the right to speak; they will be represented in the same way as the member states, i.e. one representative of the government and two representatives of their parliament; those candidate countries which have not yet signed their accession treaty will not participate in the convention's consensus when the convention prepares its final report. the president of the convention will be appointed by the laeken european council. the president shall be assisted by a bureau composed of representatives of the various components of the convention. the participation of the presidency-in-office is confirmed, the participation of the representatives of the two subsequent presidencies remains to be decided. finally, the secretariat of the convention will be provided by the general secretariat of the council. it will be able to rely on the help of the commission, the european parliament's secretariats and the national parliaments. there was unanimity in favour of consulting civil society through representative organisations at european and national level. the idea of a forum in the form of a separate assembly was dropped. these organisations may be heard or consulted in accordance with methods to be defined. the contributions of these organisations will form part of the official documentation sent to the members of the convention. the work of the convention will begin as soon as possible under the spanish presidency and will be completed by the european council in june 2003. as for the time that will elapse between the end of the convention's work and the start of the intergovernmental conference, this is still being considered. as regards the themes, the presidency's approach has been to build on the content of the nice declaration to develop a sufficiently broad and coherent mandate, which will serve as a basis for the presidency's work. the presidency agrees with the recommendations made by the rapporteurs, mr leinen and mr méndez de vigo. these themes are grouped into five open and neutral groups of questions: the objectives and content of the union's policies, the distribution of competences between the union and its member states, the democratic legitimacy of the system, and the union's capacity to decide and conduct policies. the prime minister will present a draft of the laeken declaration during his visit to the capitals. in this draft, the topics that the convention could address will be presented in the form of questions and choices, so as to enable delegations to make informed decisions. in conclusion on this important chapter, i would like to make the following remarks. whatever the content of the laeken declaration, the convention will retain control of its agenda. it would be futile, i think, to try to confine it to a pre-defined mandate. (applause) i would like to thank the presidency has been busy clarifying and declining the nice themes, where the declaration was deliberately drafted in a relatively open way. nothing proposed by the presidency should be interpreted as a mandate for the future intergovernmental conference. the terms of reference of this conference will be decided in accordance with the procedures laid down in the treaties. finally, the objective of the laeken declaration is to ensure that the convention's methodology bears fruit and that its results are taken up by the 2004 intergovernmental conference. the debate on the future of europe must also aim to make the european union closer, more transparent and more effective. in this respect, the council took note with interest of the report by mrs kaufmann on the white paper on european governance. this report contains valuable information. i share the concern to ensure that the increased involvement of civil society actors in the functioning of the union does not come at the expense of the central role that representative and politically responsible authorities must play. i now turn to the european security and defence policy. the european council will receive a report from the presidency on progress made. work has indeed progressed well in terms of improving military capabilities and strengthening civilian capabilities, as demonstrated by the capability conferences held on 19 and 20 november. as regards the declaration on the operational character of the esdp, the union is faced with the following dilemma: either it is unable to do so because of a veto imposed by a nato member who is not a member of the union, or it declares itself operational without - in the absence of access to nato resources - this declaration being based on real capabilities. in both cases, i would point out that the credibility of the union is, of course, at stake. the third approach advocated by the presidency would be to declare that the union will decide on a case-by-case basis on the response to a crisis, depending on the military and civilian means and capabilities at its disposal. that is the european security and defence policy.
president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the laeken summit must be an important stage in the process of european integration. you will be voting today on two reports which concern the very articulation of the european project and the direction it will take in the years ahead: the report by mr leinen and mr méndez de vigo on the future of the union and the report by mr kaufmann on european governance. to address these issues, we must first answer some fundamental policy questions: what are the new challenges facing the union, both internally and externally? how can the union's institutional architecture be simplified? how can the different responsibilities be shared and the national parliaments involved? the organisational form, in fact, cannot be an end in itself, but must be functional to the objectives we intend to achieve; it must reflect the project of society that the vast majority of european citizens want. the communication on the future of the union which we will be presenting before the laeken council will be based on these very considerations, which i believe are also to be found in both reports under discussion today. first, let us look at the report on the future of the union. if the union were to limit itself to the policies it managed in the 1960s or 1970s, the current institutional framework would probably be adequate. but the political point is something else: citizens are asking the union to do much more; the european union is a global community of nations, and its members are called upon to solve complex problems, which only the present size of the union can successfully tackle. the current institutional structures, however, are not able to respond effectively to these new challenges. reform of the institutional system is therefore needed to make the union more effective in taking the decisions that citizens expect. we cannot continue to raise new expectations without providing ourselves with the means to meet them. we must therefore introduce institutional reforms that go beyond what was envisaged in nice. we must also preserve the essence of the community method, based on the institutional triangle, the real mechanism that has enabled the european community's success story for fifty years: i would like to see a balanced approach based on a strong parliament, a strong council, a strong commission and, even if it goes beyond the triangle, i would say a strong court of justice. it is the only way we can combine efficiency and democracy. it must, however, be renewed and adapted to the new european reality and the union's new priorities. the european parliament has been very active in this area since the beginning of the year. the democratic dimension of the method of reforming the treaties must be strengthened. in particular, there is a strong demand that the involvement of democratically elected representatives should not be limited to the ratification of the basic texts of our union. in the present legal situation, with the limitations we have, the best solution is to have the intergovernmental conference - which i hope once again will be short and decisive - preceded by thorough preparation by the institutions and the national and european parliaments. in two weeks' time, the european council in laeken will take a historic decision, convening the convention to prepare the intergovernmental conference. a convention modelled on the charter of fundamental rights is a good answer to the need to strengthen the role of peoples in building a union which, from its very origins, is a union of states and a union of peoples. this formula, which was proposed by the commission and the european parliament at the beginning of the year, has gradually won over supporters and has been adopted by those member states which, just a few months ago - let us recall what happened in gothenburg - were very reluctant or opposed to accepting it. the convening of a convention, its composition and organisation, and the broadening of the union's constitutional reform agenda, are the key issues at the heart of the laeken declaration. these aspects are analysed in the draft resolution which is before you today. i would first of all like to congratulate the rapporteurs, mr leinen and mr méndez de vigo, on their excellent report on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs. the european commission broadly agrees with much of the report. parliament and the commission agree that we must start with the four points of nice, but as the report shows, they cover more aspects than a first reading might suggest. it is, however, unthinkable to impose taboos and limits on the discussions of a convention in which the majority of members are parliamentarians. all issues that offer adequate support will therefore have to be addressed. it is rather on certain aspects of the composition of the convention that the commission invites the european parliament to give further thought. as you know, there is strong support for the idea that the president of the convention should be appointed by the european council in laeken. i too, on behalf of the commission, support this position, because it is not enough that the convention exists, nor that it functions properly: the convention will have to convince the member states. and a president appointed by the european council, who enjoys the confidence of the heads of state and government, will be able to create much more easily the necessary climate of confidence between the convention and the european council. we fully support the proposal to ensure that the president of the convention also takes part in the work of the intergovernmental conference. there is a difference, however, because the commission is more in favour of a smaller bureau than the draft resolution on which you are voting today, with one representative for each member. the bureau shall organise the work of the convention. it is not possible for all opinions, trends and interests to be represented. the draft resolution calls for the convention to adopt unanimously a single and coherent proposal which can be the sole basis for negotiation and decision by the intergovernmental conference. i hope so and i would be very happy if that were to happen, but we must also be realistic. it is objectively possible that we cannot reach a broad consensus unless we lower our ambitions very much, or too much. i therefore prefer to go into the igc today with stronger and weaker options, to preserve the possibility of reaching strong responses, rather than letting the level of ambition within the convention drop, even before the work of the conference has begun. finally, i see that we agree to ask that the intergovernmental conference finish its work before the start of the electoral campaign for the next european elections. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, we are living through a fundamental change in the life of the union: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. that is why, at the beginning of my mandate, i had indicated that governance reform, i.e. improving the way we work on permanent treaties, was one of the commission's strategic objectives. i would therefore like to speak briefly about the kaufmann report on governance reform. first of all, i would like to congratulate mrs sylvia kaufmann, the chairman of the committee on constitutional affairs, mr napolitano, and the whole of the european parliament on the speed and efficiency with which the work was carried out, in which no less than ten parliamentary committees took part. we have significant points of convergence here too. both our institutions believe that there is a need to critically review and, if necessary, reform governance at european level. the european parliament is in favour of the creation of an interinstitutional working party, as proposed in my speech of 2 october. the commission is ready for this dialogue, which we hope the council will also participate in, at least as regards the matters within the competence of all three institutions. i have repeated this point today, a few hours ago, at the trilogue meeting, and i hope that progress can be made on this. the european parliament also agrees with the commission that budgetary procedures should be simplified and the council's activities made more transparent. finally, and most importantly, the commission and parliament agree that the central political reference point for governance issues must remain the aspect of democratic legitimacy, to which the aspect of efficiency - albeit of paramount importance - must remain subordinate. the kaufmann report also raises a number of parliament's concerns. i would like to stress, first of all, that the commission's proposals in the white paper are aimed at strengthening the democratic process and thus at strengthening the role of the european parliament. i am not going to change my view: the european parliament is the central element of democratic legitimacy, without which there can be no real support from european citizens. but let us also examine the concerns. firstly, there is the fear that civil society will override the european parliament. i can assure you that this is not the intention of the commission, because it was the commission which proposed that each institution should return to its original tasks and redefine its respective powers. secondly, the european parliament - and this is the commission's view - is the highest democratic expression of european civil society and the natural representative of its institutions. at the same time, the commission must make informed decisions in the process of drawing up legislative proposals. it cannot therefore dispense with appropriate consultations - i repeat, consultations - with economic and social operators, with the scientific and technical world and with cultural figures. it is therefore necessary to rationalize and structure a dialogue which has long been a constant feature of our way of working. i have read the kaufmann report very carefully on this point and i can assure you that we will take the most careful account of the indications - including those of method - which it contains. the commission has no intention of calling into question the prerogatives of the european parliament as a co-legislator, nor has it ever done so. our proposals on co-regulation and self-regulation are aimed solely at preventing practices which have been in existence for many years from proceeding in anarchy and falling into the abuses which you have yourself pointed out. the commission's proposals are aimed at this. in addition, our proposals would stipulate that the use of co-regulation would be decided on a case-by-case basis, after the european parliament has given its opinion. i have already said that the criteria and limits for the use of these new legislative instruments should be the subject of debate - and possibly agreement - between the institutions, preferably within the framework of the interinstitutional working party i proposed on 2 october. that's why this group is so important. the same approach should apply to the use of framework directives, i.e. legislative acts of principle and guidance which confer on the commission and the administrations responsible for implementation in the member states a wider competence to adopt implementing rules. i have already expressed the commission's conviction that parliament, together with the council, must have a simple legal instrument which enables the legislator to monitor and control the actions of the executive. there are various national experiences from which we could draw inspiration to improve the implementation of community policies and to enable the legislative authority to give effective guidance and control to the executive authority. this too requires thorough negotiation between the three institutions. i have already had occasion to say that the mechanism of the legislator's call-back of the commission's implementing measures is perhaps not the best possible device, or at least it needs to be considerably deepened. however, it is precisely in view of this objective that the commission is actively considering other options and hopes to present concrete proposals, preferably during the interinstitutional debate which i have called for. i also confirm that it would be inappropriate to decide on a concrete action plan on how to legislate within the community - what is commonly called better regulation - before all the institutions have discussed it. for this reason, in accordance with the undertaking given to you, the commission intends to approve in the coming days only a consultation document which will allow the interinstitutional dialogue to focus on certain priority measures, also suggested by the intergovernmental group chaired by mr mandelkern. we will also work to ensure that the laeken european council follows this approach and invites the institutions to reach the coordinated strategy desired in lisbon by june 2002. finally, i would like to clarify a few points concerning the action of the regulatory agencies. i agree with you that we must avoid fragmenting the executive and weakening democratic controls. moreover, the commission cannot continue to assume full political responsibility for the activities of agencies over which it has only partial influence. we therefore propose that a general model of agency be defined to ensure balanced representation in parliament, the council and the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. ladies and gentlemen, two weeks ago we presented and discussed programmes of the union. in addition to enlargement and the reform of the treaties, there are other items on the agenda of the laeken european council on which i should like to dwell very briefly. the full and effective implementation of the tampere mandate, on which we will present an assessment to the european council. the process started has been generally positive and should be developed with such as immigration or visas, which should be overcome with stronger political will. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the challenges we face and recent international events confirm the relevance key to building the new europe. it is therefore its renewal and strengthening that the future reforms of the treaties must aim at. this situation for many years, but little or nothing has been done. the convention on the protection of the community's financial interests, signed in cannes some six years ago, and the protocols thereto have not yet been ratified by all the member states and are therefore not in force. in spite of all the appeals and resolutions of parliament and some of the summit declarations of the council, we still have no community european legal area to protect the community budget, not even a clear definition of the concept of fraud against community funds, let alone the conduct of investigations and the imposition of penalties which must be equally effective, proportionate and dissuasive. in this situation of deadlock, the commission has now submitted a proposal for a directive which takes up the elements of the 1995 convention and incorporates some of them into the protocols, and which is also a proposal which the european parliament had already made at the time before the 1995 summit. the commission rightly relies on article 280 (4) of the treaty of amsterdam, which obliges the community to contribute actively to the protection of its funds. the aim was to overcome the pillar. we should not get bogged down in legal analysis, but give a clear signal. we are serious about criminal law protection against criminal misuse of european funds. we welcome the commission's directive. why would you do that? directives impose objectives on the member states, while regulations also provide the instruments for achieving these objectives. the proposal for a directive aims to - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr fiori, for his excellent work. i think he has made kind of automation, and we do not yet have the means to control this area. there's nothing to add to that. the so-called therapeutic cloning of embryos leads to reproductive cloning and must therefore
