i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the first human cloning trials in the united states must be a reminder to us today to clearly and unequivocally stop any human cloning. the distinction between therapeutic and reproductive cloning is a semantic trick. in both cases, an embryo is created, discarded, destroyed and used as a raw material. we must therefore oppose cloning, because the deliberate creation of life for research purposes is a violation of human dignity. man must never become a means to an end. human life is not a commodity. it must not be reduced to a commodity, and the production of human embryos as spare parts is incompatible with human dignity, but for us, and this must be made clear today, human dignity clearly takes precedence over research. therapeutic cloning is a precursor to reproductive cloning and has a knock-on effect. we must have a clear ban on therapeutic cloning, otherwise we cannot stop the danger of an escalation in the worldwide abuse of embryos. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the matter. again, this is basically therapeutic cloning. we must therefore send a clear signal today that we do not want a society in which women become egg suppliers and embryos are turned into lucrative commodities. we have a clear alternative to embryonic stem cell research with adult stem cell research, and therapeutic cloning is no longer necessary. the commission has also been very clear in its approach to patenting, and we must expect it to put an end to the current state of confusion about what can be patented and to give the member states clear guidance on this matter, because we must not turn the discovery of human life into an invention. human life is not created by third parties. so we need a clear signal. europe cannot be an ethical minefield. we need clear ethical boundaries. we must not have loopholes in the law, and for us human dignity must clearly be our guiding principle!
mr president, after about a year of intensive study of the findings of human genetics and their influence on medicine, after countless hearings and discussions during information visits, i am today one less hopeful. i'm disappointed, to say the least. the ad hoc committee on human genetics and new medical technologies has not achieved the goal i had hoped for. the report adopted by the committee will not provide the basis for coherent biotechnology legislation in the member states of the european union, which many of us, including myself, have been hoping for. it is a matter of the council's being able to take a decision on the matter. these pieces won't fit together so well in the end. i therefore ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to at least prevent the worst. let us decide what takes into account the social, economic and legal aspects in a balanced way and in no way overturns narrow ethical boundaries. the european parliament must not fail in this. we have to set standards here. in representative democracy, the task of setting standards is the responsibility of the directly elected parliament, not the responsibility of governments or even forces that are not primarily committed to the common good. the german and french governments set the stage for a common position on the economic and ethical issues raised by biotechnology at the consultations held in nantes last weekend. i quote from a german government document: 'such a vote between germany and france could be the prelude to a wider vote at european level.' the european parliament can cut the road and start today. the human genetics committee, as we call it for short, has carefully compiled the necessary information and the spectrum of assessments. the whole parliament must now show the way to the future of the biotechnological revolution for science, medicine and industry in the member states of the union. but we must not fall into the trap of a false belief in progress. not every progress made by man is also progress for mankind. but we must not submit to ideologies or dogmas, let alone try to establish new ones. many feel so insecure about their moral standing that they would like to forget it. but there is a lot of clarity here. sometimes we just don't see it. for example, a fertilized human egg can become only a human and nothing else. so from the moment the male sperm is united with the female egg, human dignity is protected. this absolute fundamental right has been written down again and again, most recently at the beginning of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. we just have to stick to it. in this context, we cannot accept cloning for any purpose, whether reproductive or therapeutic. you can't do that! this also excludes the possibility of using embryos for research purposes or even of producing them. the medical ethics of helping and healing, but also the view of the catastrophic consequences in all respects, forbid targeted interventions in the human germline. i would like to leave it at that. we must respect a number of other limits when we vote this afternoon. but we must also acknowledge the progress in the biological sciences today. if they are properly promoted, they may bring us closer to the dream of victory over disease and suffering, and we should be promoting the alternatives in the field of adult stem cells, for example, much more than we are doing now. i think that's where the future is.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the future of the community. i thank mr fiori for his comprehensive report. we are now in a state of conflict between the breathtaking progress of modern medicine and the ethical foundations of our society. the deciphering of the human genome, the assignment of function to genes, new techniques in medicine and now also stem cell therapy are opening up revolutionary new possibilities for curing very specific diseases. but at the same time, our political responsibility is growing. the task of politics is to define clear boundaries and to give a clear value orientation. we must not allow scientific progress and the resulting hopes for treatment to erode ethical boundaries. the act company has put us in front of a fait accompli this week with the creation of a human embryo by nuclear transfer. this is a clear violation of ethical boundaries. it is therefore urgent that we send a clear signal from the european parliament to protect human dignity against frontiers and taboo research. it is therefore necessary to speak out clearly against the reproductive and therapeutic cloning of human embryos, against any interference with the human genome and against the production of human embryos for research purposes alone. this prohibition must apply to both private and public research. in the field of stem cell research, i am opposed in principle to research on embryos that consume. however, i think that research on the 72 embryonic stem cell lines that existed before 1 august 2001 is acceptable in basic research. instead of making life available in general, research on foetal and adult stem cells must be given special encouragement as an alternative. every human being has the right to uniqueness. we must be very firm in our political defence of this right in the future.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the discussion we're having here touches on the fundamental questions of being human. is there a right to health for life? is there a right to a female child, or a right to a healthy female child, or in the end, a right to eternal life, of course, in health? new techniques are available. many promises of salvation are made to us. they have not been proven, at least not in the field of embryonic stem cell research. do we really want to be blinded by selfish research interests? do we want to be used by industry for its commercial interests? the term "therapeutic clones" is a scam. it can also be used for reproduction. the production of clones or the use of so-called surplus embryos for the purpose of weaning, for the use of stem cells, is this ethically acceptable? no, it is not acceptable! it's more like a modern form of cannibalism. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. there are viable alternatives, adult stem cells, stem cells from umbilical cord blood. these techniques are already proving to be very successful in practical applications, far more successful than embryonic stem cell research. these alternatives are ethically sound. politics is called upon to set limits. science is not able to do this, because it does not want to. we have to decide! we must be brave in the face of all opposition! no use of embryonic stem cells, cloned or surplus, it doesn't matter. no interference with the human germ line. no selection, no choice between worthwhile and worthless lives, but support for research in the search for alternatives. let us be brave and set firm limits. it's about time!

the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. the fight against fraud against the european union's finances is a high priority for the commission. the commission has the european parliament as its main ally. the commission has today unanimously approved the green paper on the criminal law protection of the community's financial interests and the creation of a european public prosecutor's office, which i have tabled. the commission has sent a strong political signal by adopting this green paper just before the laeken european council. we have already made some progress in the fight against fraud. this applies in particular to cooperation with the member states. olaf is doing a good job here. the commission has also done a lot in the area of prevention, for example in future all legislative proposals will be examined by olaf for their resistance to fraud. on the other hand, the criminal law dimension of european fraud prevention remains seriously deficient. we need a consistent european approach to law enforcement. the prosecution of crossborder fraud against the community budget still too often takes place at the frontiers of not just 15 but 17 different legal systems, and with enlargement the number will increase. there is no effective instrument to ensure that administrative investigations by olaf and also by national investigations lead to prosecution, rather than fail at the borders. the commission had therefore already proposed the creation of a european public prosecutor for the criminal protection of the communities' financial interests in september 2000 for the intergovernmental conference in nice. the european public prosecutor would be something entirely new in terms of quality. it would be a truly innovative step in the fight against fraud in criminal law. the heads of state or government did not, however, take up the commission's proposal at the time. but this is too important a subject to be left in the closet. i have therefore decided to draw up a green paper to clarify the proposal for a european public prosecutor and to show how this could work in practice. the time until the next reform of the treaties should therefore be used to the full to respond to the questions and the scepticism in the member states which have repeatedly asked for the concrete form of this system. the ec treaty itself is intended to regulate only the appointment of the european prosecutor, his dismissal, his tasks and the main features of the office. all other modalities, such as the status and functioning of the public prosecutor, are to be regulated by secondary law. the green paper is now addressing these questions. how and on whose initiative does the public prosecutor act? what are his powers? who controls the actions of the prosecutor? how does it work with national law enforcement authorities? what is the legal status and organisation of the fiscal prosecutor? the green paper discusses various options on these issues. the commission also expresses its preferences, which form a coherent system. what is the general approach proposed by the commission? what are the guidelines of the green paper? the commission's general approach is to regulate at european level only what is strictly necessary and to make use of national law and systems as far as possible. our proposals thus fully respect the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality. the fiscal prosecutor would bring significant added value to the fight against fraud in criminal law without upsetting national justice systems. what does that mean in detail? the proposal is original in that the european public prosecutor centrally directs and coordinates the investigation and prosecution at european level, but is itself decentralised and decisive for the concrete measures of the principle of mutual recognition. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the establishment of a european union agency for fundamental rights. the eppo shall inform the european parliament and the council of the outcome of the investigation. the legal proceedings themselves, including the delivery of the judgment, are to be conducted in accordance with national law. the commission proposes a decentralised structure of the public prosecutor's office. the european public prosecutor should rely in the member states on so-called 'national delegated prosecutors' who have a european mandate. the european prosecutor should be able to use the wide range of national investigative tools in the field of procedure. the prosecutors should therefore seek the assistance of national or regional law enforcement authorities, such as the criminal police. the application of the principle of mutual recognition is intended to make such investigative measures automatically valid throughout the community. the same applies to the admission of evidence and the judicial review of the european prosecutor's actions. for example, a search requested in one member state and authorized by a national judge under national law, or a telephone surveillance, would be valid throughout the community. this approach respects national legal systems. at the same time, the principle of mutual recognition ensures that the common investigation area becomes a reality. the commission also considers that the national legal system is sufficient for judicial review of the european prosecutor's actions and that a european criminal court is not necessarily necessary. the commission also considers that there is no need to create an autonomous european criminal code for the criminal cases to be prosecuted by the european public prosecutor. we are proposing a minimum level of harmonisation, but one which goes beyond the level of the proposed directive on the protection of the community's financial interests and thus also beyond the criminal offences as regulated by the 1995 convention. we want to cover all crimes against the financial interests of the communities, including, for example, fraud in tenders or breach of official secrets to the detriment of the communities' interests. we also believe that there should be uniform rules on penalties and limitation periods. the european ombudsman has been consulted on the drafting of the green paper on the role of the european ombudsman. i think we have struck a good balance here, which may convince some sceptics. the concept of the european public prosecutor fits seamlessly into the perspective of a europe of law. i worked on the green paper in close cooperation with commissioner vitorino. here, too, olaf's services were in constant contact with the services of mr vitorino's directorate-general. the new breakthroughs we have finally made in the area of judicial cooperation in criminal matters between the member states will create a favourable framework commission. – i am very grateful to the rapporteur, mr trakatellis, the members of parliament and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy for their work on this important and ambitious programme. this programme is important because protecting and improving public health is at the very centre of our citizens' concerns and their expectations. the recent terrorist attacks have underlined the need to strengthen and extend the existing community preparedness and response mechanisms. many of the amendments tabled are in line with our broad view of public health and how we should address it at community level. we can accept 38 of the 60 amendments – 28 in full and a further 10 in part. i should like to concentrate on a few key areas where some clarification of the commission's position may be of help. first, the implementation of the programme. the success of the programme will depend on the availability of resources and expertise. the commission will do everything it can to ensure the necessary, effective coordination by establishing the appropriate structural arrangements. putting these in place requires, in our view, a step-by-step approach. firstly, the commission services are engaged in the process of restructuring in order better to reflect the main areas of the programme. secondly, in order to strengthen the commission's capacity to coordinate actions, we intend to outsource some administrative and technical assistance. for the longer term, we are looking at the possibilities to set up an executive agency. however, this will have to await the adoption of the commission's proposal for a regulation on such agencies which i hope will be adopted in the fairly near future. in the light of this, i can accept amendment no 8 which calls for the appropriate structural arrangements to ensure the effectiveness and cohesion of measures and actions in the programme and to promote cooperation between the member states. however, i am unable to accept amendments nos 6, 34 and 57 which impose a deadline on the commission to carry out this work, and propose the creation of a coordination centre. this constrains the exercise of the commission's executive powers under the treaty. having said that, i hope that parliament will accept the commission's firm commitment to proceed as rapidly as we can on the establishment of the structural arrangements to ensure effective coordination and monitoring. the second area on which i would like to focus is the programme's budget. the commission's proposal was for a total budget of eur 300 million over a period of six years. amendment no 36 increases this amount to eur 380 million. the council's common position proposes a budget of eur 280 million. the decision on this matter is for the council and the european parliament, as the budgetary authority. i would simply say that the commission is keeping to its original proposal which, in our view, provides a reasonable figure for the implementation of the programme. i cannot, therefore, accept amendment no 36. this amendment and the last part of amendment no 56 also set limits on how we spend the programme budget. such restrictions undermine the essential principle that the programme must be flexible and able to respond to new concerns and threats to health, as they arise. recent events have clearly demonstrated the need to retain such flexibility. therefore we cannot accept these amendments. before i leave the issue of the budget, there is one point i want to make. the council and parliament stressed the need to put in place new structural arrangements to ensure effective coordination. this was not included in the composition of the original proposal in the budget. in view of this, when we put forward our opinion on the amendments adopted, we intend also to present a revised financial sheet for that programme. this would incorporate an increase in the budget line for expenditure on resources, for technical assistance and support which will be required for the structural arrangements. i wish to turn now to the amendments concerning the scope and structure of the programme. amendments nos 7, 13, 25, 30, 44, 46, 50, 52 and part of amendment no 58 touch on a variety of subjects, such as giving support to regional and national centres of excellence in various fields. complementary therapeutic methods – developing guidelines for medicine and healthcare interventions as well as actions to improve diet and eating habits. these amendments cannot be accepted since they cover areas under the responsibility of member states. moreover, there are a number of amendments that require specific comments. amendments nos 41 and 59 seek to impose an obligation for the commission to report annually to parliament on the implementation of the programme. parliament will be informed on a regular basis of the development of the programme through both the comitology rules and the evaluation process foreseen in article 12 of the common position. therefore, we cannot accept these amendments. amendment no 42 cannot be accepted since it limits the scope of the health information system by linking it explicitly to the right of patients to receive certain information on their illnesses and treatment. i stress, however, that i favour the concept of the promotion of patient rights and i am following the policy on this, which is included in the health forum and – you will note – is specifically referred to in the legislation at recital 3. finally, there is a group of seven amendments that we cannot accept because they take away the flexibility necessary for the implementation of the programme or because they duplicate provisions of the common position. these are amendments nos 9, 10, 23, 27, 28, 35 and 43. on the other hand, there are a number of amendments proposing important new actions that will reinforce the broad objectives and aims of the programme. to name just a few, amendment no 48 and part of no 26 that cover activities to counter health threats, including terrorists acts. amendment no 47 which covers the development of a vaccination and immunisation strategy. as these amendments, as well as amendments nos 3, 11, 29, 31, 45 and 60 will serve to strengthen the programme and improve its effectiveness, they are all acceptable to the commission. i should add that applicant countries can join in and that is provided for. furthermore, i also want to mention the reference made to the extent to which it is necessary to acquire information on diseases and disabilities, as mr prodi mentioned. i can, of course, confirm that this particular programme can deal with these issues, particularly under the first strand of the programme dealing with information and data collection. let me, in conclusion, madam president, repeat my appreciation for all the constructive work that the rapporteur and the committee have put in on shaping the future of public health policy in the eu. for those points where difficulties remain, the commission is, of course, ready and willing to assist in finding solutions.

help of the international community is now at risk. we want to see two states living side by side, peaceful and prosperous. today, that prospect seems all too distant. the number of deaths keeps increasing and so, less importantly, does the record in physical and economic damage. the world bank has estimated that the palestinian economy has suffered losses of between usd 155 million and 165 million in physical damage and usd 2.4 billion of gross national income since september last year. the number of palestinians living below the poverty line on less that usd 2 per day will have risen from 600 000 to between 1.2 million and 1.5 million by the end of 2001. even worse, the world bank projects more than 50% of the population may fall below the poverty line by the end of this year. the economic decline and the non-transfer of taxes owed to the palestinian authority by israel have caused a fall in palestinian revenues from a monthly average of usd 91 million to usd 22 million. palestinians lost more than 100 000 jobs in israel and about 66 000 jobs in the west bank and the gaza strip as a result of israel's closure policy. but the israeli economy is also suffering, which is not surprising when one considers the extent of economic interchange that was taking place before the current intifada. according to recent forecasts, the year 2001 is going to be one of the worst years since the 1950s for the israeli economy. this is mainly caused by the global economic slowdown but also by the current political security crisis. preliminary figures indicate that one in five israelis live below the poverty line, absolute numbers are up by 10% compared to last year and the rate of unemployment stood at 9.3% in the third quarter. what is the european union's stance, given this dramatic undermining of political and economic stability in the middle east? we understand israel's longing for security. we respect the fact that it is the israeli government's duty to try to provide safety for its citizens and we also understand palestinian frustration over the continuous military occupation and the remorseless spread of settlements. on monday, as the minister has just pointed out, the general affairs council discussed these issues with shimon peres and nabil sha'ath. as ever, they were extremely eloquent in what they said. the council's declaration reaffirms israel's irrevocable right to live in peace and security within internationally recognised borders and the need for the establishment of a viable and democratic palestinian state and an end to the occupation of the palestinian territories. the way chosen by people like the late prime minister rabin was to find a negotiated solution leading to two states with the 1967 line roughly as their shared border, jerusalem as capital of both, and a solution to the refugee issue acceptable to both israelis and palestinians. unfortunately forces on both the palestinian and israeli sides have been working against this goal. they have set out quite deliberately to destroy the achievements of the oslo process. it is our collective duty to try to stop them doing so. the only way of returning to meaningful negotiations is to embark once and for all on the path laid out in the mitchell report. the council on monday strongly encouraged the parties to take the first steps to end this devastating and self-fuelling cycle of violence that we have seen over the last 14 months. i confirm our strong call for the parties to implement the mitchell report without delay. it is crucial to apprehend extremists and continue fighting those terrorist groups opposed to the peace process, as the minister said. the union must continue to press the palestinian authority to take concrete steps to arrest and bring to justice those who commit terrorist acts. this is why the council on monday called clearly for the dismantling of the terrorist networks of hamas and jihad. and it is equally crucial that israel withdraws its military forces, ends the extra-judicial killings, and ends the closures and restrictions on palestinian people, particularly the senseless bombing of property and infrastructure. it is difficult to see how the destruction of the gaza airport, the destruction of an eu-funded forensic laboratory and the destruction of vast areas of arable land can help fight terrorism or increase israel’s security. i would strongly argue the opposite. in the world bank report, they state 'that the main proximate cause of the recession is closure'. removing, or significantly easing closure is the most important requirement if further decline is to be arrested and economic pressure removed from the palestinian population. continued economic hardship will make people easier prey for extremists. we need to persuade israel that its security will be increased, not hampered, by allowing the palestinian economy to develop so as to give people a reason to hope for a better future. where in history is there an example of poverty and economic decline leading to greater security and political moderation? let me add to this an argument put by henry siegman – a senior fellow at the council on foreign relations in new york and a distinguished expert on the middle east – in the article in the international herald tribune today, which i strongly recommend to all members of this house. mr siegman wrote as follows: 'policies which reinforce the despair of palestinians by killing their hope for an end to the occupation will inevitably fuel escalating violence'. we must not allow ten years of political and financial investment to be wasted. the european union has contributed more than eur 3 billion to the west bank and gaza strip since 1994. some may say unfairly that the european union is only a payer and not a player. i have heard that remark in this chamber. but what we have done is to provide some grounds for hope – and in recent months to prevent further economic misery and to keep the palestinian authority barely alive and in place by providing eur 108 million in budgetary aid over the last 14 months. some people have criticised us for that, although members of the israeli government have explicitly supported these efforts in the past. we have worked to maintain the only viable partner in peace that israel can find and we should continue to support the palestinian authority, especially in its fight against terrorism. although the palestinian authority has made mistakes and must correct them, the palestinian authority is the only structure that can provide stability in the palestinian territories. it is the provider of necessary basic services and in the end the guarantor for a minimum of security for both the palestinians and the israelis. if the palestinian authority is disabled, we will face a situation of anarchy where hamas and jihad will no doubt gather increasing support and local extremist committees will compete in an escalation of violence. it is utterly absurd to suggest that by doing this we are funding terrorists. our funding actually helps to strengthen the secular administration against the real terrorist organisations. we have put a considerable number of safeguards in place that allow us to monitor the use of our funds. the most important of these is the regular checking and reporting by the international monetary fund on the austerity budget agreed by the palestinian authority. i want to make this point very strongly. the european union has done more than anyone else to promote elections, the fight against corruption, and the rule of law in the palestinian territories. there is much further to go. but how do we best promote decency, moderation and pluralism? by allowing public services in the palestinian territories to collapse or by trying to keep them going against the odds and by trying to promote reform? the alternative to the palestinian authority is palestinian anarchy. however long and difficult the road, we should remain committed to supporting moderates, whoever they are and while – thank god – they still exist, on both sides of this tragic feud. some commentators have referred to the problems in the middle east as one of the root causes of terrorism – or they have pointed out that the palestinian-israeli conflict has been and is abused as a cheap excuse for violence or as a wicked justification for committing evil criminal acts. the international community needs to take action now to help resolve this potentially explosive situation. the risk of wider regional spillover is very real and we must use every means to prevent a return to the time when the palestinian cause was pursued largely through terrorism. one final point. today the focus is mainly on afghanistan. but increasingly it will shift to the middle east. if we are to solve the problems there, it is no good dwelling in the past, exchanging half-truths, casting blame, arguing about what mr arafat should have done at camp david or what mr sharon should not have done on the holy mount. what is past is past. peace will only come if there is a real and brave and lasting commitment to achieving it, looking ahead to a brighter future, ignoring those who try to derail the whole process through terrorist acts of violence and by disproportionate military responses. that is the way progress was made in the past, for example by mr rabin. it must be the path that we europeans advocate for the future. (applause)

corresponding development opportunity. the council and the commission are aware that this european parliament is prepared to contribute to important solutions, including in the financial field, if president of the commission. - madam president, mr prime minister, ladies and gentlemen, i am particularly honoured to be taking part in this debate, just after the laeken summit. in laeken we took a big step towards the europe we want: a more democratic, more open europe, in which our citizens are finally beginning to identify fully. i would first like to pay tribute to the belgian presidency of the council for the way it has conducted the work of the six months, and in particular the work which led to the laeken declaration. laeken has launched a new constitutional phase in the construction of europe, a phase in which this parliament and the national parliaments can play a key role. the new process will be open, transparent and will help give our fellow citizens a better understanding of the fundamental issues at stake in europe today. the stakes, in the context of enlargement and globalisation, are very high. i see the road traced in laeken as the only way to ensure democratic legitimacy, to ensure that the union can pursue integration and enlargement without risking that citizens will then reject the solutions adopted by governments. the enlargement of the european union is an irreversible process which is already well advanced. we must not forget that this is one of the main reasons for the convention. without institutional change, the enlarged union would remain inexorably stalled. without an open debate, there is a risk of losing the support of the citizens of the union and the candidate countries. we should not underestimate the importance of the fact that the applicant countries are involved for the first time in an institutional process with constitutional implications. it is their future, no less than the future of the present 15 member states, that is being decided. the results of the laeken european council, however, are not limited to the launching of the convention. the events of 11 september have reminded us of what those who want to abuse freedom can do to destroy it, and the support given by the council to our activities in the field of home affairs will help us to achieve our objective of building an area of freedom, security and justice in the european union. work on a common policy on immigration and asylum has been given a new impetus. the european council called for the commission's communication on illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings to serve as a basis for an action plan. in this context, as i proposed in my recent speech in bruges, the european council invited the council and the commission to explore ways of enabling effective cooperation between those who guard the union's external borders, and to consider the possibility of establishing a common mechanism or a common border control service. i regret that the laeken council was unable to go further in resolving the question of future european agencies. let me be clear - i too agree with what prime minister verhofstadt said - this is not a drama. however, as we have already seen on other occasions, we are forced to conclude that the unanimity rule simply hinders the decisionmaking process. one point must be clear by now. the 'community method' has made the union what it is: the eu is a union of peoples and a union of states, which requires an innovative decision-making structure, with common institutions and a single voice for all countries, large and small. the community method has served to promote efficiency and democratic legitimacy. we just have to adapt and reinforce it. this is in order not to lose the support of public opinion and also in the interest of the efficiency of our actions. our fellow citizens are sick of this kind of trading. they are more interested in whether the much-heralded european food safety authority is really able to start work than in where the seat is. i therefore confirm that the authority will start its activities on 1 january 2002 at its provisional - i stress, provisional - seat in brussels. the citizens can no longer wait for the establishment of a body dedicated to the protection of their health. in this respect, the commission intends to continue to attach the utmost importance to its relations with parliament. we have improved our procedures and our way of working, but in the last few weeks we have seen that this process of building reports and procedures has not yet achieved the objectives that we all set ourselves. it will be our task to work together to achieve these quickly and to base the second part of the legislature on a complete synergy between the commission and parliament. the objective we set ourselves in lisbon in march 2000 was to make the union the most competitive and dynamic economy in the world within 10 years. at the same time, we are committed to ensuring that it becomes a more equitable society that is responsive to the needs of all. i am pleased that the laeken council agreed to give priority to these objectives. barcelona must therefore be a significant and irreversible step forward in consolidating and developing the european social model. but we shall have occasion to discuss this again in the course of the preparations for that summit. the european council reaffirmed the strategic importance of the galileo satellite navigation project, which can catalyse innovation and competitiveness. nor could it have been otherwise, since just a month ago the member states of the european space agency - 13 of which are member states of the european union - committed eur 550 million to participate in the project. a different decision would have sent a contradictory signal to a project which is vital to our future and our independence. the european council has clearly set out the dates and objectives for the first half of 2002: now it's time to conclude without further ado. our credibility is at stake, the credibility of the council and parliament is at stake. the commission is therefore ready to help in order to meet the commitments made and finally move to the concrete development phase, taking into account all the technical and financial aspects of the project. the convention must meet expectations, ladies and gentlemen, and must bring about a change that will enable us to look with confidence to a complex and difficult future. it will not have to reinvent the union, it will not have to re-think the acquis communautaire; the european council in brussels on 14 and 15 december adopted a resolution on the future of the union. the establishment of the convention is a deliberate break with the past. our aim is that it can draw on the ideas and experiences of many, not just a few. our goal is to have it in the light of day, not in a closed room. in the convention, the commission will act as the guardian of the treaties and as the bearer of the community spirit. equality between all the member states and balance between the union's institutions are the best guarantee of a fair and efficient europe. moreover, if we look at the latest eurobarometer data, we can clearly conclude that our citizens are getting closer to europe and its institutions, even faster than we thought. at the latest by 2004, but probably before that date, the convention's contributions will be examined by an intergovernmental conference, after which the citizens of the old and new member states will elect their representatives to this assembly. let us therefore prepare ourselves for these important and important deadlines.
